School of Mathematical Sciences Guizhou Normal University Guiyang, China Email: lizhumath@pku.edu.cn Preface 

The roots of a polynomial can form a field, and the length of an orbit can determine the degree of an irreducible polynomial. In the theory of finite fields, these two phenomena have a common origin: in characteristic p, the Frobenius map x 7 → xp preserves addition and multiplication and organizes algebraic elements by their periods under iteration. Starting from this connection, this book develops the basic theory and constructions of finite fields through root sets, conjugate orbits, and linear actions. The existence of finite fields is the starting point. By adjoining roots a finite number of times, we make Xpn

− X split completely. The algebraic properties of Frobenius give its root set a field structure, while the absence of repeated roots and the degree of the polynomial determine its size. This construction presupposes neither an algebraic closure nor the existence of irreducible polynomials of a prescribed degree. Conversely, every finite subfield S satisfies 

∏

> a∈S

(X − a) = X|S| − X. 

Thus the form of this root polynomial expresses finiteness, closure under the field oper-ations, and a common period of the elements. Once the base field k = Fq is fixed, the orbits of the relative Frobenius map σ : x 7 →

xq give conjugacy, the orbit lengths give degrees, and the fixed points of its iterates give subfields; extending the base field changes the step size along these orbits. At the same time, σ is a k-linear operator, and a normal basis represents it as a cyclic shift. Thus conjugacy in field theory, periods in group theory, and cyclic structure in linear algebra are different descriptions of the same Frobenius action. The bound on the number of roots repeatedly rules out impossible relations of low degree, providing a common tool for proving the cyclicity of the multiplicative group, the nonvanishing of the trace map, and the existence of cyclic vectors. These descriptions of the same Frobenius action have different strengths and are not interchangeable. An orbit length determines the field degree of an element, but not the dimension spanned by its conjugates. Even when several orbits separately form normal bases, choosing elements from different orbits may produce a short linear relation. iii Preface 

Likewise, the set of distinct roots recovers a monic squarefree polynomial but does not retain all information about repeated factors. Connecting models therefore requires identifying both their common structure and the information each one preserves. Root sets first raise a descent question: when do data written over an extension actually come from the base field? Frobenius stability answers this question for root polynomials, while equivariant functions recover the corresponding reduced quotient algebra. The Fourier coordinates of cyclic codes later satisfy the same equivariance condition; spectral components organized by cyclotomic cosets are another expression of root-set descent. Passing from the multiplicative order of one element to joint linear relations among several elements requires trace duality and determinant criteria. AVandermonde matrix formed from consecutive powers is nonsingular whenever its nodes are distinct, whereas a Moore matrix requires the nodes to be linearly independent over the base field. This distinction shows which questions orbit data settle directly and where stronger linear conditions become necessary. The trace connects field multiplication with linear duality, and linearized polynomi-als and cyclic modules then provide a common language for normal bases, operators, and recurrences. With repeated factors, coefficient pairings and derivatives supply in-formation lost by the trace pairing; in changing a generator, translation is controlled by addition in the fixed subspace, whereas reciprocation requires a separate analysis through traces and defining equations. These methods are useful not because every problem should have the same form, but because a suitable representation exposes the obstruction at hand. Examples and counterexamples repeatedly test the limits of each representation. Chapter 13 develops this representation problem in detail. It starts with the same four-element subfield requiring quadratic and cubic representatives in two power bases, then connects low-degree representations, polynomial composition, and relative traces. Following this example gives degree profiles, defects, and Hankel recovery a common concrete task. Construction and counting lead to a further question: how can local root or fiber data recover a global factorization or count? Return maps decompose an orbit length into a base-orbit length and an internal return period, with applications to composition, compression, and irreducible constructions. Character orthogonality turns trace and multiplicative conditions into expressions that can be summed. Moments of Gaussian periods record short relations in multiplicative subgroups, while joint expansions in ad-Preface iii 

ditive and multiplicative characters connect primitivity with normality. Character sums over extensions and point counts on curves in turn lead back to finite-order recurrences. Each chapter introduces the tools needed for concrete questions and returns to earlier structures where they become useful. This book is intended for advanced undergraduates, graduate students, and re-searchers with a background in abstract algebra and linear algebra. Proofs are given for the basic structure theorems and the main constructions, and elementary tools are collected in the appendices. Examples and exercises emphasize comparisons between models, the limits of hypotheses, and the roles played by the same structure in different problems. General references are [37, 26, 20]. This book may still contain omissions and errors. The authors would be grateful to readers for comments and corrections. Acknowledgments 

We thank GPT-6 Astra for assistance in preparing this book, especially in translating the Chinese version into English. vReading Guide and Notation 

Prerequisites. The reader should be familiar with the basic theory of groups, rings, fields, and finite-dimensional vector spaces. Field extensions, extension degrees, and generated subfields are defined when first used in the text. Appendix A collects material on field embeddings, restriction of scalars, algebraic extensions, and polynomial tools; proofs concerning the adjunction of finitely many roots, the extension of isomorphisms, and the existence of cyclic vectors are given in the main text. Concepts such as tensor products and cyclic modules are introduced through the models in which they will be used. 

Reading by structural themes. This book can be read by repeatedly following a few structural themes: root sets, Frobenius orbits, trace duality, and cyclic modules. Alongside understanding the proof of each result, the reader should notice how its underlying structures reappear in other problems. Begin with Chapters 1–4, and then read Chapters 6–9 together with the material in Chapter 5 on roots of unity, cyclotomic cosets, extension of the base field, and tensor-product decompositions. The aim is to connect root sets, fixed fields, conjugate orbits, trace and norm, trace duality, linearized polynomials, and cyclic modules, and to understand how the field structure, multiplicative periods, and the linear action of Frobenius interact. Next, read Chapters 10 and 11 to see how these structures lead to factorization methods, changes of representation, and constructions of irreducible polynomials. At this stage, one can also read the opening sections of Chapter 19, through Section 19.5, to separate exact-period layers from the full fixed-point sets and relate these layers to irreducible and cyclotomic polynomials. Chapters 12 and 13 study root blocks and polynomial decomposition from affine symmetries and low-degree subfield representations, respectively; Chapter 14 develops recursive constructions from these structures. Chapter 15 treats polynomial functions and fiber permutations. Chapter 16 presents shift operators, quotient algebras, traces, periods, and recovery from finite observations in one continuous sequence. Chapter 17 vii viii Reading Guide and Notation 

then applies root sets, linearized maps, and trace coordinates to coding constructions. After studying the translation invariants in Chapter 12, one can return to Section 19.6 and the sections that follow it. These explain how affine compression changes the periods of roots and how return maps recover the factor degrees before compression. The more detailed material in Chapter 5 on cyclotomic systems, compatible lift-ing, and Galois rings can be studied around specific factorization problems. Character orthogonality, Fourier duality, and adjoint operators in Chapter 18 can be read along-side Chapters 6–8; the lifting and multiplication formulas, curve point counts, and Weil bounds can be explored through specific counting problems. When studying recurrences for character sums over extension fields, it is also useful to return to the recurrences and generating functions in Chapter 16. The primitive normal basis theorem connects the cyclic modules and trace duality of Chapter 9 with the joint counts of Chapter 18. The main text develops the structural and character-sum arguments, and Appendix C supplies the arithmetic completion for all parameters. Each return to an earlier theorem provides an opportunity to reconsider the objects it organizes and the roles it plays. Frobenius orbits determine the degrees of irreducible polynomials and also organize point counts over extension fields; the trace pairing re-covers coordinates and also parametrizes additive characters; cyclic modules explain normal bases and also describe linear recurrences. As these connections emerge, the basic theorems acquire richer meaning. When comparing models, first ask what the available data already determine and which relations remain undetected. For example, root-set descent determines which spectral data come from the base field; Proposition 17.7 expresses this as equivariance of Fourier coordinates. Example 18.16 shows that normality of each orbit does not control relations across orbits. The comparison of Vandermonde and Moore matrices at 17.51 explains why consecutive zero conditions and joint column independence require different arguments. These distinctions also motivate trace-hyperplane intersections and moments of Gaussian periods. 

Organization of the arguments. The structural results are developed according to the following dependencies. Sections 5.8–5.9 extend root-of-unity orbits at a fixed modulus to local synchroniza-tion and compatible lifting across moduli. The phases of the local orbits determine the global factors, while affine return on finite fibers gives the factor degrees after lifting. The stabilization index of a nonprincipal local cyclotomic system further determines where unique lifting begins and gives power-substitution families whose irreducibility persists; see Section 5.9.5. Section 5.10 uses Galois rings to connect root-of-unity orbits in the residue field with Hensel lifting of coefficients, yielding basic irreducible factor-izations, product decompositions of quotient rings, and canonical blocks for lengths divisible by the characteristic. Chapter 17 derives the BCH distance bound from con-secutive root-of-unity zeros and then describes cyclic codes through trace coordinates. Support periods determine their indecomposable coordinate blocks; see Theorem 17.12, Example 17.13, and Proposition 17.27. Section 15.3 proves multiplicative coset rigidity through a translation-power function space and uses the hidden subfield to explain semi-linearity under global coset relabeling. It then connects with the additive stabilizers of Section 5.6, identifying the correspondence between multiple equal-difference structure and non-affine symmetries at odd prime-power moduli. Section 17.12 recovers difference orbits from spectral projections and determines the coordinate permutations common to all cyclic codes. Proposition 9.8 applies the normality criterion to base-field translates; Exam-ple 10.27 shows how reciprocation supplies a missing Frobenius component when direct translation fails. Proposition 10.9 connects Berlekamp splitting with idempotent projections, while Section 17.6 derives the distance of binary Goppa codes from support root polynomials and links the derivative criterion with multiplicative cosets, Frobenius extensions, and splitting counts. Section 6.10 translates the norm and root ratio of quadratic conjugate roots into criteria involving the constant term and a Lucas recurrence, respectively. Cyclotomic polynomials then give an optimal coefficient criterion polynomial for a fixed primitive constant term. Section 6.11 describes the root sets of families of additive cosets through the two eigenspaces of Frobenius, reducing the numbers of reducible and irreducible xii Reading Guide and Notation 

members to the numbers of solutions to hyperbolic equations and the sizes of norm fibers. Proposition 5.9 distinguishes multiplicative cosets from Frobenius orbits, and Propo-sition 6.10 gives explicit parameters for the norm-one group. Subsection 7.3.4 uses quadratic quotient algebras to unify products and sums of reciprocals attached to root sets. Subsection 15.4.4 expresses two-root coefficient fibers through projective involu-tions. Exercises 18.20 and 18.21 study distinct-element sums and products using Jacobi sums and cyclic-group exponents, respectively. The return-map lemma in Chapter 11 underlies the treatment of root-set symmetry, recursive constructions, fiber permutations, and affine compression. Section 19.7.4 com-pares the specific return maps and applicability conditions for power and affine com-pression. The treatment of subfield representations connects minimal representation degrees, root-block coefficients, and relative trace sequences through Sections 13.2–13.4. The same short trace prefix also recovers the degree profiles of divisor subfields through intermediate traces; exact counts then determine minimum generator-representation degrees, as in Corollary 13.41. Section 14.6 applies the root-fiber criterion to composition iterates. Persistent irre-ducibility is determined by multiplicative orders for power maps, by square classes in finite critical orbits for quadratic iteration, and by noncubicity in reciprocal coordinates for a cubic family in characteristic two. A general quadratic polynomial is put into standard form by affine conjugacy, with the iteration target transformed by the same change of coordinates; see Corollary 14.24. Mixed compositions are further controlled by forward-invariant sets in the base field; reciprocal additive recursion can also be interpreted as a tower of irreducible denominators for a fixed rational map. Examples in the field with 64 elements run through changes of representation, re-currence recovery, and trace-quadratic equations; another linearized root set with 64 

elements is used to compare multiplicative orders, Frobenius periods, and the dimen-sions of orbit spans. Example 17.17 also uses the root sets of two subfields of the field with 64 elements to construct a binary Goppa code of distance exactly nine. For a com-parison of these two root sets, see Section 10.8 and Example 16.9. An eight-dimensional quotient algebra is used to illustrate trace degeneracy, the periodic part of Frobenius, and multiplication recurrences, distinguishing the periodic data of different operators; see Examples 7.15 and 16.16. Exercise 7.7 further computes the radical of the trace Reading Guide and Notation xiii 

pairing using the derivative, while Exercise 16.5 separates the transient and periodic parts of a recurrence in a nine-dimensional quotient algebra. The four appendices collect algebraic preliminaries, construct an algebraic closure and describe its automorphisms and intermediate fields, provide the arithmetic verifica-tion completing the primitive normal basis theorem, and give solutions to all exercises, respectively. The structural overview, index of notation, and subject index at the end of the book serve as guides to the results and their connections. In the electronic edition, exercise numbers in the text link to the corresponding solutions, and exercise numbers in the solutions link back to the exercises. 

Notation. Throughout, p is prime and q = pr; we usually write k = Fq ⊆ E = Fqn ,

σ(x) = xq, and φ(x) = xp. The notation [E : k] denotes the extension degree, and Aut k(E) denotes the group of automorphisms fixing k pointwise. The variable X is usually used for polynomials in field elements, and T for polynomials in operators. All field homomorphisms preserve the identity element; uniqueness of a finite field of a given order means uniqueness of its isomorphism type. Intersections and composita of subfields, and comparisons of root sets, are taken in a specified common extension field. Statements allowing polynomials of degree less than a given positive integer include the zero polynomial. Contents

# Existence of Finite Fields: Characteristic, Adjoining Roots, and Fixed Points 

The order of a finite field is determined by its characteristic and its dimension over its prime field. Existence follows by showing that a Frobenius fixed-point set is closed under field operations. Successively adjoining finitely many roots provides a suitable splitting extension, and the root bound determines the size of the fixed-point set. 

# 1.1 Characteristic and the Prime Field 

Let K be a finite field. The sequence 

0, 1, 1 + 1 , 1 + 1 + 1 , . . . 

must contain a repetition, so m · 1 = 0 for some positive integer m. The least positive integer with this property is the characteristic of K, denoted by char K.

Proposition 1.1 The characteristic of a finite field is prime. If its characteristic is p,it contains a subfield naturally isomorphic to Fp = Z/pZ.

Proof. Since 1 6 = 0 , the characteristic m ≥ 2. If m = ab with 1 < a, b < m , then 

(a · 1)( b · 1) = m · 1 = 0 .

A field has no zero divisors, so a · 1 = 0 or b · 1 = 0 , contrary to the minimality of m.Thus m = p is prime. 12 Chapter 1 Existence of Finite Fields: Characteristic, Adjoining Roots, and Fixed Points 

The map Z → K, t 7 → t · 1, preserves addition and multiplication and has kernel 

pZ. Hence 0, 1, 2 · 1, . . . , (p − 1) · 1 form a subfield isomorphic to Z/pZ. Every subfield contains 1, and therefore all these elements. This is the prime field of K.We henceforth denote this prime field by Fp. Its embedding into K, that is, an in-jective field homomorphism, is uniquely determined: it sends the residue class t modulo 

p to t · 1.

# 1.2 Dimension over the Prime Field and the Order of a Finite Field 

If k is a subfield of a field E, we call E an extension field of k and E/k a field extension ; k is the base field. The addition and multiplication of E, with elements of 

k acting as scalars, make E a k-vector space: vector addition is field addition, scalar multiplication is multiplication of an element of k by an element of E, and the vector-space axioms follow from the field axioms. The dimension of this vector space is the degree of the extension E/k, denoted by 

[E : k] := dim k E. 

If [E : k] = n < ∞, then E/k is a finite extension , or an extension of degree n. A basis of E/k means a basis of E as a k-vector space. Thus [E : k] = n if and only if there exist e1, . . . , e n ∈ E such that every x ∈ E has a unique expression 

x = a1e1 + · · · + anen, a1, . . . , a n ∈ k. 

The degree depends on the specified base field. Finiteness of an extension refers to its dimension over that field; when the base field is also finite, these coordinates deter-mine the number of elements of the extension field. For general remarks on specified embeddings, bases, and restriction of scalars, see the first two sections of Appendix A. Chapter 1 Existence of Finite Fields: Characteristic, Adjoining Roots, and Fixed Points 3

Theorem 1.2 If a finite field K has characteristic p, then for some positive integer n,

|K| = pn, n = [ K : Fp].

More generally, if k is a subfield of a finite field K and |k| = q, then |K| = q[K:k].

Proof. Regard K as a vector space over k. Since K is a finite set, the process of successively choosing linearly independent elements terminates, yielding a finite basis 

e1, . . . , e n. Every element has a unique expression 

a1e1 + · · · + anen, ai ∈ k. 

Each coefficient has q possible values, giving qn elements. Taking k = Fp proves the first assertion. 

Lemma 1.3 (The tower law) Let k ⊆ L ⊆ E be fields, with both [L : k] and [E : L]

finite. Then E/k is finite and 

[E : k] = [ E : L][ L : k].

Proof. Let u1, . . . , u a be a basis of L/k, and v1, . . . , v b a basis of E/L. Expand any 

x ∈ E in the vj , and then expand each coefficient in L in the ui, to obtain

Corollary 1.4 If K has pn elements and a subfield L has pd elements, then d | n.This divisibility is necessary for the existence of a subfield. Chapter 3 proves suffi-ciency and uniqueness of the corresponding subfield. 

# 1.3 Two Identities Arising from Finiteness 4 Chapter 1 Existence of Finite Fields: Characteristic, Adjoining Roots, and Fixed Points 

Lemma 1.5 (Power maps in characteristic p) In a field of characteristic p, for any a, b 

and any integer s ≥ 0,

(a + b)ps

= aps

+ bps

, (ab )ps

= aps

bps

.

Proof. For s = 1 , all intermediate binomial coefficients (pi

) are divisible by p, and hence vanish in the field. Iteration gives the additive identity for every s. The multiplicative identity follows from commutativity of multiplication. These identities show that φ : x 7 → xp preserves the field operations. It is called the 

Frobenius map . Its s-fold iterate is φs(x) = xps

. An element satisfying φs(x) = x is a 

fixed point of this iterate; the set of all such elements is denoted by Fix (φs). We shall use this set directly in the root-set construction. 

Proposition 1.6 (The power identity in a finite field) If |K| = Q, then every a ∈ K

satisfies aQ = a.

Proof. If a 6 = 0 , it belongs to the group K× of order Q − 1. Lagrange’s theorem gives 

aQ−1 = 1 , so aQ = a. The assertion also holds for a = 0 .

Example 1.7 Z/4 Z is not a field, since 2 6 = 0 but 22 = 0 . The field of order four has characteristic 2; its additive group is isomorphic to (Z/2 Z)2, rather than Z/4 Z. A field with pn elements and the ring of integers modulo pn are distinct concepts. We have shown that the order of a finite field must be a prime power. To construct a finite field of a prescribed prime-power order, it suffices to find an extension over which a specified polynomial splits and then take the fixed points of a Frobenius iterate. We use polynomial division, the existence of irreducible factors, and Bézout’s identity. These tools over general fields, together with their proofs, are collected in Appendix A. 

# 1.4 Adjoining One Root and the Field Structure of a Quotient Ring 

Fix a monic irreducible polynomial f ∈ k[X], with deg f = d. Define A ≡ B (mod f )

if and only if f | A − B. Each congruence class has a unique representative of degree less than d. Addition and multiplication of congruence classes define 

k[X]/( f ) = {A : A ∈ k[X]}.Chapter 1 Existence of Finite Fields: Characteristic, Adjoining Roots, and Fixed Points 5

To perform these operations, carry out ordinary polynomial arithmetic and then take the remainder modulo f . Replacing representatives by congruent ones leaves sums and products congruent, so the operations are well defined. 

Proposition 1.8 (Adjoining one root) The quotient k[X]/( f ) is a field. The residue classes of constant polynomials give an embedding of k; if α = X, then 

f (α) = 0 , k[X]/( f ) = {a0 + a1α + · · · + ad−1αd−1 : ai ∈ k}.

This expression is unique, so the extension has degree d. If k has q elements, the extension field has qd elements. 

Proof. The ring axioms follow from those of k[X], and 1 6 = 0 , since a polynomial of positive degree cannot divide 1. If A 6 = 0 , then f - A. Since f is irreducible, gcd (A, f ) = 1. By Bézout’s identity, there exist U, V with U A + V f = 1 , whence U A = 1 . Every nonzero element is invertible, so the quotient is a field. No nonzero constant is divisible by f , so the map from constants to their residue classes is injective. We have f (X) = f = 0 , and uniqueness of remainders shows that 

1, α, . . . , α d−1 is a k-basis. The counting assertion follows. The constant polynomials identify k with a subfield of the quotient. Under this identification, we write k ⊆ k[X]/( f ). We shall continue to identify a base field with its image under a specified embedding. 

# 1.5 Adjoining Finitely Many Roots and Complete Splitting 

Lemma 1.9 (Constructing a splitting extension) Let k be a field and P (X) ∈ k[X]

a nonconstant polynomial. By adjoining finitely many roots, one obtains an extension field L in which P factors completely into linear factors in L[X]. The extension may be chosen to have finite degree. If k is finite, so is L.

Proof. Induct on D = deg P , proving at the same time that the extension can be chosen to have degree at most D!. For D = 1 , the root already lies in k, so take L = k.Suppose D > 1. By Lemma A.9, P has a monic irreducible factor f of degree d,where 1 ≤ d ≤ D. Adjoining one root gives the field k1 = k[X]/( f ) and the element 6 Chapter 1 Existence of Finite Fields: Characteristic, Adjoining Roots, and Fixed Points 

α = ¯X. Using the embedding defined by constant polynomials to identify k ⊆ k1, we have 

[k1 : k] = d, P (α) = 0 .

Division by X − α in k1[X] gives remainder P (α) = 0 , so 

P (X) = ( X − α)P1(X), deg P1 = D − 1.

The induction hypothesis, applied to the base field k1 and the polynomial P1, gives an extension L/k1 over which P1 splits completely, with [L : k1] ≤ (D − 1)! . Thus P splits completely over L, and the tower law gives 

[L : k] = [ L : k1][ k1 : k] ≤ (D − 1)! D = D!.

If k is finite, then |L| = |k|[L:k] < ∞. Each induction step removes one linear factor, so the argument also applies to polynomials with repeated roots. 

Remark 1.10 The construction adjoins roots of the specified polynomial, using an irreducible factor of the remaining polynomial at each step. The existence of such a factor follows by induction on degree, and its degree is determined by the factorization. 

# 1.6 The Field Structure of Frobenius Fixed Points 

Lemma 1.11 (The root bound) A nonzero polynomial of degree D over a field has at most D distinct roots in any extension field. 

Proof. Induct on D. A nonzero constant has no roots. If D > 0 and a is a root, polynomial division gives P (X) = ( X − a)Q(X), with deg Q = D − 1. Every root b 6 = a

satisfies (b − a)Q(b) = 0 , and is therefore a root of Q. The induction hypothesis bounds the total number of roots by D.A nonzero polynomial with no repeated roots in a splitting extension is called sep-arable ; if its irreducible factorization has no repeated factor, it is called square-free .The first condition always implies the second. Over a finite field they are equivalent, since irreducible polynomials have no repeated roots, as we shall prove in Corollary 3.13. Chapter 1 Existence of Finite Fields: Characteristic, Adjoining Roots, and Fixed Points 7

Corollary 1.12 (Separability of the power polynomial) In characteristic p, for every integer n ≥ 1, the polynomial Xpn

− X has no repeated roots. 

Proof. By the derivative criterion for repeated roots (Proposition A.16), it suffices to note that (Xpn

− X)′ = −1.

Theorem 1.13 (The root-set construction) For every prime p and positive integer n,there exists a field with exactly pn elements. 

Proof. Consider P = Xpn

− X over Fp. Lemma 1.9 gives a finite extension L/Fp over which P splits completely. Set

= a}.

Thus E is closed under subtraction, multiplication, and inversion of nonzero elements, and is a subfield of L.The splitting extension L supplies all the roots; closure under field operations makes their set a subfield. Its order is determined by the degree and separability of P , inde-pendently of the chosen splitting extension. 

Corollary 1.14 (Construction over a specified base field) Let k be a given field with 

q elements. For every m ≥ 1, there exists an extension field E ⊇ k with |E| = qm and 

[E : k] = m.

Proof. Choose an extension of k over which Xqm

− X splits, and let E be the set of all its roots. Since qm is a power of p, the preceding closure argument applies, and

Example 1.15 (The field of order four) X2 + X + 1 has no root in F2, and is therefore irreducible. Adjoin a root α, and write F2[α] for the set of all A(α), with A ∈ F2[X].Polynomial division gives 

F2[α] = {0, 1, α, 1 + α}, α2 = α + 1 .

Thus α3 = 1 and α4 = α, so all four elements are roots of X4 − X. In this exam-ple, the explicit model obtained by adjoining a root agrees directly with the root-set construction. 

# 1.7 The Root Polynomial of a Finite Subfield 

For a finite subset S of a field K, the monic polynomial with simple roots 

RS (X) = ∏

> a∈S

(X − a)

records precisely all elements of S. When S is itself a subfield, this polynomial is completely determined by |S|.

Proposition 1.16 (The root polynomial of a finite subfield) Let K be a field, and let 

S ⊆ K be a finite subfield with |S| = pn. Then 

∏

> a∈S

(X − a) = Xpn

− X. 

In particular, finite subfields of the same order in a common extension field coincide. 

Proof. By Proposition 1.6, every a ∈ S satisfies apn

= a. Thus RS divides Xpn

− X.Both are monic of degree pn, so they are equal. If two finite subfields have the same order, the formula identifies both as the complete root set of the same polynomial in K,so they coincide. 

Example 1.17 (Root sets, multiplicities, and the standard root polynomial) In char-acteristic two, 

X7 − X = X(X3 − 1) 2.

In a splitting extension, its distinct roots are zero and the three cube roots of unity, that is, the elements satisfying x3 = 1 . Together they form F4. The root zero has multiplicity one, whereas each of the three nonzero roots has multiplicity two. Replacing every multiplicity by one gives the monic polynomial X(X3 − 1) = X4 − X. Thus the intrinsic Chapter 1 Existence of Finite Fields: Characteristic, Adjoining Roots, and Fixed Points 9

description of a finite field concerns the set of all distinct roots and its monic polynomial with simple roots; specifying the root set alone does not recover the multiplicities of the original polynomial. 

Remark 1.18 (Closure of fixed points and determination of their number) If τ : K →

K is a field homomorphism preserving the identity, then Fix (τ ) = {x : τ (x) = x} is a subfield. Indeed, for x, y ∈ Fix (τ ), we have τ (x − y) = x − y and τ (xy ) = xy , and, when x 6 = 0 , τ (x−1) = τ (x)−1 = x−1. Neither finiteness of K nor surjectivity of τ is required. In characteristic p, take τ = φn for an integer n ≥ 1. Its fixed points satisfy a nonzero polynomial equation, so there are only finitely many. If this polynomial splits completely, separability further shows that their number is pn. Closure under the operations, the root bound, and complete splitting play three distinct roles in the argument.

# Uniqueness and Generators of Finite Fields 

Matching roots determines the isomorphism type of a finite field, while the root bound forces its multiplicative group to be cyclic. These facts yield field generators, irreducible polynomials of every degree, and quotient-ring coordinates, connecting intrinsic struc-ture with computational models. 

# 2.1 Minimal Polynomials and Fields Generated by One Element 

Let k ⊆ E be fields and S ⊆ E. The intersection of all subfields of E containing k ∪ S

is denoted by k(S) and is called the subfield generated by k and S. This family contains E, and its intersection is closed under the field operations. Thus k(S) exists and is the smallest subfield containing k ∪ S. For S = {α1, . . . , α r}, we write k(α1, . . . , α r);when S is empty, k(S) = k. If E = k(α), then E/k is a simple extension , and α is a field generator. For α ∈ E, also write 

k[α] = {A(α) : A ∈ k[X]}.

This is the subring generated by k and α, namely the smallest subring of E containing both. Hence k[α] ⊆ k(α). The two notations record polynomial evaluation and field generation, respectively. The next proposition shows that they coincide when α is algebraic over k.11 12 Chapter 2 Uniqueness and Generators of Finite Fields 

Definition 2.1 An element α of an extension field of k is algebraic over k if A(α) = 0 for some nonzero A ∈ k[X]. A nonzero polynomial A satisfying A(α) = 0 is an 

annihilating polynomial of α over k. Choose an annihilating polynomial of least degree and divide it by its leading coefficient. The resulting monic polynomial is the 

minimal polynomial of α over k, denoted by mα,k .

Proposition 2.2 Suppose that α is algebraic over k and that m = mα,k has degree d.Then: (1) m is irreducible, and for A ∈ k[X], A(α) = 0 if and only if m | A;(2) the minimal polynomial is unique; (3) k(α) = k[α];(4) evaluation induces 

k[X]/( m) ∼= k(α), A 7 −→ A(α),

and 1, α, . . . , α d−1 is a basis of k(α)/ k. In particular, 

[k(α) : k] = deg mα,k = d. 

Proof. If m = AB , with both A, B of positive degree, then A(α)B(α) = 0 . A field has no zero divisors, so one of these values is zero. The corresponding factor has degree less than deg m, contradicting minimality. Thus m is irreducible. For any A ∈ k[X], division with remainder gives A = Qm + R, where R = 0 or deg R < d . If A(α) = 0 , then R(α) = 0 , and minimality forces R = 0 , so m | A. The converse follows immediately by evaluation. If another monic polynomial m1 of least degree vanishes at α, then m | m1. Since both are monic of the same degree, m1 = m.Consider the evaluation homomorphism ev α : k[X] → k[α], A 7 → A(α). The divisi-bility criterion shows that its kernel is precisely the ideal (m). Consequently, 

A 7 −→ A(α)

is well defined, surjective, and injective on k[X]/( m), and preserves addition, multi-plication, and the identity. Since m is irreducible, the quotient is a field, so k[α] is also a field. It contains k and α, and hence contains the smallest such subfield k(α).Conversely, A(α) ∈ k(α), so k[α] = k(α).Division with remainder shows that 1, α, . . . , α d−1 span this field. A nontrivial k-linear relation among them would give a nonzero annihilating polynomial of degree less than d, contradicting minimality. Thus they form a basis. Chapter 2 Uniqueness and Generators of Finite Fields 13 

The same terminology applies to evaluating polynomials at linear operators. Let 

A : V → V be a linear operator on a finite-dimensional k-space. For g(T ) = ∑ 

> i

ciT i,define g(A) = ∑ 

> i

ciAi, with A0 = id V . A nonzero g ∈ k[T ] satisfying g(A) = 0 is an annihilating polynomial of A. If only g(A)v = 0 is required, it is an annihilating polyno-mial of the vector v relative to A. The monic polynomials of least degree satisfying these two conditions are called the minimal polynomial of A and the minimal annihilating polynomial of v relative to A, respectively. Such polynomials exist: if dim k V = N , the linear operators form a space of dimension N 2, so id V , A, . . . , A N 2

are linearly depen-dent. The resulting operator relation also annihilates every specified vector. Division with remainder, as in Proposition 2.2, proves uniqueness of the monic polynomial of least degree. The first condition requires vanishing on the entire space, and the sec-ond only on a specified vector. Both minimal polynomials must be distinguished from general annihilating polynomials.

# 2.3 Matching Roots and Uniqueness of Splitting Fields 

Definition 2.4 Let P ∈ k[X] be nonconstant. An extension field E is a splitting field of P over k if P splits completely over E and E is generated by k and all the roots of P .Lemma 1.9 constructs an extension over which the polynomial splits. The subfield generated by all its roots in that extension is a splitting field. Successively matching roots proves uniqueness up to isomorphism. 

Proposition 2.5 (Matching roots between splitting fields) Let τ : k → k′ be an isomorphism, let E/k be a splitting field of P , and let E′/k′ be a splitting field of P τ .Then τ extends to an isomorphism E → E′.

Proof. Write the distinct roots of P as α1, . . . , α t, so that E = k(α1, . . . , α t). Starting with τ , suppose that an embedding 

τi : k(α1, . . . , α i) −→ E′

has been constructed. Regard it as an isomorphism from its domain onto its image. Let m be the minimal polynomial of αi+1 over the current domain. Since P (αi+1 ) = 0 ,Proposition 2.2 gives m | P . Applying τi coefficientwise yields 

mτi | P τ .

The right-hand side splits completely in E′, so mτi , which has positive degree, has a root 

β in E′. The one-step extension lemma gives the next embedding τi+1 . After finitely many steps, we obtain σ : E → E′.Chapter 2 Uniqueness and Generators of Finite Fields 15 

It remains to prove surjectivity. Over E, write P as a product of linear factors, retaining multiplicities. Applying σ to the coefficients and roots gives a complete fac-torization of P τ over σ(E). Thus every root of P τ belongs to σ(E). Since E′ is generated by k′ and these roots, we have E′ = σ(E).

Theorem 2.6 (Uniqueness up to isomorphism of finite fields of the same order) Any two fields with pn elements are isomorphic by an isomorphism fixing their prime fields. Thus each prime power pn determines exactly one isomorphism type of finite field, denoted by Fpn .

Proof. If |E| = pn, Proposition 1.16 identifies all elements of E with the complete root set of Xpn

− X. Hence E is a splitting field of this polynomial over Fp. The same holds for any other field with pn elements, and Proposition 2.5 gives an isomorphism. Existence was established in Theorem 1.13. 

Corollary 2.7 (Uniqueness over a specified base field) Let k be a specified field with 

q elements, and let E, E ′ be fields with qm elements containing k. Then there is an isomorphism E → E′ fixing k pointwise. 

Proof. Both are splitting fields of Xqm

−X over k. Apply the root-matching proposition to id k.

Example 2.8 (An isomorphism need not be unique) In the field with four elements, let α satisfy α2 + α + 1 = 0 . The other root of this polynomial is α + 1 . The one-step extension lemma gives an automorphism fixing F2 and sending α to α + 1 . This differs from the identity. Thus uniqueness of the isomorphism type does not imply uniqueness of the isomorphism. Having determined the isomorphism type, we turn to generators within the field. The root bound constrains the least common multiple of the element orders in a finite multiplicative group, and this constraint suffices to prove cyclicity.

Proof. First, (ab )rs = 1 . If (ab )t = 1 , then at = b−t lies in both 〈a〉 and 〈b〉. Its order divides both r and s, so it is the identity. Thus r | t and s | t, and coprimality gives 

rs | t.

# 2.5 The Root Bound and Multiplicative Cyclicity 

Theorem 2.11 (Cyclicity of finite multiplicative subgroups of a field) Every finite subgroup of the multiplicative group K× of a field K is cyclic. In particular, if |E| = Q,then E× is cyclic of order Q − 1.

Proof. Let G ⊆ K× be a finite subgroup, and let M be the least common multiple of all its element orders. Every g ∈ G satisfies gM = 1 , so all elements of G are roots of 

XM − 1. The root bound gives |G| ≤ M .On the other hand, G is abelian, so Lemma 2.10 gives an element h of order M . Its cyclic subgroup has M elements, so M ≤ | G|. Therefore 

|G| = M = |〈 h〉| ,

and hence G = 〈h〉.Chapter 2 Uniqueness and Generators of Finite Fields 17 

This proof uses a special property of fields: a polynomial of degree M cannot have more than M roots. A general finite abelian group has no analogous restriction. For example, (Z/2 Z)2 has four elements, each of order at most two. 

Definition 2.12 A generator of the multiplicative group of a finite field E is a prim-itive element of E. If |E| = Q, a primitive element ζ satisfies 

E× = {1, ζ, ζ 2, . . . , ζ Q−2}, ord (ζ) = Q − 1.

Corollary 2.13 Let |E| = Q and t ≥ 1. The equation xt = 1 has exactly gcd (t, Q − 1) 

solutions in E.

Proof. Write x = ζj , with j taken modulo Q−1. Then xt = 1 is equivalent to (Q−1) | tj ,which holds for exactly gcd (t, Q − 1) residue classes. 

Example 2.14 (Primitive elements in the field with nine elements) Let E = F3(α),where α2 = −1 = 2 . Since X2 + 1 has no root in F3, this is indeed a field with nine elements. We have α2 = 2 and α4 = 1 , so α has order four and is not primitive. However, 

(1 + α)2 = 2 α, (1 + α)4 = 2 , (1 + α)8 = 1 ,

so 1+ α has order eight and is primitive. Thus an element generating the whole extension field need not generate its multiplicative group. 

# 2.6 Successively Increasing the Multiplicative Order: Gauss’s Method 

The cyclicity proof also gives a finite construction. Suppose that a ∈ E× has order m.If m < |E×|, choose b /∈ 〈 a〉, and denote its order by s. Then s - m: otherwise b and all 

m elements of 〈a〉 would be roots of Xm − 1, contradicting the root bound. For each prime dividing m or s, choose the larger prime power appearing in their factorizations; if they are equal, choose the one from m. Let d be the product of those chosen from m, and e the product of the remaining ones, with an empty product equal to 1. Then d | m, e | s, gcd (d, e ) = 1 , and de = lcm (m, s ). The element 

c = am/dbs/e18 Chapter 2 Uniqueness and Generators of Finite Fields 

has order de > m . Replace a by c and repeat. The order strictly increases, so the process eventually yields a primitive element. This is a finite construction; its computational complexity also depends on determining element orders and factoring integers. 

Example 2.15 In F13 , the elements 3 and 5 have orders 3 and 4, respectively. These orders are coprime, so 3 · 5 = 2 has order 12 , giving a primitive element of F13 .A multiplicative primitive element also generates the whole extension field. Its minimal polynomial therefore converts an already constructed finite field into a quotient-ring model and yields irreducible polynomials of every degree. 

# 2.7 Primitive Elements Make Finite Extensions Sim-ple 

Proposition 2.16 If k ⊆ E are finite fields and ζ is a primitive element of E, then 

E = k(ζ).

Proof. The subfield k(ζ) contains 0 and all nonnegative integral powers of ζ. These powers comprise all nonzero elements of E, so the subfield is E.

Theorem 2.17 (Existence of irreducible polynomials of every degree) Let k be any finite field, with |k| = q. For every n ≥ 1, there is a monic irreducible polynomial of degree n in k[X].

Proof. By Corollary 1.14, first construct a field E with qn elements containing k. By Theorem 2.11, choose a primitive element ζ of E. Then E = k(ζ). Set f = mζ,k . This polynomial is monic and irreducible, and deg f = [ k(ζ) : k] = [ E : k] = n. 

The root-set construction establishes the existence of finite fields, while the minimal polynomial of a primitive element supplies quotient-ring coordinates. These describe the intrinsic field structure and a concrete computational model, respectively. Chapter 2 Uniqueness and Generators of Finite Fields 19 

Theorem 2.18 (Quotient-ring representations of finite fields) Let k be a field with q

elements. (1) If f ∈ k[X] is monic and irreducible of degree n, then k[X]/( f ) is a field with qn

elements containing k.(2) Every field with qn elements containing k is isomorphic to such a quotient. In fact, for every monic irreducible f of degree n, it is isomorphic to k[X]/( f ) over k.

Proof. The first assertion is Proposition 1.8. For the second, choose a primitive element of E and its minimal polynomial. Proposition 2.2 gives a quotient-ring representation. For any other monic irreducible f of degree n, the quotient ring and E are both exten-sions of k with qn elements, so Corollary 2.7 gives a k-isomorphism between them. 

# 2.8 Quotient-Ring Coordinates and Finite-Field Arithmetic 

Let f ∈ k[X] be monic and irreducible, with deg f = n ≥ 1. In k[X]/( f ), write α = X

for the residue class of X. The elements of the quotient ring are residue classes of polynomials. Choosing the unique representative of degree less than n for computation gives coordinates 

a0 + a1α + · · · + an−1αn−1.

Existence of the representative follows from division with remainder. Uniqueness follows because the difference of two distinct representatives cannot have degree less than n

while also being divisible by f . Thus the vector space kn supplies coordinates for all elements, while multiplication also depends on the chosen polynomial f .Writing rem f A for the remainder of A upon division by f , the coordinate operations are 

A + B = rem f (A + B), A · B = rem f (AB ).

If A′ = A + U f and B′ = B + V f , then the differences between A′ + B′ and A + B,and between A′B′ and AB , are divisible by f . Thus these operations are independent of the representatives. Associativity and distributivity descend from the corresponding polynomial identities. 20 Chapter 2 Uniqueness and Generators of Finite Fields 

Let 0 6 = A with deg A < n . Irreducibility gives gcd (A, f ) = 1 , and the extended Euclidean algorithm yields 

U (X)A(X) + V (X)f (X) = 1 .

Evaluation at α gives U (α)A(α) = 1 , so the inverse is represented by rem f U . The field operations are therefore reduced to arithmetic in the base field, polynomial division, and Bézout’s identity. 

Example 2.19 (A field with sixteen elements) Take f = X4 + X + 1 ∈ F2[X]. It is nonzero at 0, 1, so it has no linear factor. The only monic irreducible quadratic in 

F2[X] is X2 + X + 1 : a monic quadratic without a root must have constant term 1, and evaluation at 1 then forces the linear coefficient to be 1. Modulo X2 + X + 1 , we have 

X3 ≡ 1 and X4 ≡ X, so f ≡ 1. A reducible quartic without a linear factor must have an irreducible quadratic factor. Hence f is irreducible. Consequently, 

E = F2[α], α4 = α + 1 

has sixteen elements, each uniquely expressible as a + bα + cα 2 + dα 3, with coefficients in F2. For example, 

(1 + α2)( α + α3) = α + α5 = α2,

since α5 = α2 + α. Moreover, the order of α divides fifteen and is not 1, 3, 5: the degree-four minimal polynomial implies α3 6 = 1 , and the same degree argument gives 

α5 = α2 + α 6 = 1 . Thus α has order fifteen and is also a primitive element.

Remark 2.21 An irreducible polynomial ensures that a root generates an extension of the prescribed degree, but does not ensure that the root generates the multiplicative group. A monic irreducible polynomial whose root is a primitive element of the resulting finite field is called a primitive polynomial . The proof of Theorem 2.17 in fact produces primitive polynomials of every degree. By uniqueness of finite fields of the same order, irreducible polynomials of the same degree give quotient-ring models with the same k-isomorphism type, although their reduction relations generally give different multiplication rules in coordinates. Let f, g ∈

k[X] be monic irreducible polynomials of degree n. Choose a root b of f in k[Y ]/( g).Then 

k[X]/( f ) −→ k[Y ]/( g), A(X) 7 −→ A(b)

is a k-isomorphism by the one-step extension lemma. Conversion between these coordi-nate systems requires such a choice of root; simply identifying the respective polynomial bases need not define a field isomorphism.

# Frobenius: Subfields, Conjugates, and Descent of Root Sets 

The fixed points of Frobenius determine subfields, and its orbits determine minimal polynomials. Relating functions on root sets to the Frobenius action makes factorization the algebraic expression of orbit decomposition. Write q = pr, and fix a field k with q elements. A specified finite extension is denoted by E/k, with |E| = qm and [E : k] = m recording its order and degree. When comparing subfields, intersections, and composita, we first specify a common finite extension containing the fields in question; any change of this ambient extension will be stated. 

# 3.1 The Order of Frobenius and the Extension De-gree 

Definition 3.1 On a field of characteristic p, the map φ : a 7 → ap is called the absolute Frobenius map . For E/k, the map 

σ : E −→ E, a 7 −→ aq = φr(a)

is the relative Frobenius map over k.25 26 Chapter 3 Frobenius: Subfields, Conjugates, and Descent of Root Sets 

Proposition 3.2 The map σ is an automorphism of E, fixes k pointwise, and has order exactly m. Its fixed elements are precisely those of k:Fix (σ) = {a ∈ E : aq = a} = k. 

Proof. Lemma 1.5 shows that σ preserves addition, multiplication, and 1. If σ(a) = σ(b),then (a − b)q = 0 , so a = b. Thus σ is injective; an injection on a finite set is surjective, so σ is an automorphism. For a ∈ k, we have aq = a, so σ fixes k.Every element of E satisfies aqm

= a, and hence σm = id. If σt = id for some 

1 ≤ t < m , all qm elements of E would be roots of Xqt

− X. Since qm > q t, this contradicts the root bound. Therefore ord (σ) = m.Finally, Xq − X has at most q roots, and all q elements of k are roots. Thus the fixed elements of σ are precisely the elements of k.

# 3.2 Cyclicity of the Automorphism Group 

Theorem 3.3 

Aut k(E) = 〈σ〉 = {id , σ, . . . , σ m−1}, Aut k(E) ∼= Z/mZ.

Proof. These m powers of Frobenius are distinct k-automorphisms. Conversely, choose a primitive element ζ of E, so that E = k(ζ). The minimal polynomial of ζ over k has degree m. Any k-automorphism is uniquely determined by the image of ζ, which must be a root of this minimal polynomial. The polynomial has at most m roots, so there are at most m such automorphisms. Comparing the two bounds proves the assertion.

# 3.5 Orbits, Conjugates, and Minimal Polynomials 

Let τ be a permutation of a finite set. The orbit of an element a is {a, τ (a), τ 2(a), . . . },obtained by repeatedly applying τ . The least positive integer d for which τ d(a) = a

is the period of a; its orbit has exactly d elements. A subset preserved setwise by the permutation is called stable. If it consists of one orbit, the action on that subset is transitive. On the other hand, two algebraic elements are conjugate over a base field if they have the same minimal polynomial over that field. The following theorem identifies this algebraic condition with membership in the same Frobenius orbit.

An element whose distinct Frobenius conjugates form a basis of the whole extension over the base field is called a normal element . This notion is developed in Chapter 9. Remark 3.16 (The full collection of orbits and a single orbit) The polynomial Xqn

−X

collects all orbits whose lengths divide n, whereas an irreducible polynomial records just one orbit. An individual orbit is generally not closed under addition or multiplication. For example, the two roots of X2 + X + 1 in F4 have product one, which does not belong to that orbit. Taking the union of all orbits whose lengths divide n gives the full fixed-point set of σn. Chapter 19 further decomposes this set into exact-period layers and separates them by polynomial elimination. In any common finite splitting extension, Fqn consists exactly of all elements whose periods divide n. The set of elements of period exactly n > 1 does not contain one, and hence is not itself a field. Both the field structure of a root set and divisibility of degrees are governed by Frobenius: preservation of the operations makes the fixed-point set closed, while the orbit theorem identifies the extension degree of an element with its least period.

# 3.7 Descent of Root Sets and Decompositions of Function Algebras 

Preservation of the field operations makes the fixed points of Frobenius a subfield. For a monic polynomial with simple roots, whether its coefficients lie in the base field is determined by Frobenius stability of its root set. The latter principle both identifies irreducible polynomials and turns factorization into a direct-product decomposition of a function algebra. Here “descent” means that a polynomial initially written over an extension has all its coefficients in the base field. 

Theorem 3.19 (Descent of root sets) Let k = Fq ⊆ L = FqN , let σ(a) = aq, and let

Proof. Apply σ to every coefficient, and denote the resulting polynomial by σ(RS ).Then

A monic polynomial with simple roots is uniquely determined by its root set. Hence 

σ(RS ) = RS if and only if σ(S) = S. The elements of L fixed by σ are precisely those of k, so the former equality holds if and only if every coefficient belongs to k. Finally, 34 Chapter 3 Frobenius: Subfields, Conjugates, and Descent of Root Sets 

apply Theorem 3.11 to each orbit: the root polynomial ∏

Stability here means setwise preservation; it does not require each root to be fixed. For a monic nonconstant separable polynomial, having coefficients in the base field is equivalent to stability of the root set; under this condition, irreducibility is equivalent to transitivity of Frobenius on the roots. The assumption that the polynomial is monic fixes its leading coefficient, which the root set alone cannot determine. For example, if 

c ∈ L \ k, the root set {0} of cX is stable, but cX /∈ k[X].For a monic polynomial with repeated roots, coefficient descent is still characterized by the root multiset: Frobenius must preserve both roots and their multiplicities. Asingle root orbit, however, no longer implies irreducibility. For example, the square P 2

of an irreducible polynomial P still has just one orbit of distinct roots, but is reducible. Irreducible polynomials over finite fields are automatically separable, so the simple-root condition in the orbit criterion cannot be omitted. Let sets S, T carry maps τ : S → S and ρ : T → T , respectively. A map h : S → T

satisfying 

h ◦ τ = ρ ◦ h, 

is called equivariant with respect to τ, ρ . This equality says that h respects the speci-fied iteration; induction gives h◦τ j = ρj ◦h for every j ≥ 0. If both τ, ρ are permutations, it holds for every integer j. More generally, if a group G acts on both S, T , a map h is 

G-equivariant if 

h(g · s) = g · h(s) (g ∈ G, s ∈ S).

For the action of a cyclic group generated by a specified permutation, it suffices to check the equality for the generator. When both maps are denoted by σ, the condition is abbreviated to hσ = σh , with the two occurrences of σ acting on their respective sets. Equivariance expresses compatibility with the specified actions; it does not itself require h to preserve addition or multiplication. We shall use both maps of sets and algebras of functions. A k-vector space equipped with an associative multiplication and an identity, with multiplication k-linear in each variable, is called a k-algebra . An algebra homomorphism is a k-linear map preserving multiplication and the identity. The function algebras below are commutative, with Chapter 3 Frobenius: Subfields, Conjugates, and Descent of Root Sets 35 

pointwise operations; operations in a direct product of algebras are likewise performed coordinatewise.

Corollary 3.32 (Frobenius similarity type and algebra isomorphism type) Two nonzero finite-dimensional commutative reduced k-algebras are isomorphic if and only if their Frobenius maps are similar as k-linear operators. 

Proof. An algebra isomorphism commutes with taking q-th powers, so it conjugates one Frobenius operator to the other. Conversely, similar operators have equal underlying dimensions and equal fixed-space dimensions for every iterate. Theorem 3.31 then recovers the same field components and multiplicities. What is recovered here is the algebra’s isomorphism type. A given Frobenius-equivariant linear isomorphism need not preserve multiplication; Example 8.10 gives a concrete counterexample.

Example 3.34 (Nilpotent multiplication cannot be recovered this way) Let q ≥ 3, and take 

A = k[ε]/( ε3) × k, A′ = k[ε]/( ε2) × k[ε]/( ε2).

The algebra A contains a nilpotent element (ε, 0) with nonzero square, whereas every nilpotent element of A′ has square zero. deg g. These integer data can thus be recovered directly from g, giving the number of irreducible factors of each degree. The individual factors can then be separated by the methods in Chapter 10. 

# 3.10 Frobenius Descent of Multivariate Linear Fac-tors 

The essence of root-set descent is that a Frobenius-stable collection of factors gives a polynomial over the base field, while one orbit gives an irreducible factor. For multi-variate polynomials, the same idea applies when the polynomial splits completely into linear factors over an extension. The phrase polynomial splitting into linear fac-tors describes the form of the factorization; the linear factors are not assumed to be distinct. The following orbit formulation gives one form of Carlitz’s criterion; see [1, Chapter 13]. Let E = FqN , and let σ act coefficientwise on E[X1, . . . , X m], fixing the variables. For a nonconstant affine linear polynomial M = c0 + ∑mj=1 cj Xj , take the smallest index

conjugates of L divide f . Thus f = FLQ, with Q ∈ E[X1, . . . , X m]. Applying σ and canceling the nonzero factor FL gives σ(Q) = Q, so Q ∈ k[X1, . . . , X m]. Irreducibility forces Q = c ∈ k×. The reverse implication follows from the irreducibility of FL already proved. In one variable, a normalized linear factor is X − α, and (3.4) is the orbit product for the minimal polynomial. In several variables, Frobenius instead organizes the coef-ficients of linear factors; the product of conjugates gives the same descent mechanism. In particular, the linear factors of an irreducible polynomial splitting into linear factors are necessarily distinct in a splitting extension.

# Element Representations, Multiplicative Orders, and Polynomial Orders 

The multiplicative order and Frobenius period of an element describe the cyclic sub-group and the field extension it generates, respectively. Quotient-ring coordinates and multiplication matrices make these invariants accessible to polynomial computations, while repeated factors record the contribution of powers of the characteristic. 

# 4.1 Coordinates for Computing with Field Elements 

Fix k = Fq ⊆ E = Fqn . If E = k(α), every element has a unique expression 

x = x0 + x1α + · · · + xn−1αn−1, xi ∈ k. 

This is called a polynomial basis representation . The relation mα,k (α) = 0 reduces higher powers to lower ones. Addition is coordinatewise, multiplication consists of poly-nomial multiplication followed by reduction, and inversion uses the extended Euclidean algorithm. This algorithm records the coefficients of linear combinations during suc-cessive divisions, thereby obtaining the coefficients in Bézout’s identity. The chosen α

need only generate the extension, not the multiplicative group. If a primitive element ζ is chosen, every nonzero x is uniquely expressible as ζj ,where j ∈ Z/( qn − 1) Z. This is the exponent representation ; the exponent class j

is the discrete logarithm of x to base ζ, denoted by log ζ x. In this representation, multiplication adds exponents, inversion negates them, and taking an integer power multiplies the exponent by that integer. Addition of field elements requires further 55 56 Chapter 4 Element Representations, Multiplicative Orders, and Polynomial Orders 

information. For example, when 1 + ζt 6 = 0 , define the Zech logarithm 

Z(t) = log ζ (1 + ζt).

Then ζi + ζj = ζi+Z(j−i). If 1 + ζj−i = 0 , the sum is zero. In practice, addition can use a Zech logarithm table or a conversion to polynomial basis coordinates. If k ⊆ L ⊆ E, choose a basis ui of L/k and a basis vj of E/L, and write elements as ∑ 

> i,j

aij uivj . Lemma 1.3 guarantees uniqueness; this is a tower representation .These representations describe the same field. Choosing coordinates does not change minimal polynomials, conjugacy orbits, or element orders. 

# 4.2 The Regular Representation by Multiplication 

Choose a basis of E/k. For a ∈ E, let Ma denote the matrix of the linear map x 7 → ax .Then 

Ma+b = Ma + Mb, Mab = MaMb, M1 = I. 

This representation is injective, since Ma = 0 implies a · 1 = 0 . For nonzero Ma, its inverse is Ma−1 . Thus a 7 → Ma embeds E into a matrix algebra, with image a subfield isomorphic to E. This embedding is the regular representation of the field. If E = k(α) and mα(X) = Xn+cn−1Xn−1+· · · +c0, then, in the basis (1 , α, . . . , α n−1),the matrix Mα = A is called the companion matrix of mα: its first n − 1 columns record α · αj = αj+1 for 0 ≤ j < n − 1, and its last column is (−c0, . . . , −cn−1)t.Consequently, E ∼= k[A]. If B is the matrix of Frobenius, then 

BM aB−1 = Maq .

Thus conjugate field elements give similar multiplication matrices. Chapter 6 uses this relation to determine traces, norms, and characteristic polynomials. 

Proposition 4.1 (Conjugacy of matrix models in the same dimension) Let [E : k] = n,and let V be an n-dimensional k-space. If ρ : E → End k(V ) is a unital k-algebra homomorphism, there is a k-linear isomorphism S : E → V such that 

ρ(a) = SM aS−1 (a ∈ E).

Thus every matrix model of a field in dimension equal to its extension degree is obtained from the regular representation by one simultaneous change of basis. Chapter 4 Element Representations, Multiplicative Orders, and Polynomial Orders 57 

Proof. Choose 0 6 = v ∈ V , and define S(x) = ρ(x)v. If x 6 = 0 , then ρ(x) has inverse 

ρ(x−1), so S(x) = 0 would force v = 0 , a contradiction. Hence S is injective, and equality of dimensions makes it an isomorphism. For a, x ∈ E, we have ρ(a)S(x) = 

ρ(ax )v = S(Max), proving the conjugacy relation. The regular representation therefore preserves all multiplication relations simultane-ously. For every h ∈ k[T ], we have h(Ma) = Mh(a), so the annihilating polynomials of the multiplication matrix are exactly those of the field element. For the resulting equal-ity of minimal polynomials, see Exercise 4.6. A change of basis alters matrix entries but preserves the same system of matrix relations.

## 4.6.1 Projective Order and Minimal Binomial Multiples

# 4.7 Reciprocal Polynomials and Inverse-Root Orbits 

For a monic polynomial f of degree d with f (0) 6 = 0 , define its monic reciprocal polynomial by 

f ∨(X) = Xdf (X−1)

f (0) .

Its roots are the inverses of the roots of f , with the same respective multiplicities, and 

(f ∨)∨ = f . A polynomial satisfying f = f ∨ is called self-reciprocal . This operation preserves irreducibility, since taking reciprocals of a nontrivial factorization again gives a nontrivial factorization. 

Proposition 4.20 Let f 6 = X be monic and irreducible. If f = f ∨, then either 

f = X − 1 or X + 1 , or deg f = 2 s and every root α satisfies αqs+1 = 1 . Conversely, if a root of a monic irreducible polynomial of degree 2s satisfies this equality, then f = f ∨.

Proof. Self-reciprocity is equivalent to α−1 lying in the same Frobenius orbit as α, for some root α. If α−1 = α, then α = ±1, giving a linear polynomial. Otherwise write 

α−1 = αqj

, where 0 < j < d = deg f . Taking the qj -th power again gives αq2j

= α,so d | 2j. Since 0 < 2j < 2d, we have 2j = d. Thus d = 2 s, j = s, and αqs+1 = 1 .Conversely, the stated equality places the inverse in the original orbit, so the two monic minimal polynomials coincide. In exponent coordinates, inversion is i 7 → − i, and Frobenius is i 7 → qi . They commute, so inversion sends an entire Frobenius orbit to another orbit. If α has order 

e, its conjugates and the conjugates of its inverse are, respectively, 

{αqj

: j ≥ 0}, {α−qj

: j ≥ 0}.

These roots determine f and f ∨, respectively. Thus reciprocity is an involution on irreducible polynomials, whose fixed points are precisely the self-reciprocal irreducibles; all remaining irreducibles occur in pairs. 66 Chapter 4 Element Representations, Multiplicative Orders, and Polynomial Orders

Proof. The inverse is a conjugate if and only if qj ≡ − 1 ( mod e) for some j, giving the first equivalence. Since e > 2, the element −1 has order two. The cyclic group 〈q〉 of order d has an element of order two if and only if d is even, in which case its unique element of order two is qd/2 . This proves the second equivalence. The criterion requires inversion exactly halfway around the orbit; even degree alone is insufficient. For example, ord 8(3) = 2 , but 3 6 ≡ − 1 ( mod 8) . Thus irreducible quadratics over F3 whose roots have multiplicative order eight are not self-reciprocal. The polynomial X2 + X + 2 from Example 2.22 and its reciprocal X2 + 2 X + 2 form such a pair. # Roots of Unity, Base Extension, and Tensor Product Decompositions 

On roots of unity, Frobenius acts by multiplication on exponents; extending the base field changes the step size. Cyclotomic factorization, intersections, and composita are therefore governed by the same period calculation, while tensor products record all components of the factorization. For Galois rings, residue-field orbits and Hensel lifting further determine the factors associated with roots of unity and the direct product decomposition of quotient rings. 

# 5.1 The Splitting Field of the Roots of Unity 

Let N be a positive integer with gcd (N, q ) = 1 . In an extension in which XN − 1 splits, put 

μN = {ζ : ζN = 1 }.

The elements of μN are called N -th roots of unity . This set is a multiplicative group. The derivative N X N −1 shows that the roots are simple, so |μN | = N . By Theorem 2.11, 

μN is cyclic; an element of order N is called a primitive N -th root of unity .

Proposition 5.1 The splitting field of XN − 1 over Fq is Fqs , where s = ord N (q). For 

N = 1 , we set s = 1 .

Proof. Choose a generator ζ of μN . Every root is a power of ζ, so the splitting field is 

Fq(ζ). Proposition 4.4 gives its degree s.If N = paM , where p - M , then

The Chinese remainder theorem (CRT) over the integers identifies the unit group modulo 2`a with that modulo `a. If a modulus has two distinct odd prime divisors, its unit-group decomposition under the CRT has at least two components of even order; each contains an element of order two, so their direct product has at least three elements of order two and cannot be cyclic. The same argument applies when the modulus is divisible by both four and an odd prime. If 2a | M with a ≥ 3, the four distinct units modulo 2a

1, −1, 1 + 2 a−1, −1 + 2 a−1

all square to one, so this unit group is not cyclic. The CRT makes it a direct factor of the unit group modulo M . Since a quotient of a cyclic group is cyclic, the latter group is not cyclic either. The remaining moduli are exactly those listed.

# 5.6 Multiple Equal-Difference Structure of Cyclo-tomic Cosets and Binomial Descent 

Extending the base field splits a Frobenius orbit into suborbits with a larger step size. For roots of unity, some suborbits also form complete equal-difference blocks, whose root polynomials are binomials. This relation explains the additive symmetry within exponent orbits, the forced zero coefficients of the factors, and the appearance of lower-degree polynomials suited to computation. Throughout this section, fix gcd (N, q ) = 1 ,and retain the notation Ci = {iq j mod N : j ≥ 0} and MCi .For multiple equal-difference structure and its correspondence with binomial factor-ization, see [71]. We describe these decompositions uniformly using complete additive cosets. 

## 5.6.1 Complete Equal-Difference Root Blocks and the Coarsest Partition 

Definition 5.19 For r | N , a set 

B = b + Nr Z/N Z =

{

b, b + Nr , . . . , b + ( r − 1) Nr

}

is called a complete equal-difference block of size r. A partition of a nonempty set into disjoint complete equal-difference blocks of the same size is called a multiple equal-difference decomposition . Each block must be a complete coset of the corresponding additive subgroup; an arbitrary segment of a finite arithmetic progression need not satisfy this condition. The decomposition records neither the order of the blocks nor Chapter 5 Roots of Unity, Base Extension, and Tensor Product Decompositions 81 

the starting point of a block. The case r = 1 gives the singleton partition. A partition is finer than another if each of its blocks is contained in a block of the latter. Apartition coarser than every admissible partition is called the coarsest partition . For a nonempty set C ⊆ Z/N Z, its additive stabilizer is 

H+(C) = {u ∈ Z/N Z : C + u = C}.

Proposition 5.22 (An additive-stabilizer criterion for a multiplicative orbit) Let R =

Remark 5.34 (Equal-difference orbits and sparsest defining equations) Let C be a

Starting from an arbitrary degree-n generator α, one may therefore ask whether a low-degree rational function

## 5.6.4 Three-Sparse Factorizations and Images under Root Squar-ing 

For a positive integer n, call Xn − 1 3-sparse over k if each of its monic irreducible factors over k has at most three nonzero terms. This concerns the number of terms of each irreducible factor, not of Xn − 1 itself. The constant terms of these factors are nonzero, so 3-sparsity means that every irreducible factor is a binomial or trinomial. Let q = pe, and write n = pam, where gcd (m, p ) = 1 . Since 

Xn − 1 = ( Xm − 1) pa

,

3-sparsity depends only on m, not on the multiplicities of the factors. Multiple equal-difference structure gives a sufficient condition for a 3-sparse fac-torization: if the coarsest equal-difference decomposition has at most two blocks, the outer polynomial in (5.10) has degree at most two and retains at most three nonzero terms after power substitution. In odd characteristic, this arithmetic condition is also necessary [13]. 

Theorem 5.39 (A criterion for 3-sparsity in odd characteristic) Let q be an odd prime power, p = char k, and write n = pam, where gcd (m, p ) = 1 . Then 

Xn − 1 is 3-sparse over k ⇐⇒ rad (m) | q2 − 1.

d = 1 , its factor is linear. If d > 1, then ρ = ord rad (d)(q) divides two. The value ωCi

given by Theorem 5.26 also divides two: the additional dyadic factor two can occur only when ρ = 1 , since q2 ≡ 1 ( mod 4) . Taking r = κCi in Proposition 5.31 gives

## 5.6.6 Cyclotomic Polynomials of Low Order and Coefficient Re-currences 

When the square-free kernel of the index divides q + 1 , roots of unity of low order can first be treated in the quadratic extension, where Frobenius acts by inversion. When the dyadic part remains unchanged, coefficients of factors of higher-index cyclotomic polynomials can therefore be obtained recursively from coefficients of quadratic factors at lower indices. For the stabilization that produces factors at higher indices from those at lower indices by power substitution, see [63] and Proposition 5.69. ## 5.6.7 Unions of Orbits, Root Power Sums, and the Maximum Composition Exponent 

Transitivity of the multiplicative action on a single cyclotomic coset ensures that each complete equal-difference block extends to a partition of the whole coset. For a union of cosets, existing blocks may merge and produce translation periods absent from each constituent coset. The maximum monomial composition exponent of the entire root set is still determined by its additive stabilizer; root power sums give another way to compute this stabilizer.

# 5.7 Base Extension and Tensor Product Decomposi-tions 

Extending the base field replaces σ by an iterate and may therefore split one orbit into several. The tensor product gives an algebraic expression of this phenomenon. For finite extensions E/k and F /k, E ⊗k F is the vector space generated by symbols x ⊗ y subject to bilinear relations, with multiplication defined by (x ⊗ y)( x′ ⊗ y′) = xx ′ ⊗ yy ′. If (ei)

and (fj ) are bases of the two fields, then (ei ⊗ fj ) is a basis of the tensor product, whose dimension is therefore [E : k][ F : k].Chapter 5 Roots of Unity, Base Extension, and Tensor Product Decompositions 105

The compositum corresponds to just one component of the tensor product; the tensor product also records the other ways in which the two fields can agree on their common subfield.

# 5.8 Synchronization of Local Orbits and Explicit Fac-torization of Roots-of-Unity Polynomials 

Conjugate orbits of roots of unity can first be calculated at pairwise coprime moduli and then combined by the Chinese remainder theorem. In the combination, the local orbits advance simultaneously; even when all local orbits are specified, they may yield more than one global orbit. Choose ζ to be a primitive fifteenth root of unity that is a root of X4 + X + 1 . Then

Together with the two unit orbits above, they recover all five irreducible factors in the earlier example of fifteenth roots of unity. For each orbit determined in (5.19), the multiple equal-difference structure of Sec-tion 5.6 can further compress the root product and determine the least extension degree over which all its factors are binomials. Local representatives enumerate and label the orbits; multiple equal-difference structure describes the additive symmetry within each orbit. Together they give an explicit factorization of roots-of-unity polynomials. For 

N = 1 , the exponent set consists of one singleton orbit, with factor X − 1.

# 5.9 Cyclotomic Systems and Compatible Factor Lift-ing 

When moduli increase along a divisibility chain, power maps between roots of unity re-late cyclotomic cosets at different levels. A cyclotomic system records this compatibility and corresponds to a compatible tower of irreducible factors. Fix q = pe; all moduli below are coprime to p. For cyclotomic systems and their classification in prime-power directions, see [73]. We describe their lifting structure by return permutations on finite fibers [75]. 

## 5.9.1 Reduction Maps and Compatible Systems 

To compare different moduli, write an orbit modulo m as 

Cm(γ) = {qj γ mod m : j ≥ 0}, τm(γ) = |Cm(γ)|,

and let Cm be the finite set of all such orbits. Theorem 5.5 gives 

τm(γ) = ord m/ gcd (m,γ )(q), ord 1(q) = 1 .

If m | n, reduction commutes with multiplication by q, inducing a map 

πn,m : Cn −→ C m, Cn(γ) 7 −→ Cm(γ).

It is surjective: choose a representative of a parent orbit, lift it to an integer modulo n,and take its orbit. For l | m | n, we also have πn,l = πm,l πn,m .

## 5.9.2 Affine Return on a Lifting Fiber 

A fiber of a map consists of all elements mapped to a specified point; see Section 6.2. 

Theorem 5.61 (Lifting cyclotomic cosets by return maps) Let m | n, r = n/m, choose

## 5.9.4 Admissible Digits and Compatible Representatives 

If each step of the divisibility chain multiplies by one prime, so Ni+1 = `iNi with 

`i 6 = p, the return permutations give coordinates at successive levels. Fix an initial representative 0 ≤ γ0 < N 0, and put τ0 = τN0 (γ0). At step i, denote (5.20) by Ti, let 

D(Ti) be the set of least nonnegative representatives of its orbits, and define recursively 

ki ∈ D(Ti), γi+1 = γi + Niki, τi+1 = τi | Orb Ti (ki)|. (5.24) Call (ki)i≥0 an admissible digit path . Every path gives a system with initial term 

CN0 (γ0), and every such system has exactly one path: given the parent orbit and its representative, the return-lifting theorem puts all child orbits in bijection with D(Ti),so both the successive choices and their inverses are unique. The recursion also ensures 

0 ≤ γi < N i, γi+1 ≡ γi (mod Ni).

Thus it produces compatible representatives, not just compatible orbits. Any divisibility chain can be refined by factoring each successive quotient into primes and inserting finitely many intermediate levels. The orbit at an intermediate level is uniquely determined by reduction from a higher level, so this refinement preserves the original compatibility information. For local systems, take N0 = m and `i = `. For total systems, take N0 = 1 and a sequence of lifting primes in which every ` 6 = p occurs infinitely often. Then every n coprime to p divides some Ni, and its orbit is obtained by reduction from that level; all sufficiently high levels give the same result. Chapter 5 Roots of Unity, Base Extension, and Tensor Product Decompositions 121 

A compatible representative γi need not be the coset leader λNi (γi) of the entire orbit CNi (γi). Choosing the coset leader independently at each level still represents the same system, but may violate γi+1 ≡ γi (mod Ni), so the original digit recursion cannot simply be continued with those representatives. For subsequent returns, retain the representatives chosen in (5.24). A total system restricts to a local system along each prime-power chain starting at modulus one, but these local systems generally do not uniquely determine the total system. The CRT decomposition in Section 5.8 shows that, after fixing the local orbits, their relative phases under simultaneous traversal must also be recorded. For example, the two global unit orbits modulo fifteen have the same local images modulo three and five; these phases may change at higher prime-power levels. Compatible systems link local-to-global combination at one level with factor lifting across levels. 

## 5.9.5 Stable Growth of Local Systems 

Once a prime direction is fixed, the lengths in a compatible system are determined by the first deviation and the local multiplicative orders. We give the exact level from which all lifts are unique and translate it into a substitution formula for irreducible factors. This local classification is given in [73, 75]. Let ` 6 = p be prime, let gcd (m, p` ) = 1 , and fix a base-level orbit Cm(γ), with 

0 ≤ γ < m . Put

ηi ≡ γ (mod m), ηi ≡ 0 (mod `i).

The orbits Pi = CNi (ηi) are compatible and have length τ at every level. We call 

(Pi)i≥0 the principal cyclotomic system above Cm(γ). It is the unique system whose coordinate modulo `i is zero at every level. For any system (Ci)i≥0 different from the principal system, there is a unique u ≥ 0

such that 

Ci = Pi (0 ≤ i ≤ u), Cu+1 6 = Pu+1 .

We call u its deviation depth . At level u + 1 , every index in the orbit is divisible by 

`u but not by `u+1 ; compatibility preserves this valuation at all higher levels. 122 Chapter 5 Roots of Unity, Base Extension, and Tensor Product Decompositions
