# 5.10 Galois Rings and Lifting of Roots-of-Unity Fac-tors 

Over a finite field, roots-of-unity factors are determined by Frobenius orbits. Over a Galois ring of characteristic ps, roots of unity of order coprime to p retain the same or-bit structure, while the coefficients of their factors are uniquely determined by coprime Hensel lifting. When p | n, the residual root orbits correspond to canonical comax-imal blocks. For the standard theory of Galois rings, see [62]; for lifting cyclotomic cosets and multiple equal-difference structure, see [76]. Below, s is the exponent in the characteristic ps, and q = pr is fixed. 

## 5.10.1 Quotient Ring Models and Coprime Hensel Lifting Chapter 5 Roots of Unity, Base Extension, and Tensor Product Decompositions 129 

Definition 5.74 (Galois rings and basic irreducible polynomials) Let p be prime, s, r ≥

1, and let P ∈ (Z/psZ)[ T ] be monic of degree r, with irreducible reduction P modulo p.The ring 

A = ( Z/psZ)[ T ]/( P )

is called a Galois ring , denoted by GR (ps, r ). Its isomorphism type depends only on 

p, s, r . A polynomial G ∈ A[X] is called basic irreducible if it is monic and G ∈ Fq[X]

is irreducible. Here and below, reduction is coefficientwise modulo p. The second parameter r is the degree of the residue field over Fp. In particular, GR (p, r ) ∼= Fpr and GR (ps, 1) ∼= Z/psZ.A commutative ring with a unique maximal ideal is called a local ring ; its quotient by that maximal ideal is called its residue field . A commutative ring whose ideals are totally ordered by inclusion is called a chain ring .

Proposition 5.75 (Units, the residue field, and the ideal chain) The ring A has charac-teristic ps, cardinality psr , and unique maximal ideal pA , with A/pA ∼= Fq. An element 

u ∈ A is invertible if and only if u 6 = 0 . Every nonzero element determines a unique 

0 ≤ j < s for which it can be written as pj u with u a unit. All ideals form the chain 

A ⊃ pA ⊃ · · · ⊃ ps−1A ⊃ psA = 0 , Ann A(pj ) = ps−j A (0 ≤ j ≤ s).

Proof. Monic division shows that the images of 1, T, . . . , T r−1 form a basis of A over 

Z/psZ. Thus its characteristic is ps, its cardinality is psr , and its quotient modulo p is 

Fp[T ]/( P ) ∼= Fq. If u 6 = 0 , lifting its inverse gives uv = 1 + pw . Since (pw )s = 0 , a finite geometric sum gives the inverse of 1 + pw , so u is a unit. Conversely, a unit reduces to a unit. The least p-adic valuation among the basis coordinates of a nonzero element is j < s ; after extracting pj , the remaining element has nonzero reduction. Thus j is unique, and the least such j in a nonzero ideal determines that ideal as pj A. The same basis coordinates directly give the annihilator identity. The nonunits are exactly pA , so it is the unique maximal ideal. 

Lemma 5.76 (Hensel lifting of simple roots) Let f ∈ A[X], and suppose a ∈ Fq

satisfies f (a) = 0 , f ′(a) 6 = 0 . There is a unique a ∈ A with f (a) = 0 and a mod p = a.This process is called Hensel lifting .

Proof. If aj satisfies f (aj ) ≡ 0 ( mod pj ), 1 ≤ j < s , then f (aj )/ pj mod p is well defined: any two quotients differ by an element of Ann A(pj ) = ps−j A ⊆ pA . Put 

aj+1 = aj + pj δj , δj = −f (aj )

pj f ′(a)−1 in Fq.130 Chapter 5 Roots of Unity, Base Extension, and Tensor Product Decompositions 

On expansion, all correction terms of degree at least two contain p2j and vanish modulo 

pj+1 , so f (aj+1 ) ≡ 0 ( mod pj+1 ). Every lift must satisfy the same linear correction equation, so each level is unique. Iteration to j = s gives the desired root; for s = 1 ,the result is immediate.

In general, if ideals I, J in a commutative ring R satisfy I + J = R, choose u ∈ I

For t ∈ T (A), both φ(t) and tp are Teichmüller representatives of the same residue class, so φ(t) = tp. A ring homomorphism preserves p, giving the digit formula. The map φr reduces to the identity, and the same root uniqueness gives φr = id. The reduction has order r, so φ has order exactly r. The digit formula shows that every digit of a fixed element reduces to an element of Fp. Applying the same simple-root lifting and digit expansion within Z/psZ shows that these elements form precisely that subring. This proof also shows that the isomorphism type of a Galois ring is independent of the choice of P . In another quotient ring with the same parameters, send α by a residue-field isomorphism to a root of P , then lift it uniquely to a root of P , obtaining a ring homomorphism. Its reduction modulo p is an isomorphism, and the image of every nonzero element pj u, j < s , remains nonzero, so it is injective; equality of cardinalities makes it an isomorphism. For a positive integer d, the same method embeds A in S = GR (ps, rd ): first embed the residue fields Fq ⊆ Fqd , then lift the corresponding simple root of P . Distinct ξb have distinct reductions, so their differences are units; hence the factors

Example 5.86 (The coset twist in residue degree two) Take R = GR (4 , 2) =(Z/4 Z)[ ω]/( ω2 + ω + 1) . Here ω3 = 1 , and the residue field is F4. For X6 − 1,we have pa = 2 and m = 3. The four-cyclotomic cosets modulo three are

BC1 = ( X − ω)2, FC1 (X2) = ( X − ω 2)2.

Omitting 2C1 = C2 assigns the block for C2 to C1, although the product of all blocks remains unchanged. Also, BC1 = ( X − ω)( X + ω); these two linear factors have the same reduction modulo two and are not comaximal. Moreover, 

BC1 − (X − ω)2 = 2 ω(X − ω) 6 = 0 .

Thus this smallest nontrivial residue-field extension displays the coset twist, Chinese remainder decomposition into blocks, and repeated-root factorization within a block at once.

Inside a block, we still have X3 − 1 = ( X − 1)( X2 + X + 1) , but these two factors are not comaximal: their reductions modulo 3 are X − 1 and (X − 1) 2. # Trace, Norm, and Conjugate Coordinates 

Sums and products along conjugate orbits give trace and norm. They are also the trace and determinant of multiplication operators and govern Frobenius difference equations. Equivariant splitting of the trace further reveals the interaction between the character-istic and the extension degree. 

# 6.1 Orbit Sums and Orbit Products

They are also called the relative trace and relative norm over k. When k = Fp is the prime field, Tr E/Fp is called the absolute trace .Frobenius cyclically permutes the terms in the sum and product, so both values are fixed by σ and hence belong to k. The trace is k-linear, and the norm on E×

is a homomorphism of multiplicative groups. For c ∈ k, we have Tr E/k(c) = nc and NE/k(c) = cn. Here n denotes its image in the field, which may be zero. If d = [ k(a) : k], the conjugate orbit has only d distinct elements, but the definitions above still have n terms. # 6.2 Surjectivity and Fiber Sizes 

For a map h : S → T and a fixed element t of the target, the set of all elements mapped to t,

h−1(t) = {x ∈ S : h(x) = t}

is called the fiber of h over t. Here h−1(t) is the preimage of the singleton {t}; it does not require h to have an inverse. Fibers may be empty; the nonempty fibers are disjoint and their union is the whole domain S. For example, the trace fiber over c ∈ k

is {x ∈ E : Tr E/k(x) = c}, and the fiber of the norm on the multiplicative group over 

c ∈ k× is {x ∈ E× : NE/k(x) = c}. A fiber is always understood relative to a specified map and domain. Chapter 6 Trace, Norm, and Conjugate Coordinates 145 

Theorem 6.3 The trace Tr E/k : E → k is surjective, with qn−1 elements in each fiber. The norm N E/k : E× → k× is also surjective, with (qn − 1)/( q − 1) preimages of each nonzero value. 

Proof. The trace is given by the nonzero polynomial X + Xq + · · · + Xqn−1

, whose degree qn−1 < q n prevents it from vanishing at every element of E. Thus it is a nonzero linear map to the one-dimensional k-space k, and is surjective. Its kernel has dimension 

n − 1. If x0 has trace c, then Tr (x) = c is equivalent to x − x0 ∈ ker Tr, so the fiber is 

x0 + ker Tr, of size qn−1.Choose a generator ζ of E×. The element N E/k(ζ) = ζ(qn−1)/( q−1) has order q − 1,and hence generates k×. If N (x0) = c 6 = 0 , then N (x) = c is equivalent to x−10 x ∈ ker N. Thus the fiber is the multiplicative coset x0 ker N, whose size follows by counting kernel and image of the group homomorphism. 

Remark 6.4 When p | n, we have Tr E/k(1) = 0 , but the trace map is still nonzero. A linear operator P with P 2 = P is called a projection; it maps the whole space onto im P

and acts identically on that image. The trace operator itself need not be a projection: viewing k as a subspace of E, it satisfies Tr 2 = n Tr. Only when p - n does n−1 Tr define a projection onto k.

Example 6.5 In E = F3(α), with α2 = −1, we have α3 = −α. For x = a + bα ,Tr E/F3 (x) = 2 a, NE/F3 (x) = a2 + b2.

In F4/F2, however, Tr (1) = 0 ; if β2 + β + 1 = 0 , then Tr (β) = 1 .

Norm preservation and linear structure. The nonzero norm fibers are multiplica-tive cosets of ker N E/k. If a k-linear map T : E → E preserves the norm of every element, then T (x) − T (y) = T (x − y), so it also preserves the norm of every nonzero difference. A condition on norm fibers thus becomes a compatibility condition between addition and multiplication. When |k| > 2, such a map must be multiplication by a norm-one element followed by a k-automorphism; see Exercise 6.13. This is the finite-field case of Lenstra’s norm-form theorem [33, Theorem 4]; the solution explains the mechanism using the difference-quotient rigidity established later. 146 Chapter 6 Trace, Norm, and Conjugate Coordinates 

# 6.3 Compatibility of Multiple Norms and Joint Fibers 

When norms to two subfields are prescribed separately, surjectivity of each norm does not ensure that one element realizes both values. Their norms to the intersection must agree; multiplicative cyclicity turns this into compatibility of integer congruences. The following result also appears in [27, Lemma 3.1]. Let d1, . . . , d s | n, and put Li = Fqdi ⊆ E. Given nonzero values ai ∈ L×

Li ∩ Lj . The elements x ∈ E× simultaneously satisfying N E/Li (x) = ai form the joint fiber of the norm map x 7 → (NE/Li (x)) i.

# 6.4 Two Hilbert 90 Identities 

Theorem 6.8 (Additive and multiplicative Hilbert 90) We have ker Tr E/k = {bq − b : b ∈ E},

ker (NE/k : E× → k×) = {bq−1 : b ∈ E×}.

Proof. For every b, Tr (σ(b) − b) = 0 , by cancellation in the sum. The kernel of σ − id is 

k, so its image has k-dimension n − 1. The trace kernel has the same dimension; hence the two coincide. Similarly, N (σ(b)/ b) = 1 . The homomorphism b 7 → bq−1 has kernel k×, so its image has (qn − 1)/( q − 1) elements, exactly the size of the norm kernel. 148 Chapter 6 Trace, Norm, and Conjugate Coordinates 

Example 6.9 (A Frobenius difference equation with trace-zero right-hand side) Reuse 

E = F9 = F3(α), α2 = −1, from Example 3.12; the new question concerns the image and fibers of the Frobenius difference. For x = u + vα , we have 

x3 − x = ( u − vα ) − (u + vα ) = vα. 

Thus the image is the one-dimensional space F3α, while ker (x 7 → x3 − x) = F3. Also, Tr (u + vα ) = 2 u, so the trace-zero space is likewise F3α. The solutions of x3 − x = α are 

α, α + 1 , α + 2 , while x3 − x = 1 has no solution. This exhibits both the image identity in Hilbert 90 and the coset structure of each nonempty fiber. Thus xq −x = a is solvable in E if and only if Tr E/k(a) = 0 , and then has q solutions. For a 6 = 0 , the equation xq−1 = a is solvable if and only if N E/k(a) = 1 , and then has 

q − 1 solutions. These equations turn additive orbit differences and multiplicative orbit ratios, respectively, into one condition over the base field.

# 6.5 Trace, Differences, and Equivariant Decomposi-tion 

Put D = σ − id. Additive Hilbert 90 and surjectivity of the trace together give 

0 −→ k −→ E D

−−→ E Tr E/k

−−−−→ k −→ 0. (6.6) Exactness means that the image of each map is the kernel of the next. This expresses two facts: Frobenius differences annihilate base-field constants, and an element is a Frobenius difference if and only if its trace is zero. Let σ act on the two copies of E,and let the identity act on the two copies of k. All maps above are then equivariant. In particular, equivariance of P : E → k means P σ = P ; viewing its values in E, this is also equivalent to P σ = σP .

Proposition 6.11 Regard Tr = Tr E/k as a linear operator taking values in E. Then Tr 2 = n Tr. If p - n, there is a Frobenius-equivariant direct-sum decomposition

n Tr : E → k,

Proof. For c ∈ k, we have Tr (c) = nc . Since Tr (x) ∈ k, this gives Tr (Tr (x)) = n Tr (x).If p - n, then P 2 = P and P |k = id, while P σ = P = σP , giving the direct sum. The space ker Tr is D-stable, and ker (D|ker Tr ) = k ∩ ker Tr = {0}.

Finite dimensionality gives invertibility. If p | n, every base-field element has trace zero, so k ⊆ im D. Suppose such a map 

P exists. Since its values lie in k, commutation means P σ = P , and hence P D = 0 .But 1 ∈ im D, so P (1) = 0 , contradicting P |k = id. When p | n, the k-vector space E still admits a complement to k, but no such complement is Frobenius-stable. # 6.10 Root Ratios and Coefficient Criteria for Primi-tive Quadratics 

For a monic irreducible quadratic, the trace and norm of a root determine the linear and constant coefficients, while the multiplicative order of the ratio of its conjugate roots is its projective order. Translating the multiplicative order of this ratio into coefficient conditions gives primitivity criteria, counts with fixed constant term, and the minimal binomial multiple. For related descriptions of primitive quadratics, see [60, 61]; for background on Lucas atoms, see [52]. The following construction of optimal determining polynomials over finite fields is given in [69]. Throughout this section, fix 

k = Fq of characteristic p, and put N = q + 1 .

## 6.10.1 Root Ratios, Recurrence Remainders, and Projective Or-der 

In the context of binomial multiples, projective order is also called binomial order ;the quasi-order in [60] has the same definition. Chapter 6 Trace, Norm, and Conjugate Coordinates 157 

Proposition 6.23 (Quadratic primitivity and root ratios) Let f = X2 +bX +c ∈ k[X],with c 6 = 0 , and let its roots be θ1, θ 2. Then f is primitive if and only if c generates k×

and ord (θ1/θ2) = q + 1 .

Proof. If f is irreducible, its roots are θ, θ q, and θq+1 = c. Proposition 4.17 gives its projective order as ord (θ/θq); Proposition 4.16 then gives the equivalent conditions for primitivity. Conversely, if the root ratio has order q + 1 , then f is irreducible: otherwise both roots lie in k, and their ratio has order dividing q − 1, which cannot equal q + 1 .The equivalence above then applies.

Expressing it as a function of a parameter for the pair is called norm descent here.

# Trace Duality, Bases, and Coordinate Recovery 

The trace pairing identifies field elements with linear functionals, and conjugate coor-dinates express this pairing as a matrix. Dual bases recover coordinates, while relative trace is adjoint to subfield inclusion, linking subfield structure to linear orthogonality. 

# 7.1 Nondegeneracy of the Trace Pairing 

Fix k = Fq ⊆ E = Fqn . Define the trace pairing by 

B(x, y ) = Tr E/k(xy ).

It is a symmetric k-bilinear form. A bilinear form is also called a bilinear pairing. The 

radical of a symmetric pairing B is rad B = {x ∈ E : B(x, y ) = 0 for every y ∈ E}.

A pairing is nondegenerate if its radical is zero. Vectors in the radical pair to zero with every vector. A linear functional is a linear map to the base field. The space 

E∨ = Hom k(E, k ) of all such maps is the dual space. 

Theorem 7.1 The trace pairing is nondegenerate: if B(x, y ) = 0 for every y ∈ E,then x = 0 . Thus every k-linear functional λ : E → k has a unique expression λ(x) = 

Tr E/k(ax ), with a ∈ E.

Proof. If x 6 = 0 , choose z with Tr (z) = 1 by surjectivity of the trace, and set y = z/x.Then B(x, y ) = 1 . Hence the pairing is nondegenerate. The map E → Hom k(E, k ),

a 7 → (x 7 → Tr (ax )) , is therefore injective. Its domain and codomain both have dimension 

n, so it is an isomorphism. 171 172 Chapter 7 Trace Duality, Bases, and Coordinate Recovery

# 7.3 Coefficient Pairings, Derivatives, and Algebra Trace 

When the conjugate roots are distinct, interpolation expresses the coefficient functional as a trace. Quotient algebras with repeated factors still retain the coefficient functional, but its relation to the trace involves an additional derivative factor that may fail to be invertible. 

## 7.3.1 The Derivative Formula and Nondegeneracy 

For a finite-dimensional commutative k-algebra A, define its algebra trace by Tr A/k(u) = tr (Mu), Mu(v) = uv. 

The right-hand side is the matrix trace of a linear operator and is independent of the basis. If k is finite and A/k is a finite field extension, Proposition 6.22 identifies it with the field trace defined by the conjugate orbit. 

Theorem 7.7 (Coefficient pairings, derivatives, and algebra trace) Let k be any field, let f ∈ k[T ] be monic with deg f = d ≥ 1, and put A = k[T ]/( f ) and α = T . Proposition 7.8 (The algebra trace pairing and separability) Let k be any field, let

(7.5) These conditions are also equivalent to separability of f , that is, to having no repeated roots in a splitting field. If moreover k = Fq, they are equivalent to A being reduced, and to u 7 → uq being an automorphism of A. When these conditions hold, the coefficient functional in Theorem 7.7 satisfies

.Chapter 7 Trace Duality, Bases, and Coordinate Recovery 177 

Proof. By the trace formula in Theorem 7.7 and nondegeneracy of the coefficient pairing, an element u pairs to zero with every v under the trace pairing if and only if f ′(α)u = 0 .Thus nondegeneracy of the trace pairing is equivalent to injectivity of multiplication by f ′(α). Finite dimensionality makes this equivalent to surjectivity, and hence to invertibility of f ′(α). Bézout’s identity makes this equivalent to gcd (f, f ′) = 1 . The derivative criterion identifies gcd (f, f ′) = 1 with separability of f ; the base field need not be finite here. Now assume k = Fq. Finite fields are perfect, so f is separable if and only if f has no repeated irreducible factor. If f has no repeated factor, the Chinese remainder theorem expresses A as a product of finite fields, so A is reduced. If f has repeated factors, let r be the product of its distinct monic irreducible factors. Then r(α) 6 = 0 , but a sufficiently high power of this element is zero, so A is not reduced. The equivalence between reducedness and invertibility of Frobenius follows from Theorem 3.23. Finally, replacing u by u/f ′(α) in (7.4) gives the last formula. Write Bλ(u, v ) = λ(uv ) and BTr (u, v ) = Tr A/k(uv ). The trace formula gives 

BTr (u, v ) = Bλ

(f ′(α)u, v ).

Thus passing from the coefficient pairing to the trace pairing amounts to applying the multiplication operator Mf ′(α) to the first argument. Nondegeneracy of the coefficient pairing uses only standard remainders and their leading terms; it does not require distinct roots. For the trace pairing to remain nondegenerate, this additional multipli-cation operator must be invertible. With repeated factors, the operator has a nonzero kernel, so the trace pairing loses information in some directions. The coefficient pairing therefore applies to every monic nonconstant polynomial, whereas nondegeneracy of the algebra trace pairing is characterized exactly by separability. Over a finite base field, Proposition 7.4 is the case in which A is a field. In the square-free but reducible case, the algebra trace is the sum of the traces of the field components, and the derivative-normalized coefficient formula still holds. Section 16.2 uses the coefficient pairing to parameterize the solution space of a recurrence, retaining the nilpotent structure associated with repeated factors. 178 Chapter 7 Trace Duality, Bases, and Coordinate Recovery 

Corollary 7.9 (A trace criterion for reduced algebras) Let A be a finite-dimensional commutative k = Fq-algebra. Then A is reduced if and only if its algebra trace pairing is nondegenerate. 

Proof. If A is reduced, Theorem 3.23 expresses it as a product ∏ 

> i

Ei of finite fields. The multiplication matrices are block diagonal, so the algebra trace is the sum of the component field traces. Each field trace pairing is nondegenerate, and so is their direct sum. Conversely, if A is not reduced, choose a nonzero nilpotent element u. For every 

v ∈ A, commutativity implies that uv is nilpotent, so the multiplication operator Muv is nilpotent and has matrix trace zero. Thus u pairs to zero with every v, and the pairing is degenerate.

We use the definitions of local ring and residue field on page 129. An ideal m is called a nilpotent ideal if me = 0 for some positive integer e, that is, if every product of e of its elements is zero. For a monic irreducible polynomial P ∈ k[T ] and a positive integer e, put 

RP = k[T ]/( P e), m = ( P ), KP = k[T ]/( P ).

Bézout’s identity shows that an element of RP is invertible if and only if its image modulo P is nonzero. Thus the nonunits form exactly m. The quotient RP /m ' KP is a field, and no proper ideal contains a unit, so m is the unique maximal ideal. Moreover, 

me = 0 . This model retains both the field associated with an irreducible factor and the nilpotent structure recorded by its multiplicity.

If p - ei, the exponent of Pi in gcd (f, f ′) is exactly ei − 1; if p | ei, it is ei. Comparing degrees gives the second formula, including the case f ′ = 0 .Formula (7.6) shows that the algebra trace takes the residue-field trace in each component, weights it by the multiplicity, and sums the results. The trace pairing vanishes whenever one argument is nilpotent. If the multiplicity vanishes in the base field, the entire residue-field contribution vanishes as well. Section 16.2 retains the coefficient functional λ precisely to distinguish these directions and their shift action. The unit norm equation in Chapter 9 is likewise first solved over the residue field; lifting errors must then be corrected in the nilpotent ideal (Lemma 9.54). Thus residue-field traces and multiplicities determine the algebra trace, whereas solving unit norm equations also requires the original local ring. 

Remark 7.12 (The role of perfectness in the reducedness criterion) The coefficient pairing and derivative formula of Theorem 7.7 hold over any base field, as does the separability criterion in Proposition 7.8. Identifying separability further with reduced-ness of the quotient algebra uses perfectness of the base field. For example, take an indeterminate u and put k = Fp(up) and E = Fp(u). Example A.6 in the appendix proves that 

E ' k[T ]/( T p − up), [E : k] = p. 

This algebra is a field and hence reduced, but its defining polynomial has zero deriva-tive, so (7.4) gives Tr E/k = 0 . Surjectivity of Frobenius over finite fields ensures that irreducible polynomials are separable, excluding this reduced but inseparable case. ## 7.3.3 The Periodic Part of Frobenius and the Reduced Quotient 

In a finite-dimensional commutative algebra, the ideal of nilpotent elements is the nil-radical . The following proposition also proves that these elements form an ideal and realizes the reduced quotient inside the original algebra by means of periodic points of Frobenius. 

Proposition 7.13 (The periodic part of Frobenius and the reduced quotient) Let 

A 6 = 0 be a finite-dimensional commutative k = Fq-algebra, and put 

F : A −→ A, F (a) = aq, n = {a ∈ A : am = 0 for some m ≥ 1}.

Write 

Aper = {a ∈ A : F m(a) = a for some m ≥ 1}.

Then n is an ideal, Aper is a reduced k-subalgebra, and 

A = Aper ⊕ n, Aper 

> ∼

−−→ A/n. (7.8) The first identity is a direct sum of k-vector spaces; the second is induced by restricting the natural quotient map. For sufficiently large r,ker F r = n, im F r = Aper .

There is a positive integer N such that F N is an algebra projection onto Aper with kernel 

n. Moreover, Aper is the unique k-subalgebra mapped isomorphically onto A/n by the natural quotient map. 

Proof. Since A is commutative and k = Fq, F is both an algebra homomorphism and a 

k-linear map. Finite dimensionality ensures that the ascending chain of kernels and the descending chain of images both stabilize. Choose r ≥ 1 such that both are stable from step r onward, and put B = im F r. Each ker F j is an ideal. An element is nilpotent if and only if some iterate of the q-th power map sends it to zero, so 

n = ⋃

> j≥1

ker F j = ker F r.

This also proves that n is an ideal. Stability of the image gives F (B) = B. Thus F |B is surjective on a finite-dimensional space, hence bijective. The set B is finite, so all its elements are periodic under F .Conversely, if F m(a) = a, choose jm ≥ r; then a = F jm (a) ∈ B. Hence B = Aper . In particular, the periodic points form a unital k-subalgebra. 182 Chapter 7 Trace Duality, Bases, and Coordinate Recovery 

If a ∈ B ∩ n, then F r(a) = 0 . Since F r|B is injective, a = 0 . The rank–nullity theorem gives dim B + dim n = dim A, whence A = B ⊕ n. The quotient map restricted to B is therefore a bijective algebra homomorphism. Since B has no nonzero nilpotents, it is reduced. Reducedness of the quotient can also be checked directly: if am ∈ n, then 

a is nilpotent, so a ∈ n.Let M be the order of the permutation F |B , and choose N ≥ r with M | N . For the unique decomposition a = b + u with b ∈ B, u ∈ n, we have F N (a) = b. Thus F N

is the required projection and satisfies (F N )2 = F N .Finally, suppose a subalgebra C ⊆ A maps isomorphically onto A/n under the quotient map. Then C is reduced. Its Frobenius is injective, hence bijective by finiteness. Every element of C is therefore periodic, giving C ⊆ B. Both have dimension dim (A/n),so C = B.

## 7.3.4 Quadratic Quotient Algebras and Product Coordinates of Root Sets 

Reduction of a root polynomial modulo a low-degree polynomial retains only part of the root-set data. A quadratic quotient turns these data into a norm-one product, a ratio of two values, or a sum of reciprocals. The factorization type of the modulus determines which form occurs. ## 7.3.5 Weighted trace forms and symmetric multiplication matri-ces 

Let E = Fqn and k = Fq. For λ ∈ E×, define the nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form 

Bλ(x, y ) = Tr E/k(λxy ).

Relative to a nondegenerate symmetric pairing B, a linear operator A is called self-adjoint if B(Ax, y ) = B(x, Ay ) for all x, y . Equivalently, A∗ = A; the general definition and existence and uniqueness of the adjoint map are given at 7.4 below. 

Proposition 7.19 (Self-adjoint multiplication and simultaneous symmetric matrices) For all a, x, y ∈ E, one has Bλ(ax, y ) = Bλ(x, ay ). Moreover, there exist λ ∈ E× and a k-basis of E in which the matrices of all multiplication operators ma : x 7 → ax are symmetric. 

Proof. Self-adjointness follows from λaxy = λxay . It suffices to give some Bλ an or-thonormal basis. We use the classification criterion in Lemma 7.25 below; its proof is independent of this proposition. Fix a k-basis, let Gλ be the Gram matrix of Bλ, and set D1 = det G1 ∈ k×. If Mλ is the matrix of multiplication by λ, then Gλ = G1Mλ, so det Gλ = NE/k(λ)D1.

When q is odd, surjectivity of the norm allows a choice of λ making this determinant a nonzero square; Lemma 7.25 then supplies an orthonormal basis. When q is even, 

Bλ(x, x ) = Tr (λx 2) is not identically zero, since the trace pairing is nondegenerate and squaring is bijective. The form is therefore nonalternating, and the same lemma again supplies an orthonormal basis. In such a basis the Gram matrix is the identity, so self-adjointness makes every Ma equal to its transpose. 

Remark 7.20 The weighted form need not equal the ordinary trace form B1. Simul-taneous symmetry of multiplication matrices does not assert that the ordinary trace pairing admits a self-dual basis. For the standard classification of bilinear forms see [45].

# 7.6 Existence of Self-Dual Bases 

A basis equal to its dual basis, that is, satisfying Tr (bibj ) = δij , is called a self-dual basis . No normality condition is imposed here. 

Lemma 7.25 On a finite-dimensional space of positive dimension over a finite field 

k, a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form admits a basis with identity Gram matrix if and only if: (1) in characteristic different from two, its Gram determinant is a square in k;(2) in characteristic two, it is not an alternating form, that is, some v satisfies B(v, v ) 6 =0.

Proof. First suppose the characteristic is not two. If B(v, v ) = 0 for every vector, then 

2B(x, y ) = B(x + y, x + y) − B(x, x ) − B(y, y ) = 0 

for all x, y , contradicting nondegeneracy. Thus one can choose v with B(v, v ) 6 = 0 .Every vector x has a unique decomposition 

x = B(x, v )

B(v, v ) v +

(

x − B(x, v )

B(v, v ) v

)

∈ kv ⊕ (kv )⊥.

The restriction to the orthogonal complement remains nondegenerate: a vector there orthogonal to both the complement and v is orthogonal to the entire space and hence is zero. Induction gives a diagonal Gram matrix with nonzero entries. For any a, b ∈ k×, the sets {ax 2 : x ∈ k} and {1 − by 2 : y ∈ k} each contain (q + 1)/2 

elements, so they intersect. Thus the binary diagonal form ax 2 + by 2 represents 1, and a line with Gram coefficient 1 splits off. Its orthogonal complement is a nondegener-ate line whose coefficient has square class ab , since a change of basis multiplies the determinant by a nonzero square. Applying this operation successively to two as yet unnormalized diagonal entries gives diag (1 , . . . , 1, c ), where c has the square class of the original determinant. If the determinant is a square, scaling also gives coefficient 1 on the last line. Necessity follows from the same change-of-basis formula for determinants; the conclusion includes the one-dimensional case. Now suppose the characteristic is two. The form with identity matrix is not alter-nating, so this condition is necessary. If some v satisfies B(v, v ) 6 = 0 , the squaring map is bijective on a finite field, so v can be scaled to have self-pairing 1. The same orthog-onal decomposition successively splits off unit lines until the orthogonal complement is 190 Chapter 7 Trace Duality, Bases, and Coordinate Recovery 

zero or is a nondegenerate alternating space. A nondegenerate alternating space decom-poses into two-dimensional blocks: choose u 6 = 0 and, by nondegeneracy, choose v with 

B(u, v ) = 1 . The matrix on (u, v ) is then ( 0 1 1 0 ); split off this block and apply induction to its orthogonal complement. At least one unit line kw has already been obtained. If u, v is an alternating block orthogonal to w, then 

w + u, w + v, w + u + v

each have self-pairing 1, and their pairwise pairings are 1 + 1 = 0 . Their Gram matrix is the identity, so they are linearly independent and form a basis of this three-dimensional space. Thus one unit line and one alternating block can be replaced by three unit lines. Repeating this for each block gives an orthonormal basis of the entire space. 

Theorem 7.26 The extension Fqn /Fq admits a self-dual basis if and only if q is even or both q, n are odd. 

Proof. If q is even, B(x, x ) = Tr (x2) = Tr (x)2. The trace is surjective, so the form is not alternating; the preceding lemma gives a self-dual basis. Suppose q is odd. Choose any k-basis b0, . . . , b n−1 and put 

V = ( bqi 

> j

)0≤i,j<n , D = det V. 

Theorem 6.21 shows that V is invertible, so D 6 = 0 . The Gram matrix is V TV and has determinant D2. Raising D to the q-th power cyclically permutes the rows of V ,so Dq = ( −1) n−1D. If n is odd, then D ∈ k and the determinant is a square. If n is even, then D /∈ k; but any square root of D2 in k would have to equal D or −D, a contradiction. The determinant is therefore a nonsquare. The preceding lemma proves the result. This criterion comes from the Frobenius action on the determinant of the matrix of conjugates. Self-duality is a coordinate condition, whereas normality requires the basis vectors to form a single Frobenius orbit. # Linearized Polynomials and Operator Algebras 

Finite-dimensional subspaces of finite extensions have linearized root polynomials. Com-position corresponds to operator multiplication, while the condition that the coefficients lie in the base field determines whether the operator commutes with Frobenius. Trace adjoints relate kernels to images. 

# 8.1 Polynomial Representations of Linear Maps 

Let k = Fq ⊆ E = Fqn , as before. Whenever all roots of a polynomial are considered in this chapter, we work in a finite extension over which it splits completely; when considering a kernel on E, we take only the roots belonging to E. A polynomial of the form 

L(X) = a0X + a1Xq + · · · + asXqs

, ai ∈ E, 

is called a q-linearized polynomial . If as 6 = 0 , then s is its q-degree; its ordinary degree is qs. The map L is k-linear on every extension field containing its coefficients, since the qth-power map preserves addition and fixes k. Its zero set is therefore a linear subspace, called the root space of L.

Proposition 8.1 The roots of a nonzero linearized polynomial of q-degree s form a 

k-vector space of dimension at most s. The polynomial has no repeated roots if and only if a0 6 = 0 .

Proof. The root set is the kernel of a linear map and hence is a subspace. The usual bound on the number of roots gives at most qs roots, so the dimension is at most s.The derivative is the constant a0. If it is nonzero, there are no repeated roots. If it is 193 194 Chapter 8 Linearized Polynomials and Operator Algebras 

zero, all exponents are divisible by p; taking pth roots of the coefficients in the finite coefficient field expresses L as the pth power of a nonconstant polynomial, so it has repeated roots. If a0 6 = 0 , then L has qs distinct roots in its splitting field, so its full root space has dimension exactly s; its kernel in a fixed field E may have smaller dimension. Section 8.5 treats all roots and their multiplicities, while Corollary 9.11 describes the kernels in finite extensions when the coefficients lie in k.

Theorem 8.2 (Polynomial representations of all linear maps) Every k-linear map 

A : E → E has a unique representation 

A(x) = a0x + a1xq + · · · + an−1xqn−1

, ai ∈ E. 

Proof. The coefficient tuples form an n2-dimensional k-space, and End k(E) also has dimension n2. If two representations define the same function, their difference vanishes on all qn elements of E, whereas a nonzero difference polynomial has degree at most 

qn−1 and cannot have so many roots. The map from coefficient tuples to linear maps is therefore injective, and comparing dimensions proves surjectivity.

# 8.3 Composition and Operator Polynomials 

Multiplication of linear maps means composition, rather than pointwise multiplication of their values. For example, (aX q) ◦ (bX q) = ab qXq2

, which generally differs from 

(bX q) ◦ (aX q). Thus linearized polynomials with coefficients in E generally do not commute under composition. When all coefficients lie in k, define, for a(T ) = ∑ aiT i ∈ k[T ],

La(X) = ∑ aiXqi

.

Then La+b = La + Lb and Lab = La ◦ L b. The constant polynomial 1 corresponds to the identity map X. On E, we have La = a(σ), where σ(x) = xq.

Theorem 8.8 (Kernel dimension and the greatest common divisor) For a ∈ k[T ], let 

h = gcd (a, T n − 1) be the monic greatest common divisor. Then ker (a(σ) : E → E) = ker h(σ), dim k ker a(σ) = deg h. 

In particular, a(σ) is invertible if and only if gcd (a, T n − 1) = 1 .

Proof. Since T n − 1 6 = 0 , the monic greatest common divisor h is defined even when 

a = 0 . Bézout’s identity gives h = ua + v(T n − 1) . Evaluating at the operator σ and using σn = id yields 

h(σ) = u(σ)a(σ).

Thus ker a(σ) ⊆ ker h(σ). Conversely, a = hc gives a(σ) = c(σ)h(σ), so the kernels agree. Write T n − 1 = hb . The correspondence between ordinary multiplication and lin-earized composition gives

(Lh(X)).

− X as an ordinary polynomial. The latter splits over E with no repeated roots, so all roots of Lh also lie in E and are simple. If d = deg h, then deg X Lh = qd, so its root space contains exactly qd elements and has dimension d. This includes h = 1 : in that case Lh = X and the kernel is {0}.Finally, a(σ) is invertible if and only if its kernel is zero, equivalently deg h = 0 , or

Example 8.10 (Commuting with Frobenius need not preserve multiplication) Let 

E = F16 and σ(x) = x2, and take A = 1 + σ + σ2. Since T 4 − 1 = ( T + 1) 4 and 

(1 + T + T 2)|T =1 = 1 , the polynomials 1 + T + T 2 and T 4 − 1 are coprime. Theorem 8.8 therefore shows that A is invertible. It commutes with σ and satisfies A(1) = 1 . If A

also preserved multiplication, it would be an automorphism of E/F2, hence some σj

with 0 ≤ j < 4. The nonzero polynomial 1 + T + T 2 − T j would then annihilate σ,although its degree is at most three, contradicting the fact that the kernel of k[T ] → k[σ]

in Theorem 8.9 is (T 4 − 1) . Thus an invertible linear map fixing the identity and commuting with Frobenius need not be a field isomorphism. 

# 8.5 Root Multiplicities and Composition Division 

If L(X) = ∑si=h aiXqi

and ahas 6 = 0 , take the unique qhth root of each coefficient in the finite coefficient field to obtain 

L(X) = M (X)qh

, M ′(X) 6 = 0 .

In a splitting extension, every root has multiplicity exactly qh, and the distinct roots form an Fq-space of dimension s − h. Conversely, if a nonzero polynomial splits com-pletely in a specified extension, its distinct roots form a finite Fq-space V , and every root has the same multiplicity qh, then the polynomial must be cL V (X)qh

and hence is linearized. The condition that all roots have the same multiplicity, a power of q, is essential; the condition that the root set be a subspace is not sufficient by itself. 

Theorem 8.11 (Right composition division) Let L, M be q-linearized polynomials over the same finite extension, with M 6 = 0 . There are unique q-linearized polynomials 

Q, R over that field such that 

L = Q ◦ M + R, R = 0 or deg q R < deg q M. 

Moreover, divisibility M | L as ordinary polynomials holds if and only if L = Q ◦ M .

Proof. Let the leading terms be aX qs

and bX qt

, with s ≥ t. Subtracting 

(a/bqs−t

)M (X)qs−t

cancels the leading term. Repeating finitely many times proves existence. The q-degree of a nonzero composition is the sum of the q-degrees, so subtracting two division identities proves uniqueness. Every term of Q(M (X)) is divisible by the ordinary polynomial M (X). Thus if M | L, then M | R; the remainder 200 Chapter 8 Linearized Polynomials and Operator Algebras 

has smaller ordinary degree and must be zero. Conversely, if L = Q ◦ M , the same termwise divisibility gives M | L.Older literature calls composition “symbolic multiplication.” For coefficients in Fq,

La ◦L b = Lab , so symbolic factorization is ordinary factorization of operator polynomials; over a larger coefficient field, composition is generally noncommutative, and its order must be specified. 

Proposition 8.12 (Minimal linearized polynomial) Given a finite field K ⊇ Fq and an element β algebraic over K, there is a unique monic nonzero q-linearized polynomial 

M ∈ K[X] of least q-degree such that M (β) = 0 . It is called the minimal linearized polynomial M of β over K. The q-linearized polynomials with coefficients in K van-ishing at β are exactly those of the form Q ◦ M , where Q ∈ K[X] is also q-linearized; in this case M is called a right factor under composition. 

Proof. The element β lies in a finite field, so some XqN

− X vanishes at it. Choosing the least degree proves existence. Right composition division of any other annihilat-ing polynomial leaves a remainder vanishing at β, which must be zero by minimality. Subtracting two monic polynomials of least degree proves uniqueness. 

Remark 8.13 (Roots of the minimal linearized polynomial) Let |K| = Q, and take all K-conjugates β, β Q, . . . of β in a finite extension. Write V for their Fq-linear span. The Qth-power map preserves V , so the coefficients of LV are fixed by the Qth-power map and belong to K. Every nonzero linearized polynomial with coefficients in K

vanishing at β also vanishes at all its K-conjugates and hence, by Fq-linearity, on V . Its ordinary degree is therefore at least |V |. The polynomial LV attains this degree, so the minimal linearized polynomial is exactly LV . The ordinary minimal polynomial has the conjugate orbit as its root set; the minimal linearized polynomial has the linear span of that orbit as its root set. When the coefficient field is exactly k = Fq, this M corresponds to the Frobenius annihilator polynomial μβ defined in the next chapter, namely M = Lμβ . Its root set is the linear span of the conjugate orbit, whereas the root set of the ordinary minimal polynomial is the conjugate orbit itself. Proposition 8.14 (Invariant subspaces and operator factors) Let h ∈ k[T ] be monic, with deg h ≥ 1 and h(0) 6 = 0 , and let W be the space of all roots of Lh. The Frobenius-invariant k-subspaces of W correspond bijectively to the monic divisors of h:

d | h ←→ {x : Ld(x) = 0 }.

Proof. The monic root polynomial LV of an invariant subspace V has coefficients in 

k, so it equals some Ld. Since V ⊆ W and the roots are simple, we have ordinary divisibility Ld | L h. Right division under composition over k gives a linearized quotient with coefficients in k, say Lc. Thus Lh = Lc ◦ L d = Lcd ; comparing the coefficients of each Xqi

gives h = cd . The same composition identity proves the converse, and uniqueness of the root-set polynomial establishes the bijection. In particular, W has no nonzero proper invariant subspace if and only if h is irre-ducible in k[T ].

Chapter 9 arranges the Frobenius conjugates of a single element in a Moore matrix; a column permutation converts it into a multiplication matrix in a cyclic algebra (Proposition 9.32). Furthermore, if a, b ∈ k[T ] are not both zero, then gcd (La, Lb) = Lgcd (a,b ), (8.3) where all greatest common divisors are monic. This identity follows directly from the Euclidean algorithm. If b 6 = 0 , division with remainder in k[T ] gives a = cb + r, and then 

La = Lc ◦ L b + Lr.

Since Lc(Y ) has no constant term, the ordinary polynomial Lb(X) divides Lc(Lb(X)) ,so gcd (La, Lb) = gcd (Lb, Lr).

Following the Euclidean algorithm for a, b reduces the left side to the linearization of the last nonzero remainder. Multiplication by a nonzero base-field constant commutes with linearization, so monic normalization gives (8.3). If b = 0 , the identity follows directly by monic normalization. The argument takes place in the ordinary polynomial ring and thus preserves both roots and their multiplicities; it also shows that, for base-field coefficients, the ordinary greatest common divisor agrees with the greatest common right divisor under composition.

## 8.6.1 Quotient Multiplication and Trace Duality 

Definition 8.19 For k-subspaces U, V ⊆ E, the product of subspaces is defined by 

U V = span k{uv : u ∈ U, v ∈ V }.

The linear span is part of the definition; U V need not equal the set of individual products. 

Definition 8.20 Given a k-subspace W ⊆ E, define the quotient multiplication map for each a ∈ E by 

Ta,W : W −→ E/W, x 7 −→ ax + W. 

These maps depend k-linearly on a; the resulting parameter map is 

ΦW : E −→ Hom k(W, E /W ), a 7 −→ Ta,W .

Here E/W is a quotient vector space, generally not a quotient ring. For a ∈ E×, the number 

IW (a) = dim k(W ∩ aW )

is called the multiplicative intersection dimension of W with its scalar multiple. 206 Chapter 8 Linearized Polynomials and Operator Algebras 

Proposition 8.21 (Kernels and duals of quotient multiplication) Put r = dim k W ,and take orthogonal complements with respect to Tr E/k(xy ). Then ker ΦW = H(W ), ker Ta,W = W ∩ a−1W, rank Ta,W = r − IW (a) (a 6 = 0) .

(E/W )∨ ' W ⊥, W ∨ ' E/W ⊥.

Proof. The equality Ta,W = 0 is equivalent to aW ⊆ W , so the kernel of the parameter map ΦW is H(W ). For a 6 = 0 , the condition Ta,W (x) = 0 is equivalent to x ∈ W ∩ a−1W .Multiplication by a maps this intersection isomorphically onto aW ∩ W , proving the rank formula. The kernel of the parameter map consists of scalars for which the entire map vanishes, whereas the kernel of one Ta,W consists of vectors whose products lie in 

W .The two quotient pairings are 

(z + W, y ) 7 −→ Tr E/k(zy ), (x, z + W ⊥) 7 −→ Tr E/k(xz ).

In the first, y ∈ W ⊥; in the second, x ∈ W . Thus both are independent of the coset representatives. Nondegeneracy of the trace pairing on E gives (W ⊥)⊥ = W and dim W ⊥ = n − r. It follows that both quotient pairings are nondegenerate on each side and give the stated duality isomorphisms. No nondegeneracy assumption on the restriction to W is needed. For x ∈ W and y ∈ W ⊥, the identity Tr E/k(( ax )y) = Tr E/k(x(ay )) 

identifies the dual map with y 7 → ay + W ⊥. A map and its dual vanish simultaneously and have the same rank, giving (8.5). Chapter 8 Linearized Polynomials and Operator Algebras 207

E, and does not require the characteristic to be coprime to the extension degree. Equation (8.6) also gives a simple product criterion: if dim k U + dim k V > n , then

# Normal Bases, Cyclic Modules, and Invariant Subspaces 

A normal basis represents Frobenius as a cyclic shift, making the extension field a concrete cyclic module. This unifies normality criteria, root-space counts, and the classification of invariant subspaces; reciprocation and the trace pairing further describe duality. Families of translates apply the unit criterion to changes of generator: the same cyclic-module model determines which primary components can be repaired and which obstructions remain unchanged. 

# 9.1 Orbit Length and the Dimension of Its Span 

A k-linear operator A : V → V makes V a k[T ]-module: the action of a polynomial 

a(T ) on a vector v is defined as a(A)v. If the iterates v, Av, A 2v, . . . of a vector v span all of V , then v is called a cyclic vector , and the corresponding k[T ]-module is called a 

cyclic module . A subspace U satisfying A(U ) ⊆ U is called A-invariant; it is precisely a submodule for this module structure. In this chapter A = σ, so a polynomial acts as a linear combination of Frobenius iterates. 

Definition 9.1 Let E = Fqn and k = Fq, and let η be a normal element. Its conjugates 

η, η q, . . . , η qn−1

form a basis of E/k, called a normal basis .A normal element has n distinct conjugates and therefore generates the extension field; the converse fails. Orbit length counts distinct elements, whereas normality re-quires these elements to be linearly independent. 215 216 Chapter 9 Normal Bases, Cyclic Modules, and Invariant Subspaces 

Example 9.2 Let F8 = F2(α) with α3 + α + 1 = 0 . The element α has degree three, but α + α2 + α4 = 0 , so it is not normal. Put η = α + 1 . Its conjugates are

Division with remainder shows that every operator polynomial annihilating a is divisible by μa; in particular, μa | T n − 1.If d = deg μa, then a, σ (a), . . . , σ d−1(a) are linearly independent and span the entire orbit. Hence deg μa = dim k〈a, σ (a), σ 2(a), . . . 〉k.

This operator polynomial generally differs from the minimal polynomial ma,k (X) of the field element. The former describes linear relations among conjugates; the latter has the distinct conjugates as its roots.

## 9.2.1 The Root Bound and Linear Nondegeneracy 

The key restriction in the normal-basis proof is that a nonzero polynomial of low de-gree cannot vanish on too large a set. For linearized polynomials, comparing ordinary degree with the cardinality of a subspace turns this restriction into linear independence. Specifically, if a0, . . . , a s ∈ E are not all zero, then 

∣∣∣∣∣{

x ∈ E :

> s

∑

> i=0

aixqi

= 0 

}∣ ∣∣∣∣ ≤ qs.

Thus this operator cannot annihilate a k-subspace of dimension greater than s. Four results already obtained use this same restriction: (1) Cyclicity of the multiplicative group. The exponent e of a finite multiplicative subgroup is attained as the order of an element, and every group element is a root of 

Xe −1. The group order is therefore at most e, while that element already generates a cyclic subgroup of e elements. The two groups coincide (Theorem 2.11). (2) Nondegeneracy of the trace pairing. The trace polynomial X+Xq +· · · +Xqn−1

is nonzero of degree less than qn and cannot vanish on all of E. Scaling a nonzero trace value by a base-field scalar gives an element of trace one; multiplication by the inverse of any nonzero element then proves nondegeneracy of the trace pairing (Theorems 6.3 and 7.1). (3) The Moore criterion. If the Moore determinant of s elements linearly indepen-dent over the base field vanished, a nonzero linearized polynomial of q-degree at most s−1 would vanish on their span of qs elements, a contradiction (Theorem 8.3). (4) Existence of normal bases. The same degree comparison excludes every opera-tor relation for σ of degree less than n, forcing its minimal polynomial to be T n − 1;the cyclic vector lemma then gives a normal basis. The root bound determines the minimal-polynomial degree, and the cyclic vector lemma converts that degree into a basis. Chapter 9 Normal Bases, Cyclic Modules, and Invariant Subspaces 221 

Preservation of the field operations by Frobenius supplies fixed points, orbits, and lin-earized structure; the root bound excludes unintended degeneracies within these struc-tures. Together they show how counting restrictions in finite fields become generation, surjectivity, and linear independence.

The n conjugates of a normal element are distinct and give different cyclic starting points of the same normal basis, so divide by n to count bases. A normal element has nonzero trace, since otherwise the sum of its conjugates would give a nontrivial linear relation. In particular, if n = pa, then T n − 1 = ( T − 1) n and there is just one normality condition: 

(T n − 1

T − 1

)

(σ)( x) = Tr E/k(x) 6 = 0 .

Thus, when the extension degree is a power of the characteristic p, the normal elements are exactly those with nonzero trace. Normality can also be forced by a stronger family of linear-independence conditions. Section 17.9 proves that, when the irreducible trace code of a multiplicative subgroup is nontrivial and MDS, the Frobenius orbit of every nonidentity element is a normal basis. The subgroup condition first excludes proper subfields, and column independence then recovers generation of the Frobenius cyclic module; see Theorem 17.53. Upgrading the normality of every nonidentity element to joint independence across a whole subgroup requires control of additive relations between different Frobenius orbits; Example 18.16 gives an explicit subgroup whose nontrivial orbits are all normal despite a three-term relation. 

## 9.3.1 The Effect of Translation on Normality 

For a fixed θ ∈ E, adding a base-field element preserves the generated field: k(θ + t) = 

k(θ). Normality, however, requires the conjugates to generate the entire cyclic module, so one must determine which generation conditions such a translation can change. Chapter 9 Normal Bases, Cyclic Modules, and Invariant Subspaces 223

When the characteristic does not divide the extension degree, a base-field trans-lation can change only the T − 1 component. When the characteristic divides the extension degree, such a translation cannot change whether any primary component is generated in full. The latter statement does not mean that every component of the element is unchanged; it means that the nonvanishing conditions deciding normality are unchanged. Consequently, changing the trace generally cannot repair a failure of gen-eration in another primary component. Example 9.16 (An identity action that cannot be realized) The identity operator on a two-dimensional space k2 cannot be realized this way. In general, the root polynomial of a Frobenius-stable subspace attains the root bound, forcing the degree of the minimal polynomial of the restricted Frobenius operator to equal the dimension of the space. # 9.6 The Lattice of Invariant Subspaces and Trace Du-ality 

A family of subspaces ordered by inclusion is a lattice if any two members have, within the family, both a largest common subspace and a smallest subspace containing them. For invariant subspaces these operations are intersection and sum; this section identifies them with polynomial greatest common divisors and least common multiples. Put F (T ) = T n − 1. A normal element θ gives an isomorphism 

k[T ]/( F ) −→ E, a 7 −→ a(σ)θ. (9.9) This is an isomorphism of k[T ]-modules, with T acting on the right as σ. In general it is not a field or ring isomorphism: the element 1 on the left maps to θ, and when 

n > 1, the polynomial T − 1 is a proper factor of F , so the ring on the left has zero divisors. This model describes the linear action of Frobenius; it does not replace field multiplication.

# 9.8 When Nonzero Trace Implies Normality 

Theorem 9.33 Let n ≥ 1. The property that every element of degree n over k with nonzero trace is normal holds if and only if one of the following conditions is satisfied: (1) n = pa, where a ≥ 0;(2) n = ` 6 = p is prime and ord ℓ(q) = ` − 1.

Proof. Write n = pam with p - m and put F = T n − 1 = ( T m − 1) pa

Φℓ is irreducible, then F = ( T − 1)Φ ℓ. The trace condition requires the first factor and degree ` requires the second, forcing μ = F . The cyclotomic orbit theorem shows that

The second factor contains a primitive mth root of unity, of order m; the multiplicity contributes pa. Thus ord (μ) = n but μ 6 = F , giving a nonnormal counterexample. If a = 0 , m > 1 and m is either composite or prime with Φm reducible, choose an irreducible factor P | Φm and put μ = ( T − 1) P . Its order is m, but its degree satisfies 

1 + ord m(q) < m : for composite degree use 1 + ϕ(m) < m , and for prime degree use reducibility of Φm. This again gives the required counterexample and exhausts the remaining cases. Nonzero trace detects the multiplicity of T − 1 in the Frobenius annihilator poly-nomial. The classification identifies the parameters for which this condition, together with full degree, forces normality. Proposition 9.8 allows base-field translation to alter only the trace condition. Ex-ercise 9.19 uses this to compare two different quantifiers: whether nonzero trace forces normality, and whether every full-degree element can be made normal by translation. 

Corollary 9.34 (Nonzero trace without a degree hypothesis) For E = Fqn and k = Fq,

(∀α ∈ E, Tr E/k(α) 6 = 0 ⇒ α is normal ) ⇐⇒ n = pa (a ≥ 0) .

Proposition 9.41 (Complete normality in characteristic-power degree) If [E : k] = pa,where p = char k and a ≥ 0, then the following conditions on α ∈ E are equivalent: α

Example 9.44 (Two intermediate traces and one free field component) Take k = F5,

Prescribing intermediate traces amounts to polynomial reduction in normal coordinates, whereas prescribing a norm imposes a condition on field multiplication. They impose different restrictions on normality. Prescribed intermediate traces specify quotient coordinates, whereas adding ele-ments of an intermediate subfield gives a coset of an ideal in the cyclic module. If πi(U ) = 0 , then Ii ⊆ (Pi). All elements of the affine component have the same image πi(α0) in the residue field: all are units or none are. Normality means that every local component is a unit. Multiplying the independent local counts gives the formula.

# 9.13 The Complete Criterion for Self-Dual Normal Bases 

This section treats normality and the trace pairing within one algebra. The key re-duction expresses changes of normal basis as units in the cyclic-module algebra and self-duality as a unit norm equation for an involution. Solvability is determined by residue-field norms and lifting through nilpotent ideals. A map whose square is the identity is an involution ; the identity map itself is allowed. A primitive normal element generates both the multiplicative group and the Frobenius cyclic module. Let k = Fq and E = Fqn , and write σ(x) = xq, N = qn − 1, and

Theorem 9.58 (Primitive normal basis theorem) For every prime power q and positive integer n, the extension Fqn /Fq has a primitive normal element. Proposition 9.59 (Primitive elements in quadratic extensions are normal) For every prime power q, every primitive element of Fq2 is normal over Fq.

## 9.14.1 Two Unit Coordinate Systems and a Joint Criterion 

Fix a primitive element ζ and a normal element θ. The two generation problems have coordinate models 

Z/N Z −→ E×, j 7 −→ ζj ,R = k[T ]/( F ) −→ E, ¯u 7 −→ u(σ)θ. 

(9.33) The first is an isomorphism from an additive group to a multiplicative group; the second is a k[T ]-module isomorphism, with T acting on E as σ. The order formula in a cyclic Chapter 9 Normal Bases, Cyclic Modules, and Invariant Subspaces 259 

group and the cyclic-module model in this chapter give 

ζj is primitive ⇐⇒ gcd (j, N ) = 1 ,u(σ)θ is normal ⇐⇒ gcd (u, F ) = 1 .

The two types of generators therefore correspond to (Z/N Z)× and R×, respectively. The models preserve different operations: exponent coordinates turn field multiplication into addition of exponents, while normal coordinates turn Frobenius into a cyclic shift. The second isomorphism generally does not preserve field multiplication, and the first does not describe field addition. Coprimality in the two coordinate systems is therefore not interchangeable. 

Proposition 9.61 (A joint criterion for primitive normal elements) For a ∈ E×, the following two conditions hold simultaneously if and only if a is primitive and normal: (1) For every distinct prime divisor ` | N , we have aN /ℓ 6 = 1 ;(2) For every distinct monic irreducible factor P | F , we have (F /P )( σ)( a) 6 = 0 .When N = 1 , the first set of conditions is empty. 

Proof. Let e = ord (a), so e | N . If e < N , choose a prime divisor ` of N /e. Then e | N /`,hence aN /ℓ = 1 . Conversely, if this equality holds, e | N /` < N , so a is not primitive. The second set is exactly the normality criterion of Proposition 9.6. Combining them proves the assertion. The first set excludes elements of multiplicative order less than N ; the second ex-cludes elements whose conjugates span a proper subspace. The multiplicative condition excludes the subgroup {a ∈ E× : aN /ℓ = 1 }, of order N /`; the normality condition excludes the subspace ker (F /P )( σ). In the cyclic-module model, this corresponds to the ideal ( ¯P ) of R, of dimension n − deg P . When p | n, the polynomial F may have repeated factors, but F /P reduces the multiplicity of P by only one, so the second set still tests the full primary structure. Taking P = T − 1 gives Tr E/k(a) 6 = 0 ; the trace condition is generally only one normality condition. Theorem 9.33 describes when nonzero trace, together with degree n over k, is sufficient for normality. 260 Chapter 9 Normal Bases, Cyclic Modules, and Invariant Subspaces 

## 9.14.2 Changing Generators and Intersecting the Two Condi-tions 

If gcd (j, N ) = 1 , the power map a 7 → aj is an automorphism of E× and therefore takes primitive elements to primitive elements. If ¯u ∈ R×, the operator u(σ) is an invertible k-linear map taking normal elements to normal elements. Indeed, if μa = F ,the cyclic-module model gives μu(σ)a = F / gcd (F, u ) = F . The first type of change need not preserve normality, and the second need not preserve multiplicative order. Frobenius preserves both: in exponent coordinates it is multiplication by q, and in normal coordinates multiplication by T ; each multiplier is a unit in its coordinate ring. The identity σM aσ−1 = Maq in the regular representation of Section 4.2 also shows how these actions are compatible within one extension field.

Separate existence of the two types of generators only says that both sets are nonempty; the primitive normal basis theorem guarantees that a single element can satisfy both sets of exclusion conditions. Such an element provides exponent coordinates for the nonzero elements and normal coordinates for the whole field. The relation between the two coordinate systems still depends on the specific field operations. 

Testing normality before sieving for primitivity. When candidates are restricted to θ + k, Proposition 9.8 first determines whether an obstruction to normality persists throughout the translate. If the family contains no normal element, it contains no primitive normal element. If it does contain a normal element, put 

Pθ = #{t ∈ k : θ + t is primitive }, P N θ = #{t ∈ k : θ + t is primitive and normal }.

When p - n, also put βθ = θ − Tr E/k(θ)/ n. Then 

P N θ =



Pθ, p | n, Pθ − 1{βθ is primitive }, p - n. 

(9.34) The indicator is one when βθ is primitive and zero otherwise; zero is not counted as a primitive element. The formula assumes that the translate contains a normal element ; it does not dispense with checking the normality obstruction. It turns the joint condition into a concrete procedure: first test generation in the cyclic module, and then apply the multiplicative-order test to the remaining candidates. It gives no estimate for Pθ, nor does it assert that every translate contains a primitive element. 

The common structure of cyclic modules, trace duality, and local counts. 

The commutative algebra A = k[T ]/( T n − 1) explains several results of this chapter. In normal coordinates, T acts by Frobenius cyclic shift, and normal elements correspond to units of A. After factoring T n − 1 = ∏ 

> P

P eP , normality means that every local component is nonzero modulo P . This explains normal-element counts, prescribed intermediate traces, and the exact invariant-affine count. The trace pairing gives the involution T 7 → T −1 and the correlation identity gα = hαh∗

> α

; self-dual normal bases and prescribed correlations are governed by unit norm equations uu ∗ = b. The additive 262 Chapter 9 Normal Bases, Cyclic Modules, and Invariant Subspaces 

and multiplicative structures must not be conflated: primitivity is still a multiplicative-order condition in E× and does not follow from being a unit in the cyclic module. Their simultaneous satisfaction is precisely the difficulty addressed by the primitive normal basis theorem.

# Frobenius Tests, Factorization, and Changes of Representation 

Irreducibility criteria test orbit lengths, fixed subalgebras separate distinct orbits, and the minimal polynomial of a fixed element determines the actual splitting values. Root-set descent thus becomes a finite sequence of linear-algebra and polynomial operations. Value fibers of fixed elements also yield idempotent projections; constructing normal el-ements compares the different effects of translation and reciprocation on linear relations among conjugates. 

# 10.1 Frobenius Criteria for Irreducibility

# 10.2 Square-Free and Distinct-Degree Factorization 

Square-free factorization first reduces the factorization of a general polynomial to that of square-free polynomials. One may then apply Berlekamp’s method directly, or first group the irreducible factors by degree and then split each equal-degree part by a randomized method. 

## 10.2.1 Separating Multiplicities 

Finite fields are perfect, so their irreducible polynomials are separable. If f ′ = 0 , every nonzero term has exponent divisible by p, and there is a unique expression f = gp. Over the coefficient field Fpr , the pth root of a coefficient a is apr−1

.The following gives the square-free factorization of a monic nonconstant polyno-mial, namely f = ∏ 

> i

zii , where each zi is monic and the zi different from 1 are square-free and pairwise coprime. (1) Put c = gcd (f, f ′), w = f /c, and i = 1 .(2) While w 6 = 1 , compute y = gcd (w, c ) and z = w/y; if z 6 = 1 , record the factor z

with multiplicity i. Then put w = y, c = c/y, and i = i + 1 .(3) After the loop, if the remaining c 6 = 1 , it is a pth power. Apply the same procedure recursively to c1/ p and multiply every resulting multiplicity by p.Correctness can be checked separately for each irreducible factor P and its multiplicity 

e: if p - e, it occurs with multiplicity e − 1 in c and once in w; the loop extracts it 270 Chapter 10 Frobenius Tests, Factorization, and Changes of Representation 

exactly when i = e. If p | e, it initially remains entirely in c and is handled by the final 

pth-root step. Every recursive call lowers the degree, so the algorithm terminates. 

## 10.2.2 Grouping by Orbit Length 

Let f be monic, nonconstant, and square-free. Distinct-degree factorization uses the fact that the roots of Xqi

− X are exactly the elements whose periods divide i.Put r = f , u = X mod r, and i = 1 . While 2i ≤ deg r, compute 

u ← uq mod r, g = gcd (r, u − X).

If g 6 = 1 , record g as the product of all irreducible factors of degree i, then put r ← r/g

and reduce u modulo the new r. If r = 1 , stop; otherwise put i ← i + 1 and continue. On exit, if r 6 = 1 , it is itself an irreducible factor. It suffices to prove the invariant: on entering step i, the polynomial r has no irre-ducible factor of degree less than i, and u records the previous Frobenius-power remain-der. Every common irreducible factor at this step has degree both dividing i and at least i, hence exactly i. If two irreducible factors remained on exit, each would have degree at least the current i, forcing deg r ≥ 2i, a contradiction. 

# 10.3 Berlekamp’s Method: Separating Orbits with the Fixed Subalgebra 

Berlekamp’s method [5] computes fixed elements in the quotient algebra by linear equa-tions and uses them to separate factors. 

Theorem 10.6 Let f = f1 · · · fs be the irreducible factorization of a square-free polynomial, and put A = k[X]/( f ). Then 

B = {h ∈ A : hq = h}

is a k-space of dimension s and is isomorphic as a k-algebra to ks.

Proof. In a finite splitting extension, let S be the root set of f . It has s Frobenius orbits. Theorem 3.20 identifies A with the equivariant function algebra and B with functions taking a constant base-field value on each orbit. Thus B ' ks, of dimension s. The Chapter 10 Frobenius Tests, Factorization, and Changes of Representation 271 

indicator function of a subset is one on the subset and zero on its complement. The orbit indicators give pairwise orthogonal idempotents in B summing to one; these are precisely the algebra elements used to separate factors. 

Example 10.7 (Separating two root orbits with one fixed element) In F2[X], put 

f = ( X + 1)( X2 + X + 1) = X3 + 1 , h = X + X2.

Modulo f , we have X3 = 1 and X4 = X, hence h2 = X2 + X4 = h. Thus h belongs to the Berlekamp subalgebra. On the component corresponding to X + 1 , we have 

h(1) = 0 ; on the other component, X2 + X + 1 = 0 gives h = 1 . Therefore gcd (f, h ) = X + 1 , gcd (f, h − 1) = X2 + X + 1 .

A fixed element takes a constant base-field value on each root orbit; distinct values separate the orbits into different factors. In the basis 1, X, . . . , X deg f −1, compute the matrix of h 7 → hq and solve hq − h = 0 

to obtain a basis of B. If dim B = 1 , then f is irreducible. If the dimension exceeds one, choose h ∈ B outside the constant subspace. For every c ∈ k, compute gcd (f, h − c)

to group the irreducible factors of f by the values on their components. Since these values are not all equal, at least two nontrivial groups result; continuing on the resulting factors gives the full factorization. The fixed subalgebra is isomorphic to a finite product of copies of the base field and is generally not a field. It records exactly how many Frobenius orbits make up the root set. For square-free f , computing the fixed-space dimensions of all Frobenius iterates and applying Theorem 3.31 also recovers the number of irreducible factors of each degree.

Proposition 10.10 (Randomized root finding for completely split polynomials) Let

Proof. The Chinese remainder theorem gives k[Y ]/( M ) ' kt, so the values of b at the roots are independent and uniform in k. In odd characteristic an attempt fails exactly when the values are all zero, all nonzero squares, or all nonsquares. Thus the failure probability is

Constructing a multiple from the affine span of the roots. These operations map values in unknown field components into a small set, after which greatest common divisors separate factors with different values. The resulting elements satisfy

## Recursive Factorization and Correctness of the Output 

Repeat the procedure on each output factor F , sampling independently and uniformly from polynomials of degree less than deg F . If deg F = d, return F : it must be irre-ducible. If deg F > d , the polynomial F is still a product of distinct irreducibles of 280 Chapter 10 Frobenius Tests, Factorization, and Changes of Representation 

degree d with at least two components, so the same success-probability bound applies. Failure only triggers resampling; success strictly lowers the degrees of both subproblems. A randomized algorithm whose running time depends on random choices, whose output is always correct, and whose expected running time is finite is called a Las Vegas algorithm . This procedure is of that type: each trial uses finitely many polynomial operations, and each recursive node needs at most two trials in expectation. A full factorization has s − 1 successful splitting nodes, so the expected total number of trials is at most 2( s − 1) . Independent retries terminate with probability one. Every split uses a greatest common divisor and exact division, and the final factors have degree exactly d;randomness therefore does not affect output correctness. This gives Cantor–Zassenhaus equal-degree factorization; see [8].

# 10.5 From Quotient-Ring Representations to Ex-plicit Isomorphisms 

The structure theorem determines the isomorphism type of a finite field; computation also requires the image of a specified generator. Root finding directly connects these two levels of information. 

Proposition 10.17 Let f, g ∈ k[X] be monic irreducible polynomials of degree n,and put E = k[X]/( f ) = k(α) and E′ = k[Y ]/( g) = k(β). Choose a root b of f in E′.Then 

Φ : E −→ E′, P (α) 7 −→ P (b)

b, b q, . . . , b qn−1

Proof. Since f | Xqn

− X, it splits into n distinct linear factors in E′, so a root b

exists. Evaluation P 7 → P (b) has kernel (f ) and therefore induces an injection from E282 Chapter 10 Frobenius Tests, Factorization, and Changes of Representation 

to E′. Both sides have dimension n, so it is an isomorphism. Every k-isomorphism is determined by the image of α, which must be a root of f ; its roots are exactly the listed Frobenius orbit. Algorithmically, apply this chapter’s factorization methods to f over E′[X] and take a linear factor. Enumerating the elements of E′ also terminates, but its qn candi-dates grow exponentially with the representation length n log q. Once a root is chosen, computing the isomorphism requires only evaluation. Precompute the coordinates of 

1, b, . . . , b n−1 in the power basis of β and use them as the columns of a matrix P . Then 

[Φ( x)] (1 ,β,...,β n−1) = P [x](1 ,α,...,α n−1).

The matrix P is invertible, and computing P −1 gives the coordinate formula for the inverse isomorphism.

## 10.5.1 Sparse Relations for a Fixed Defining Polynomial 

Changing a generator changes its minimal polynomial. For a fixed generator, one may instead allow a relation to have higher degree in order to reduce its number of nonzero terms. These are different problems. We now fix a defining polynomial and express the second problem as linear relations among powers in a quotient algebra. Chapter 10 Frobenius Tests, Factorization, and Changes of Representation 285 

Definition 10.19 (Minimum degree of a sparse multiple) Let k = Fq, and let f ∈ k[X]

be monic and nonconstant, with f (0) 6 = 0 . For an integer s ≥ 2, define 

Ls(f ) = min {deg P : 0 6 = P ∈ k[X], f | P, wt (P ) ≤ s}.

We call Ls(f ) the minimum degree of a sparse multiple of f with at most s terms. The degree is that of the multiple P , not of the multiplier P /f .In the finite quotient algebra k[X]/( f ), the element X is a unit. Hence f divides some XB − 1, and all the minima above are finite. Clearly, deg f ≤ Ls+1 (f ) ≤ Ls(f ).

A multiple attaining the minimum degree has nonzero constant term: otherwise one could divide it by X, retain divisibility by f , and lower its degree. Thus a degree-minimal binomial, after monic normalization, has the form XB − c, with c ∈ k×. By Proposition 4.17, L2(f ) is precisely the order of X in the unit group modulo base-field scalars. When f is irreducible and α is a root, divisibility f | ∑ 

> i

aiXi is equivalent to ∑ 

> i

aiαi = 0 . Thus Ls(f ) controls both the number of terms and the exponent range of a relation, whereas wq(n) allows the generator to vary. The two quantities are not interchangeable. The quantity λq(H) in Section 18.6 instead fixes the entire multiplicative subgroup and minimizes the number of terms in a relation, without an additional restriction on their exponent positions. 

Proposition 10.20 (Coefficient cancellation by a linear multiplier) Let d = deg f ≥ 2,and write f = ∑di=0 aiXi. If some coefficient is zero, then Ld(f ) = d. If all coefficients are nonzero, define the adjacent coefficient ratios by ri = ai/ai−1 for 1 ≤ i ≤ d. For 

r ∈ k×,wt ((1 − rX )f ) = d + 2 − #{i : 1 ≤ i ≤ d, r i = r}. (10.9) Consequently, when all coefficients are nonzero, 

Ld(f ) = d + 1 ⇐⇒ r1, . . . , r d contain a repeated value .

Proof. A nonzero multiple of degree d is a scalar multiple of f . This proves the first case and shows that Ld(f ) > d when every coefficient is nonzero. The constant and leading coefficients of (1 − rX )f are a0 and −ra d, both nonzero. Its coefficient of Xi is 

ai − ra i−1, which vanishes precisely when ri = r. This proves (10.9). A repeated ratio therefore cancels at least two coefficients, producing a multiple of degree d + 1 with at 286 Chapter 10 Frobenius Tests, Factorization, and Changes of Representation 

most d terms. Conversely, a multiple of degree d + 1 has a linear multiplier. If the multiplier has zero constant term, the product is a scalar multiple of Xf and still has 

d + 1 terms. Otherwise the multiplier can be normalized to 1 − rX , and (10.9) forces a repeated ratio. The ratio ri = r corresponds to the multiplier 1 − rX , whose monic form is X − r−1,not X − r. The direction of the reciprocal is fixed by the coefficient ai − ra i−1.

Corollary 10.21 (Cancellation over a smaller coefficient field) If the coefficients of f

lie in a subfield FQ ⊆ k and d ≥ Q, then Ld(f ) ≤ d + 1 .

Proof. If a coefficient is zero, then Ld(f ) = d. Otherwise the d adjacent ratios lie in the 

Q − 1 element set F×

> Q

, so two coincide. Apply the preceding proposition. 

Example 10.22 (The same multiplicative period, but different three-term relations) In F5[X], take 

f1 = X3 + 3 X2 + X + 1 , f2 = X3 + 4 X2 + X + 1 .

Their values at 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 are (1 , 1, 3, 3, 2) and (1 , 2, 2, 2, 3) , respectively. Hence both are irreducible. For a root α of either polynomial, the norm gives α31 = −1, so its multiplicative order is 2 or 62 . Degree three excludes order 2. Both roots therefore have multiplicative order 62 and projective order 31 , giving 

L2(f1) = L2(f2) = 31 .

On the other hand, direct multiplication gives 

(X2 + 2 X + 3) f1 = X5 + 2 X2 + 3 , (X + 1) f2 = X4 + 2 X + 1 .

The adjacent ratios for f1 are 1, 3, 2, with no repetition, so it has no three-term multiple of degree four. Those for f2 are 1, 4, 4. Since each polynomial itself has four terms, 

L3(f1) = 5 , L3(f2) = 4 .

The multiplicative and projective periods do not determine where the first three-term relation occurs. For general f , writing each Xi mod f as a column vector turns sparse relations into linear relations among specified remainder columns. This also explains why the mono-mial coordinates must remain fixed: a translation of the variable preserves irreducibility but usually changes the number of terms. Section 12.2 will describe the same relations by evaluations that retain root multiplicities. Chapter 10 Frobenius Tests, Factorization, and Changes of Representation 287

When q > n(n − 1) , testing any n(n − 1) + 1 distinct base-field parameters must produce a normal element. For smaller base fields, this bound alone does not guarantee a successful parameter in k.

# 10.7 Random Computation and Canonical Output 

Random factorization may discover the same factors in different orders; sorting the complete factor set still gives a fixed output. First fix a field representation: use the integer representatives 0, 1, . . . , p − 1 in Fp, and compare elements of the quotient-ring model Fp[Z]/( g) by lexicographic order on coefficient vectors (a0, . . . , a r−1). This order depends on the representation and is not compatible with field operations. 292 Chapter 10 Frobenius Tests, Factorization, and Changes of Representation 

Definition 10.28 (Pseudo-deterministic algorithms) A randomized algorithm is 

pseudo-deterministic if, for every input, there is a valid output determined by that input that the algorithm returns with probability at least 2/3 .This fixed output is called the canonical output for the input. A fixed output is compatible with the use of randomness during computation. ALas Vegas algorithm requires correct results but need not return the same result on different runs; selecting from the complete candidate set by a fixed rule can leave ran-domness affecting only running time. Rai [49] gives a pseudo-deterministic construction of irreducible polynomials of any prescribed degree. The quadratic construction below illustrates canonical selection; the general-degree construction is not developed here. 

Proposition 10.29 (A fixed nonsquare from successive root extraction) Let p be an odd prime and write p − 1 = 2 sm with m odd. Start from a = −1. If a is a square, find both roots of X2 − a and replace a by the root with the smaller integer representative; if 

a is a nonsquare, return X2 −a. The procedure stops after exactly s−1 root extractions, and the quadratic irreducible polynomial returned depends only on p.

Proof. The initial element −1 has order two. If a has order 2j and b2 = a, then ord (b)/ gcd (ord (b), 2) = 2 j , so ord (b) = 2 j+1 . The square subgroup of the cyclic group 

F× 

> p

has order 2s−1m, so an element of order 2j is a square if and only if j < s . Each root extraction therefore doubles the order, and the procedure stops exactly when the order reaches 2s. Each step makes a fixed choice from the complete pair of roots, so the whole sequence and final output are independent of random choices. The final a is a nonsquare, making X2 − a irreducible. Test whether an element is a square using a(p−1)/2 and find both roots using the random splitting in Proposition 10.10. If splitting fails, sample again; choose the smaller root only after obtaining two roots verified by substitution. The root-finding subroutine is Las Vegas, so it terminates with probability one and finite expected running time. Combining at most log 2 p root extractions with binary exponentiation gives expected bit complexity polynomial in log p for the entire construction. Suppose a known bound 

T (p) on the expected bit-operation count is available, where T (p) is a polynomial in log p. Report failure if execution has not finished after 3T (p) steps. Markov’s inequality bounds the timeout probability by 1/3 , so the probability of returning the fixed valid output within this limit is at least 2/3 .Chapter 10 Frobenius Tests, Factorization, and Changes of Representation 293
