72 = −1 7 −→ 27 7 −→ 10 , ord (72) = 2 , ord (27) = 4 , ord (10) = 8 .

Indeed, the two roots of −1 are 27 , 46 , and those of 27 are 10 , 63 ; choosing the smaller root gives the displayed sequence. Also 10 36 = (10 4)9 = ( −1) 9 = −1, so the final output is X2 − 10 . This example appears in [49, Example 2.1]; its increasing-order mechanism also parallels multiplicative period extension in Chapter 2. 

## Sparse Representations and Complexity 

The preceding costs are measured by degree or by the number of base-field operations. In a sparse representation , only nonzero coefficients and their binary-encoded exponents are stored, so input length can be much smaller than degree. For example, X2u

− 1 has just two terms, and its exponent needs only u + 1 bits; a dense representation storing all coefficients needs 2u + 1 coefficient positions. A polynomial bound in the degree need not therefore be polynomial in sparse input length. For sparse greatest common divisors, Qiu et al. [47] prove a conditional complexity obstruction in a model with the finite-field size also part of the input and exponents encoded in binary: if general sparse greatest common divisors could be computed in randomized polynomial bit time in the sparse lengths of the input and output, then NP ⊆ BPP. Here NP (nondeterministic polynomial time) consists of decision prob-lems admitting a deterministic polynomial-time verifier and a polynomial p such that every yes-instance x has an accepted certificate of length at most p(|x|), whereas no no-instance has an accepted certificate. The class BPP (bounded-error probabilistic polynomial time) consists of decision problems solvable by randomized polynomial-time algorithms with error probability at most 1/3 for every input, taken over the algorithm’s internal random choices. The conclusion uses NP * BPP as the complexity assumption and concerns finite fields varying with the input; it does not establish the same obstruc-tion over every fixed finite field. The preceding algorithms measure cost by polynomial degree, whereas this statement measures bit complexity by sparse input and output length. 294 Chapter 10 Frobenius Tests, Factorization, and Changes of Representation

# Root Fibers, Return Periods, and Irreducible Constructions 

This chapter studies maps that commute with the Frobenius actions on their source and target, namely, equivariant maps satisfying πσ = σπ . When the image is a single Frobenius orbit, the length of each source orbit is the product of the image orbit length and the corresponding fiber return period. Together with the multiplicity data of the fiber polynomials, this principle characterizes the irreducibility of composite polynomials and the degrees and multiplicities of their irreducible factors. Divisibility relations among return periods also compare the fields generated by the roots; for linearized compositions, periods in affine fibers control the least root field. 

# 11.1 Root Fibers and Equivariant Return Maps 

Let P (Y ) ∈ k[Y ] be monic and irreducible, with deg P = n, and let α be a root. Take relatively prime A, B ∈ k[X], with B 6 = 0 and A/B nonconstant, and assume that 

A − αB is nonconstant. In a finite extension L/k containing all roots of P and over which Q(X) = B(X)nP (A(X)/ B(X)) splits completely, consider the map 

h : {x ∈ L : B(x) 6 = 0 } −→ L, h(x) = A(x)/ B(x).

The second equality holds because coprimality of A, B prevents a root of the equation from making the denominator zero. These fibers lie over the roots of P and are called 

root fibers . The corresponding polynomial A − αqi

their multiplicities. Below, calling a fiber separable or irreducible means that its fiber polynomial has that property; factor multiplicities within a fiber are likewise recorded by that polynomial. Put O = {α, α q, . . . , α qn−1

Thus Frobenius maps each fiber bijectively onto the next, and its nth iterate is the first to preserve the initial fiber. The permutation obtained by restricting σn to this fiber is called the return map : it records how the original action moves elements within the same fiber after one circuit of the base orbit. The entire root set is therefore a single orbit precisely when the return map acts transitively on a fiber. The change of step shown in Figure 5.1 is here restricted to a fiber: σ moves successively through the fibers, whereas σn preserves the chosen fiber. Theorem 5.61 gave a concrete form of this mechanism in fibers arising from modulus lifting; we now formulate it as an orbit correspondence for general finite sets.

The base orbit length and fiber size are identical in the two examples; the return permutation determines their different factorization types. In general, a base orbit of length n and return cycles of lengths d1, . . . , d s give full orbits of distinct roots of lengths nd 1, . . . , nd s. Factor multiplicities still require the root multiplicities in the fiber polynomial. The following lemma proves the orbit-length correspondence. 

Lemma 11.1 (Return map of an orbit fiber) Let each of the finite sets S and O carry a permutation denoted by σ, and suppose that O is a single orbit of length n. If a surjection π : S → O satisfies πσ = σπ , then, for every a ∈ O, the σ-orbits in S

correspond bijectively to the σn-orbits in the fiber π−1(a). A return orbit of length d

corresponds to a full orbit of length nd .

Proof. The image of each full orbit is a nonempty σ-invariant subset of O, hence is all of O; thus the orbit meets the chosen fiber. If x lies in this fiber, then σt(x) lies in it if and only if σt(a) = a, that is, n | t. The intersection of the full orbit with the fiber is therefore exactly one σn-orbit. If the latter has least period d, the return times of x to itself are precisely the multiples of nd , and its least positive period is nd . Distinct full orbits are disjoint, so this correspondence is bijective. 

Theorem 11.2 (Root fiber criterion, or Capelli’s criterion) Let P ∈ k[Y ] be monic and irreducible with deg P = n, and let A, B ∈ k[X] be relatively prime with A/B

nonconstant. Take a root α of P , and assume that A − αB is nonconstant. Then 

Q(X) = B(X)nP (A(X)/ B(X))

is irreducible over k if and only if A(X) − αB (X) is irreducible over k(α). If n > 1,then deg Q = n max (deg A, deg B).304 Chapter 11 Root Fibers, Return Periods, and Irreducible Constructions 

Proof. First suppose that n > 1, and write h = max (deg A, deg B). Since α /∈ k, the leading terms of A−αB cannot cancel: if deg A 6 = deg B, the highest-degree term comes from one polynomial; if the degrees are equal and the leading terms cancel, then α is the ratio of two leading coefficients in the base field, a contradiction. The same argument applies to all conjugate roots, so 

Q(X) = 

> n−1

∏

> i=0

(A(X) − αqi

B(X)), deg Q = nh. 

Take a root β of A − αB . If B(β) = 0 , then A(β) = 0 ; but gcd (A, B ) = 1 gives a Bézout identity, and evaluating it at β yields a contradiction. Hence B(β) 6 = 0 , and 

α = A(β)

B(β) ∈ k(β).

Thus k ⊆ k(α) ⊆ k(β), and the tower law gives 

[k(β) : k] = n[k(β) : k(α)] .

If the fiber polynomial A − αB is irreducible over k(α), then [k(β) : k(α)] = h, so 

β has degree nh = deg Q over k. Its minimal polynomial divides Q and has the same degree. Hence Q is a nonzero constant times an irreducible polynomial, and is therefore irreducible. Conversely, if Q is irreducible, its root β satisfies [k(β) : k] = nh , so [k(β) : k(α)] = h.The minimal polynomial of β over k(α) divides A − αB and has the same degree, so the fiber polynomial is irreducible. When n = 1 , we have P (Y ) = Y − α, α ∈ k, and 

Q = A − αB , so the conclusion is immediate; in this case the degree is the actual degree of the nonconstant fiber polynomial in the hypothesis. For each root β in the fiber over α, the tower-law identity expresses its Frobenius orbit length over k as the product of n and its return period over k(α). Thus the analysis of a composite polynomial separates into the analysis of the original orbit and that of the fiber return map. Irreducibility, factor degrees, and factor multiplicities can all be recovered from the factorization of one fiber, so the fiber method also applies to the structural analysis of reducible composite polynomials. For a construction, first choose an irreducible P , and then choose A, B satisfying the hypotheses of the theorem. Their base-field coefficients make the fibers over conjugate roots compatible with Frobenius; these fibers cannot be prescribed independently. Adesired factor degree is the product of the base-orbit length and the least return period; knowing that one iterate returns gives only a multiple of the period. For the entire composite polynomial to be irreducible, the fiber polynomial must also have no repeated 306 Chapter 11 Root Fibers, Return Periods, and Irreducible Constructions 

roots, and the return map must traverse the whole fiber. In a recursive construction, continuing to the next step requires the data enforcing these conditions to be preserved; Chapter 14 controls them through traces, square classes, and multiplicative orders. The same return lemma also applies to linear state spaces and their quotients; Section 16.2 gives the corresponding root-space realization.

## Eliminating the Trace while Preserving Generation 

The preceding composite polynomial takes preimages under a rational function: its new root β satisfies R(β) = α. We now take the image β = R(α) of a given generator and ask when a trace condition can be imposed without shortening its Frobenius orbit. Here a generator means a field generator, with no additional requirement of primitivity or normality. Chapter 11 Root Fibers, Return Periods, and Irreducible Constructions 307

In a quadratic extension of characteristic two, k lies in the trace kernel, which has dimension one over k; hence the kernel is exactly k, and no trace-zero generator exists. # 11.5 Restrictions on Irreducibility of Affine Root Spaces 

For an affine subspace β + V , its dimension is defined as dim V . After choosing a base point β, the correspondence v ↔ β + v gives linear coordinates, but the affine subspace itself has no distinguished zero vector. In these coordinates, a map of the form v 7 → Av + c, with A linear and c fixed, is called an affine map; when A is invertible, it is an affine transformation. We shall write nonempty fibers of linearized equations as such translated spaces.

Irreducibility means that the full root set is a single orbit of length pv. Applying Proposition 11.17 to this v-dimensional affine space gives

When v ≥ 3, we have 2v−1 ≥ v+1 , so the right-hand side is at most v−1, a contradiction. When v = 2 and p ≥ 3, the right-hand side is one, again a contradiction. Thus only 

v = 1 or p = v = 2 is possible. This restriction compares the unique orbit length required by irreducibility with the upper bound for the shortest orbit length in an affine space of the given dimension. 

Proposition 11.19 (Complete form of the quartic exception) Let char k = 2 , let

The right-hand condition is exactly the quadratic trace criterion for irreducibility of 

X2 + uX + v over k. Thus the fiber polynomial is irreducible, and the root fiber theorem gives the irreducibility of L + b.

# 11.6 Root-Field Spectra and Least Root Fields 

Irreducibility requires all roots to form a single Frobenius orbit. For a reducible polyno-mial, divisibility among orbit lengths also records inclusions among the fields generated by individual roots. The fiber method can determine whether the roots of a composite polynomial form a single orbit and can also compare the extensions required by different orbits. 

Definition 11.21 (Root-field spectrum and least root field) Let k = Fq, and let f ∈

k[X] be nonconstant. Define the root-field spectrum of f over k by 

Dk(f ) = {deg P : P ∈ k[X] is monic irreducible and P | f }.

In a common finite splitting extension, if a root β0 of f satisfies 

k(β0) ⊆ k(β) for every β with f (β) = 0 ,

then k(β0) is called the least root field of f . A polynomial with this property is also called a subnormal polynomial ; see Agou [1]. 320 Chapter 11 Root Fibers, Return Periods, and Irreducible Constructions 

The root-field spectrum records only the degrees of distinct irreducible factors, not their numbers or multiplicities. What is required here is a least element under inclusion: a root field contained in every other root field, not merely a minimal element containing no smaller root field. The latter exists for every nonempty finite collection of root fields and does not characterize the property under discussion. 

Proposition 11.22 Let Dk(f ) = {d1, . . . , d s}, and put d∗ = gcd (d1, . . . , d s). The following conditions are equivalent: (1) f has a least root field; (2) there exists d0 ∈ D k(f ) such that d0 | d for every d ∈ D k(f );(3) d∗ ∈ D k(f ).When these conditions hold, the least root field is Fqd∗ . In general, the intersection of all root fields is Fqd∗ , but this intersection need not be generated by a root of f .

Proof. Every root of an irreducible factor of degree d generates Fqd . Within a common extension, Fqa ⊆ Fqb if and only if a | b, so the first two conditions are equivalent. If the second holds, then d0 divides all di, and some di = d0, so d∗ = d0. Conversely, if d∗

belongs to the root-field spectrum, it itself satisfies the second condition. The subfield intersection formula proves the final assertion. 

Proposition 11.23 (Root-field spectrum of a composite polynomial) Let P ∈ k[Y ] be monic and irreducible with deg P = n, let α be a root, and put E = k(α). For every nonconstant G ∈ k[X], we have 

Dk(P (G)) = nDE (G − α) = {nd : d ∈ D E (G − α)}. (11.3) Thus P (G) has a least root field over k if and only if G − α has a least root field over 

E. If the latter has degree d0 over E, then the former has degree nd 0 over k.

Proof. When n > 1, apply Theorem 11.3 with A = G and B = 1 : each irreducible factor hj in the fiber corresponds to an irreducible factor of degree n deg hj over the base field, and all factors arise this way. This gives (11.3); multiplicities in the fiber do not affect the identity. When n = 1 , we have E = k and P (G) = G − α, so the equality is immediate. Finally, nd 0 | nd if and only if d0 | d. Multiplication by n

therefore preserves and reflects the divisibility order, proving the equivalence of the least-root-field conditions. Chapter 11 Root Fibers, Return Periods, and Irreducible Constructions 321 

Thus, to find the least root field of a composite polynomial, one may first seek in one fiber the shortest return period dividing all return periods. For linearized polyno-mials, Lemma 11.16 guarantees its existence, and Proposition 11.17 gives a method of computation and an upper bound.

# Affine Symmetries of Root Sets 

Frobenius orbits determine irreducible factors; translations, scalings, and affine transfor-mations preserving root multiplicities determine another partition. Translation orbits yield additive decompositions, while full affine orbits give a normal form that also records the special orbit and its multiplicity. An affine symmetry of the quotient lifts to an affine transformation of the original root set only when its slope satisfies a compatibility con-dition. Here the slope of an affine transformation X 7 → aX + b is its linear coefficient a;compatibility requires scalar multiplication v 7 → av to preserve the translation subspace. Conversely, polynomial differences and coefficient comparison recover these symmetries without first finding the individual roots. This chapter recovers affine stabilizers from root multiplicities and coefficient identities, then describes factorization through orbits and Frobenius return. General polynomial decomposition need not arise from affine symmetry; Chapter 13 turns instead to low-degree representations of subfields. Fix k = Fq, with q = pr, and write σ(x) = xq for relative Frobenius. Root sets and root multiplicities are compared in a finite extension E/k over which the polynomials concerned split completely; enlarge E when necessary. We use X for polynomials in the original coordinate and Y, B as auxiliary variables. A multiset is an unordered collection in which elements may occur with multiplicity. A root multiset thus records both the roots and their multiplicities. 

Descent, factorization, and compositional blocks of root sets Descent concerns stability. Frobenius preserves root multiplicities exactly when the monic root polynomial is defined over the base field. This is Theorem 3.19 with multiplicities retained. 

Factors correspond to orbits. Each Frobenius orbit gives a monic irreducible factor; its length and common root multiplicity determine the degree and exponent, respectively. 

Composition requires complete fibers. A Frobenius-compatible partition is not enough: in the irreducible case, a candidate root block must be a complete fiber of a suitable base-field 

327 328 Chapter 12 Affine Symmetries of Root Sets polynomial; see Theorem 13.4. Stabilizers describe the symmetry of certain fibers, whereas low-degree representations do not require such symmetry. 

Sections 12.1–12.7 recover translation and affine symmetries from root multiplicities, then determine factor degrees and multiplicities by fiber return; irreducibility also yields conjugate-difference criteria, recovery on quotients, and low-degree classifications. 

# 12.1 Root Multiplicities and Three Stabilizers 

Definition 12.1 Let f ∈ k[X] be monic and nonconstant, and put n = deg f . Define its root multiplicity function by 

νf (α) = max {j ≥ 0 : ( X − α)j | f } (α ∈ E).

The set Sf = {α ∈ E : νf (α) > 0} consists of the distinct roots of f . At a point that is not a root, the multiplicity is zero; the element zero itself may or may not be a root. 

Definition 12.2 Define the additive stabilizer , multiplicative stabilizer , and 

affine stabilizer of f , respectively, by 

Vf = {b ∈ E : νf (α + b) = νf (α) for all α ∈ E},Mf = {a ∈ E× : νf (aα ) = νf (α) for all α ∈ E},

Af = {ga,b : X 7 → aX + b : a ∈ E×, b ∈ E, ν f (ga,b (α)) = νf (α) for all α ∈ E}.

The group operation is composition of transformations, namely 

ga,b ◦ ga′,b ′ = gaa ′, b +ab ′ .

For any field K, all transformations X 7 → aX + b, with a ∈ K×, b ∈ K, form the one-dimensional affine group , denoted by AGL 1(K). We call Af (k) = Af ∩ AGL 1(k)

the affine stabilizer over the base field .These groups preserve the entire root multiplicity function and may permute distinct roots; Af (k) additionally requires the transformation coefficients to lie in the base field. For an action of a group G on a set, the point stabilizer of α is Gα = {g ∈ G :

g(α) = α}. An action is called free if every point stabilizer is trivial. The base-field affine stabilizer restricts transformation coefficients, whereas a point stabilizer requires a specified point to be fixed; these are generally different. In particular, the map a 7 → ga, 0Chapter 12 Affine Symmetries of Root Sets 329 

gives a group isomorphism 

Mf ' (Af )0 = {ga, 0 : a ∈ Mf }.

The map Af → E×, ga,b 7 → a, is called the slope map . Its image is the image of the slope map , namely the set 

{a ∈ E× : there exists b ∈ E with ga,b ∈ A f }.

Here b 6 = 0 is allowed, so this image generally differs from Mf , which includes only coefficients of scalings about the origin. 

Proposition 12.3 (Substitution identity) For a 6 = 0 , we have 

ga,b ∈ A f ⇐⇒ f (aX + b) = anf (X).

In particular, b ∈ Vf ⇐⇒ f (X + b) = f (X), and a ∈ Mf ⇐⇒ f (aX ) = anf (X). All these equalities are identities of ordinary polynomials. 

Proof. The substitution X 7 → aX +b is invertible and preserves the multiplicity of every linear factor. Thus the root multiplicities agree if and only if the two polynomials differ by a nonzero constant factor; comparing leading terms gives the factor an.The factor an generally cannot be omitted. For example, scaling X 7 → aX , with 

a ∈ F× 

> qd

− X into a(Xqd

− X). Equality of values at all base-field points also cannot replace a polynomial identity, since the nonzero polynomial Xq −X vanishes throughout the base field. 

Proposition 12.4 (Finiteness and the field of the parameters) The set Vf is a finite 

Fp-linear subspace, and |Vf | | | Sf |. If |Sf | ≥ 2, then Af is finite, all its parameters already lie in the splitting field of f , and enlarging the splitting extension does not enlarge Vf , M f , Af .

Proof. Composition and inversion of translations make Vf an additive subgroup, hence an Fp-subspace. Fix α ∈ Sf . The map b 7 → α + b injects Vf into Sf , proving finiteness. A nonzero translation fixes no point, so each translation orbit has size |Vf |, giving the divisibility assertion. Take two distinct roots α, β . If an affine transformation sends them to γ, η , respec-tively, then 

a = η − γβ − α , b = γ − aα. 330 Chapter 12 Affine Symmetries of Root Sets 

The parameters therefore lie in the splitting field of the polynomial and are uniquely determined by these two images. There are only finitely many such ordered image pairs, and the same reasoning applies in every larger extension. 

Remark 12.5 (The case of a single distinct root) If |Sf | = 1 , then f = ( X − c)n;Frobenius fixes the unique root, so c ∈ k. In this case Vf = {0}, and all affine stabilizing transformations have the form X 7 → c + a(X − c). Allowing a larger field of parameters also allows more slopes a. Thus, whenever we discuss the full finite affine structure independently of the splitting extension below, we assume |Sf | ≥ 2. The results on translation differences and the common p-power do not require this assumption. 

Proposition 12.6 (Compatibility with Frobenius) We have νf (αq) = νf (α), σ(Vf ) = 

Vf , and 

σ ◦ ga,b ◦ σ−1 = gaq ,b q .

Thus Frobenius maps Af to itself and commutes with every transformation in Af (k).The latter conclusion does not in general apply to the whole of Af .

Proof. Applying coefficientwise Frobenius to the linear factorization of f leaves f un-changed, so root multiplicities are preserved. The conjugation formula follows by direct substitution; taking qth powers of the coefficients in the affine identity also shows that the right-hand transformation remains in the stabilizer. The transformation commutes with σ if and only if aq = a, b q = b.

Definition 12.16 (Support period and support-primitive core) Let f ∈ k[X] be monic and nonconstant with f (0) 6 = 0 . Its support period is sp (f ) = gcd {j ≥ 1 : [ Xj ]f 6 = 0 }.

f (X) = fsp (Xs).

Y 7 → Xs ensures uniqueness. Thus the support period is the maximum monomial com-position exponent defined on page 89, and deg fsp = deg f /s. Proposition 12.8 and the preceding proposition together describe it through root multiplicities; see Remark 12.7 for its expression in root-of-unity indices. For this terminology and its applications to decompositions of cyclic codes, see [74]. Support-primitivity requires only that the expo-nents in the support have greatest common divisor one; it requires neither irreducibility nor that the roots generate the multiplicative group. The support period also records a scalar action that may remain on the roots of a binomial. # 12.3 Translation Orbits and Additive Decomposi-tions 

Theorem 12.23 (Translation invariance and subspace composition) Let W be a finite Frobenius-stable Fp-subspace, and let f ∈ k[X]. Then 

f (X + w) = f (X) for all w ∈ W ⇐⇒ f (X) = F (LW (X)) for some F ∈ k[Y ].

The outer polynomial F is unique; if f is monic and nonconstant, so is F , and deg f =

|W | deg F .

Proof. Sufficiency follows immediately from LW (X + w) = LW (X). For necessity, take a finite extension containing W . Since f (w) = f (0) for every w ∈ W , the monic Chapter 12 Affine Symmetries of Root Sets 339 

square-free polynomial LW divides f − f (0) , so 

f (X) = f (0) + LW (X)Q(X).

For every w ∈ W , compare this identity with its translate and cancel the nonzero polynomial LW . It follows that Q is also translation-invariant. Induction on the degree gives f = F (LW ). Nonconstant substitution Y 7 → LW (X) maps nonzero polynomials to nonzero polynomials, so is injective and ensures uniqueness. Since LW ∈ k[X], applying coefficientwise Frobenius to this identity gives another decomposition with the same inner polynomial; uniqueness forces every coefficient of F

to be Frobenius-fixed, so F ∈ k[Y ].On root sets, the same conclusion appears as a product over complete additive cosets. For every α, ∏

> w∈W

(X − α − w) = LW (X) − LW (α).

If W ⊆ Vf , the multiplicities on each root coset are equal, and the multiplicity of LW (α)

as a root of the outer polynomial F equals this common multiplicity. This compositional characterization of translation-invariant polynomials also appears in [50].

Corollary 12.31 (The square-free case) When t > 1, the polynomial f is square-free if and only if e = 1 , w ∈ { 0, 1}, and H is square-free. 

Proof. Distinct fibers in the normal form are disjoint and every fiber polynomial is square-free; the assertion follows pointwise from the multiplicity formulas in the theorem. For an action of a group G on a set S, regard each orbit Gx = {g(x) : g ∈ G} as one element. The resulting set S/G = {Gx : x ∈ S} is called the orbit space . This is a quotient of sets; it does not automatically inherit any field operations the original set may possess.

## 12.4.1 Polynomial Spaces with a Fixed Scalar Multiplier

Fixing a scalar multiplier allows us to describe all polynomials satisfying the condition at once, without finding their normal forms individually.

# 12.5 Recovering the Normal-Form Data: Three Ex-amples 

Proposition 12.36 (A finite coefficient recovery procedure) Let f ∈ k[X] be monic with |Sf | ≥ 2. The following procedure determines the full affine normal form from the coefficients of f .(1) Find e from the p-adic valuations of the positive exponents occurring in the poly-nomial, and extract the unique monic root h = f 1/ e.(2) Take the monic greatest common divisor of the coefficients of powers of X in

(3) Solve the coefficient equations (12.4) in a finite splitting extension to find Af and its slope image μt. These equations may instead be solved for the lower-degree polynomial h. (4) If t > 1, take a generator a 6 = 1 of the slope image and an element ga,b ∈ A f of slope a, and compute

w with U w | h, then recover the unique expression h/U w = H(U t).

Proof. The first four steps follow respectively from the common p-power, the transla-tion coefficient formula, the affine coefficient criterion, and the center descent theorem. Divisibility in the fifth step is tested by ordinary polynomial division. Given a monic nonconstant P and a polynomial R known to belong to k[P ], the outer polynomial can likewise be recovered by removing leading terms: if deg R = m deg P and its leading coefficient is a, replace R by R − aP m, and repeat until zero. At each step the de-gree strictly decreases and the remaining polynomial still belongs to k[P ], so all outer coefficients are recovered. This procedure always terminates, although the enumeration in the third step may be large. Without first factoring f , one may take N = lcm (1 , 2, . . . , n ) and E = FqN :each irreducible factor has degree at most n, so all its roots lie in E. One can enumerate 

E× ×E and test the coefficient equations, but this general bound on the extension degree is usually much larger than the degree actually needed. By contrast, the first two steps take place entirely over k, requiring neither factorization of f nor enumeration of the elements of Vf . When f is irreducible, Subsections 12.7.2–12.7.4 give another route to the full group using specified conjugate differences and a base-field center. # 12.6 Frobenius Return and Recovery of Irreducible Factors 

Symmetry orbits and Frobenius orbits generally give different partitions. The former determine quotient polynomials and the corresponding normal forms, while the latter determine irreducible factors. Lemma 11.1 connects them: after one circuit of the base orbit, the return period in a fiber, multiplied by the base orbit length, is the degree of the original root. We now express this return map as a computable finite permutation, retaining multiplicities as well.

Here the return map is the squaring permutation induced by Frobenius on μ3; its orbits of lengths one and two give the linear and quadratic factors, respectively. Factors from the special orbit can also be recovered directly. On C = c+V , Frobenius has coordinate form 

v 7 −→ vq + ( cq − c).

Its cycle lengths are the degrees of the irreducible factors of U , all of which have multi-plicity ew in f . Together with the free fibers for each P | H, Theorem 12.46 therefore gives all irreducible factorization data of the normal form. 

# 12.7 Stabilizers of Irreducible Polynomials: Restric-tions, Recovery, and Classification 

Irreducibility requires Frobenius to act as a single cycle on all roots. This restricts the sizes of the base-field affine group and translation blocks, and also allows specified con-jugate differences to identify all translations. After passing to the translation quotient, compatible slopes and centered multiplicative orders recover the full affine group; a centered multiplicative order is the multiplicative order obtained by subtracting a can-didate center from a quotient root. This yields explicit classifications in prime degree and in the quartic case in characteristic two. 

## 12.7.1 Restrictions on the Base-Field Group and Translation Group 358 Chapter 12 Affine Symmetries of Root Sets 

Theorem 12.49 (Classification of the base-field affine stabilizer) If f ∈ k[X] is monic and irreducible with n = deg f ≥ 2, then Af (k) is cyclic and its order divides n. More precisely, it is of one of the following types: (1) the trivial group; (2) a group of order p generated by a nonzero translation; (3) a group that becomes the scaling group μd ⊆ k× after a base-field translation of coordinates, where d > 1 and d | gcd (n, q − 1) .In particular, |Vf ∩ k| ≤ p.

Proof. Take a root α of f . For each g ∈ A f (k), there is a unique j mod n such that 

g(α) = αqj

. Since g commutes with Frobenius, 

g(αqi

) = αqi+j

(0 ≤ i < n ).

Thus g acts on all roots as the jth power of the same cycle, and composition corresponds to addition of exponents. An affine transformation fixing two distinct points is the identity, giving a group embedding Af (k) ↪→ Z/nZ. This proves that the group is cyclic of order dividing n.Take a generator g(X) = aX + b. If a = 1 , then b = 0 gives the identity and b 6 = 0 

gives a translation of order p. If a 6 = 1 , then c = b/(1 − a) ∈ k, and g(X) − c = a(X − c).Its order is therefore ord (a) | q − 1, and conjugation by a base-field translation makes it a scaling group. Finally, Vf ∩ k is both a subgroup of a cyclic group and an additive group in which every nonzero element has order p, so its order is at most p.The corresponding root structures are also explicit. The translation type gives 

f = F (Xp − bp−1X), and the scaling type gives f = F (( X − c)d). In the latter case there is no factor X−c, since an irreducible polynomial of degree at least two cannot have a root c ∈ k. The outer polynomial F must be irreducible; in a converse construction, irreducibility of the inner fiber must still be checked by the root fiber criterion, since symmetry alone does not ensure irreducibility. ## 12.7.3 The Translation Quotient and Lifting Compatible Slopes

## 12.7.4 Centered Multiplicative Orders and Recovery of the Full Stabilizer 

The residual group on the translation quotient has no nonzero translations, so if non-trivial it has a unique fixed center. To test candidate centers using root values, first express the multiple equal-difference structure of Section 5.6 as a finite divisor formula.

Proof. Take γ as a primitive N th root of unity. The root index set is C = 〈q〉 ⊆ Z/N Z,of size dN . For r | N , reduction modulo N /r maps C to an orbit of size ord N /r(q), with all nonempty fibers of equal size. Every fiber of the reduction map Z/N Z → Z/( N /r)Z

has r elements, so C is a union of complete fibers if and only if dN = r ord N /r(q).This is equivalent to C being preserved by the additive subgroup of order r in Z/N Z.By Theorem 5.21, such r are exactly the divisors of κC , with maximum κC . The correspondence between index translations and multiplication of root values proves the assertion. When N = 1 , both sides are one.

## 12.7.5 Possible Group Types and Classification in Prime Degree

merely multiplies the trace by λ−1, preserving nonvanishing, so this count is independent of the representative. Multiplying the two counts gives (12.28).

All four rows have q = 3, root order 13, and irreducible degree three; since gcd (13 , 3) = 1 , their multiplicative stabilizers are all trivial as well. Their full affine groups nevertheless differ, because additive relations among root values are not determined by these multiplicative-order data. The first and third rows are reciprocal but have different group types; the third has a trivial group despite having a zero coefficient between its leading and constant terms. Thus inversion need not preserve affine stability, and the full affine group does not explain every coefficient cancellation. An inner component obtained from a translation or affine stabilizer is maximal only within the corresponding symmetry class and does not exhaust general polyno-mial decompositions. For irreducible polynomials, the next chapter gives a criterion independent of affine symmetry, using low-degree representations of subfields.

# Subfield Representations and Polynomial Decomposition 

The central question of this chapter is concrete: why can the same subfield require poly-nomial representatives of different degrees in different power bases? We first compute a quartic example, then use degree profiles, root blocks, and relative traces to explain it.

These minimum degrees were obtained directly, without a composition criterion. The abstract subfield is unchanged; its position in the successive low-degree power spaces has changed. The example raises four questions that organize this chapter: • Why does the minimum representative degree depend on the power basis when the subfield is the same? • When is the lower bound [E : K] attained in a general extension? • Why is equality equivalent to a composition of the defining polynomial? • How can relative traces detect equality and recover root blocks from finitely many data? The degree profile records the subfield’s intersections with low-degree spaces; the defect measures the departure from the optimal distribution. Hankel recovery turns a finite relative-trace prefix back into a root-block equation. We first establish the degree bound and its equality criterion, and then give the full table of tools. 

# 13.1 Low-Degree Representations of Subfields and Polynomial Decomposition 

Subfield classification determines which subfields a finite field contains, but does not specify the degrees needed to represent their elements in given coordinates. Once a generator is fixed, the power basis assigns a degree to each field element; intersections Chapter 13 Subfield Representations and Polynomial Decomposition 377 

of a subfield with the low-degree spaces record its distribution in these coordinates. This section studies such representation degrees and connects them with partitions of irreducible root sets and polynomial decomposition. Here the measure of complexity is the degree of a polynomial representative, rather than the number of field operations or bit operations required for computation. 

## 13.1.1 Power-Basis Degrees and the Degree Profile of a Subfield 

Fix k = Fq, let f ∈ k[X] be monic and irreducible with deg f = n ≥ 2, take a root α,and write 

E = k(α) = Fqn , σ(x) = xq.

Every u ∈ E has a unique polynomial representative hu ∈ k[X] of degree less than n,satisfying u = hu(α). For u 6 = 0 , define its degree in the power basis by deg α(u) = 

deg hu, and set deg α(0) = −∞ . For 0 ≤ t < n , put 

Pt(α) = span k{1, α, . . . , α t}, P−1(α) = {0}.

These spaces form the power-basis degree filtration of E, the increasing sequence of subspaces 

{0} ⊂ P 0(α) ⊂ · · · ⊂ P n−1(α) = E. 

The function deg α records the degree of the polynomial representative in the given power basis; its multiplicative behavior depends on whether reduction modulo f is needed. If 

u, v 6 = 0 and deg α(u) + deg α(v) < n , no degree reduction modulo f is needed after multiplication, so deg α(uv ) = deg α(u) + deg α(v). (13.1) Once the sum of degrees reaches n, this equality may fail. By the subfield classification theorem 3.6, for every d | n, the field E contains a unique subfield 

Kd = Fqd = {u ∈ E : σd(u) = u}.378 Chapter 13 Subfield Representations and Polynomial Decomposition 

Definition 13.2 For d | n and −1 ≤ t < n , define 

Uf,d (t) = Kd ∩ P t(α), ρf,d (t) = dim k Uf,d (t).

The function ρf,d is called the degree profile of Kd in this power basis. For d > 1,define its minimum generator-representation degree by 

κf (d) = min {deg h : h ∈ k[X], deg h < n, k (h(α)) = Kd}. (13.2) The extension Kd/k has a generator, and every element has a unique representative of degree less than n, so the minimum exists. Allowing arbitrary degrees for h gives the same minimum: first take the remainder modulo f . The value ρf,d (t) records the dimension of the whole intersection space, whereas κf (d) requires a value generating the specified subfield; the two must not be confused. When d is composite, the presence of an element of the intersection space outside the base field does not by itself imply that the space contains a generator of Kd/k.

Proposition 13.3 (Coordinate dependence and invariance) The degree profile and minimum generator-representation degree are independent of the choice of a conjugate root of f . They are also unchanged upon replacing the generator by α′ = aα + b, with 

a ∈ k×, b ∈ k. In general, they depend on the generator, not merely on the abstract field E.

Proof. If α′ = σj (α), then σj fixes k pointwise, preserves Kd, and maps Pt(α) bijectively onto Pt(α′). It also preserves degrees of elements over k, so both kinds of data are unchanged. If α′ = aα +b, binomial expansion gives Pt(α′) ⊆ P t(α), and α = a−1(α′ −b)

gives the reverse inclusion. The degree filtrations are therefore identical. Example 13.1 at the start of this chapter already shows that a general change of generator may change these data. When d = 1 , we have ρf, 1(t) = 1 for 0 ≤ t < n ; when d = n, ρf,n (t) = t + 1 and 

κf (n) = 1 . Whenever a nontrivial decomposition is considered below, assume 1 < d < n ,and write 

m = n/d = [ E : Kd].

Theorem 13.4 (Least degree and functional decomposition) Suppose 1 < d < n , d | n,and put m = n/d. Then 

κf (d) ≥ m. (13.3) Equality holds if and only if there exist monic P, h ∈ k[X] such that

f | Pβ (h), n ≤ d deg h. 

Thus deg h ≥ m. If deg h = m, divide h by its leading coefficient to make it monic; this does not change the subfield generated by its value. Denote the monic minimal polynomial of the new value by P . Then f and P (h) are monic of the same degree, and the former divides the latter, so they are equal. Conversely, if (13.4) holds, then P must be irreducible, since otherwise a nontrivial factorization, after substitution of h, would make f reducible. Thus h(α) has degree d,and uniqueness of the subfield implies that it generates Kd. This gives κf (d) ≤ m, and the lower bound yields equality. The equality theorem gives the first central criterion. Theorem 13.8 (Equivalent characterizations of zero defect) Suppose 1 < d < n and 

m = n/d. The following conditions are equivalent: (1) κf (d) = m;(2) ρf,d (m) = 2 ;(3) ρf,d (t) = 1 + bt/mc for every 0 ≤ t < n ;(4) λi = im for 0 ≤ i < d , or equivalently ∆f (d) = 0 .They are also equivalent to the decomposition in Theorem 13.4.

This proof shows why belonging to a subfield and generating it must generally be distinguished: in this argument, attainment of the lower bound m is what allows degree comparison to force every such element outside the base field to generate Kd/k. # 13.2 Duality Between Subfield Degree Profiles and Relative Traces 

Low-degree representations of a subfield are determined by its intersections with the power-basis degree spaces; trace pairing converts these intersections into orthogonality conditions. Relative trace expresses these conditions over the subfield, recovering the entire degree profile from the ranks of spans of successive trace values. Continue to assume that f ∈ k[X] is monic and irreducible with deg f = n, E = k(α), and f (α) = 0 ,and fix 

1 < d < n, d | n, K = Kd = Fqd , m = n/d. 

The degree spaces Pt(α), profile ρf,d , and defect ∆f (d) retain their definitions from the preceding section.

Define the weighted trace pairing on E by 

〈u, v 〉α = Tr E/k

( uv f ′(α)

)

An irreducible polynomial over a finite field is separable, so f ′(α) 6 = 0 ; invertibility of nonzero scalar multiplication and nondegeneracy of the trace pairing show that this pairing is nondegenerate. Write U ⊥α for the orthogonal complement with respect to it, to distinguish it from that for the ordinary trace pairing. Chapter 13 Subfield Representations and Polynomial Decomposition 391 

Proposition 13.16 (Reverse orthogonality of the degree filtration) For −1 ≤ t < n ,we have 

Pt(α)⊥α = Pn−2−t(α). (13.12) Here P−1(α) = {0}.

Proof. If 0 ≤ t ≤ n − 2, u ∈ P t(α), and v ∈ P n−2−t(α), then uv has a polynomial representative of degree at most n − 2. The leading-coefficient formula (7.1) gives 

〈u, v 〉α = 0 . Thus the right side is contained in the left. Nondegeneracy gives both sides dimension n − t − 1, so they are equal. For t = −1 and t = n − 1, the equalities are 

{0}⊥α = E and E⊥α = {0}, respectively. The weight 1/ f ′(α) turns the trace functional into the leading-coefficient functional, making the orthogonal complement of a low-degree space another low-degree space. For the ordinary trace pairing, a scalar factor 1/ f ′(α) must be inserted on the right; formula (13.12) cannot be retained unchanged.

## 13.2.3 Two Kinds of Jumps and a Trace-Rank Criterion for De-composition 

Since the trace rank increases by at most one per step and reaches d by n − 1, define the trace-rank jump positions by 

μi = min {s ≥ 0 : rf,d (s) ≥ i + 1 }, 0 ≤ i < d. 

Here the μi are integers listed in increasing order, not the integer Möbius function μ(·).

Proof. For 0 ≤ t < n , subtract (13.14) at t − 1 from the identity at t to obtain

# 13.4 Recovering Root Blocks and Representation Structure from Relative Traces 

The trace-rank function over k records the subfield degree profile; over the subfield K,the same trace values satisfy a linear recurrence. Its minimal polynomial is exactly the relative root-block polynomial, so the relative trace sequence also recovers the co-efficient rank and rational representation of the preceding section. The same matrix can admit both interpretations, but the coefficient fields and node hypotheses must not be conflated. In particular, the minimum recurrence order is not the rank of an arbitrary short prefix.

The opening example leads to the following connections within this chapter: • Defining equations and Frobenius fixed-point matrices recover intersections of sub-fields with low-degree power spaces. • Degree jumps, exact generator counts, and defects quantify the subfield’s position in the chosen power basis. • A minimum representative degree of n/d is equivalent to a polynomial composition of the corresponding degrees. • Nonconstant root-block coefficients and coefficient rank distinguish polynomial rep-resentations from rational representations allowing denominators. • Base-field ranks of relative traces and shortest recurrences over the subfield recover degree profiles and root-block equations, respectively. Chapter 13 Subfield Representations and Polynomial Decomposition 409 

The same relative trace sequence gives different information over two coefficient fields: prefix ranks over the base field k recover the degree profile of the subfield; the shortest recurrence over the subfield K recovers the relative root-block polynomial. The former records the position of the subfield in the power basis; the latter determines the root block and its coefficient space, and hence tests low-degree generator representations and functional decompositions.

# Orbit Composition, Recursive Lifting, and Trace Descent 

Direct products and tensor products of root orbits provide composition constructions, while return maps provide recursive lifting. Trace can also be used to descend con-structions from an auxiliary extension to the base field; combining these local period conditions yields irreducible polynomials of prescribed degrees. The resultant expresses the product of conjugate values as a norm, and its symmetry under interchange yields polynomial reciprocity laws. Polynomial iteration requires the root fibers to remain irreducible at every level; critical orbits and norm descent for power residues can reduce certain infinite conditions to finite tests in the base field. The following table places the one-step fiber criteria of Chapter 11 alongside the recursive and descent constructions of this chapter. Let P be monic irreducible of degree n, let α be a root, and put E = k(α). The key to a one-step construction is that the return map has a single orbit on the entire fiber; a recursive construction must also preserve the data needed for the next step. Trace descent additionally requires ruling out membership in a smaller subfield. The evaluation points in Figure 5.2 are precisely such pairs of roots, with Frobenius acting on both coordinates simultaneously. The operation on roots then sends each pair to its sum or product; distinct evaluation points may have the same im-age, so the resulting multiplicities must be retained. Moreover, f (g1g2) = ( f g1)( f g2),and the same holds in the other variable. 

Theorem 14.1 (Composition of coprime orbits) Suppose that (G, ) is a Frobenius-stable group and that Frobenius preserves its group operation. If the roots of monic polynomials f, g all lie in G, and their degrees are m, n ≥ 1, respectively, then f  g is irreducible if and only if both f, g are irreducible and gcd (m, n ) = 1 .

Proof. Distributivity of the composed-product operation over ordinary products shows that irreducibility of the result forces both f, g to be irreducible. If d = gcd (m, n ) > 1,every root pair (α, β ) has period at most lcm (m, n ) = mn /d, and its composed value has period at most this number, so it cannot be a root of an irreducible polynomial of degree mn .Conversely, suppose that f and g are irreducible and that m, n are coprime. Let 

γ = α  β have period t. Clearly t | mn . Since σmt (γ) = γ and σmt (α) = α, cancellation gives σmt (β) = β. Hence n | mt , and therefore n | t. Similarly, m | t, so mn | t. Thus 

t = mn , and the degree of the composed value over the base field equals the degree of the composed polynomial. The additive group allows zero roots; the multiplicative group requires f (0) g(0) 6 = 0 .For example, X ⊕ g = g, whereas X g = Xdeg g, so the nonzero condition cannot be Chapter 14 Orbit Composition, Recursive Lifting, and Trace Descent 417 

omitted in the multiplicative case. Any binary polynomial operation compatible with Frobenius defines a composition, but need not satisfy the irreducibility statement above: the proof uses cancellation in a group.

# 14.3 Power-Residue Symbols, Norms, and Polyno-mial Reciprocity 

Throughout this section, k = Fq. The resultant multiplies the values of one polynomial at all roots of another. When these roots form a single Frobenius orbit, this product is a norm. Taking a suitable power of the norm then determines whether an element of the residue field is a power of the prescribed exponent. Interchanging the two root sets changes the resultant only by a sign, yielding a polynomial power-residue reciprocity law [1, Chapter 9].

# 14.5 Recursive Quadratic Lifting: Self-Reciprocal Orbits 

Theorem 14.13 (The Q-transform in characteristic two) Let k have characteristic two, and let P = Xn + cn−1Xn−1 + · · · + c0 ∈ k[X] be monic irreducible with c0 6 = 0 .Retain the convention c1 = 1 when n = 1 , and suppose that Tr k/F2 (c1/c0) = 1 , Tr k/F2 (cn−1) = 1 .

Put P0 = P and Pj+1 = Q(Pj ). Then each Pj is irreducible of degree 2j n, and is self-reciprocal for j ≥ 1.

Proof. By Theorem 11.11, the first trace condition ensures that P1 is irreducible. For monic F of degree N , the constant term of Q(F ) is one, and its linear coefficient is the next-to-leading coefficient of F . Since Q(F ) is self-reciprocal, its linear and next-to-leading coefficients are equal. Thus, from P1 onward, both coefficients remain equal 426 Chapter 14 Orbit Composition, Recursive Lifting, and Trace Descent 

to cn−1. The second trace condition then ensures irreducibility of the quadratic fiber polynomial at every step. 

Example 14.14 Starting from P0 = X + 1 ∈ F2[X], we obtain successively 

P1 = X2 + X + 1 ,P2 = X4 + X3 + X2 + X + 1 ,P3 = X8 + X7 + X6 + X4 + X2 + X + 1 .

At each step, Frobenius acts transitively on the union of the two-element fibers over the preceding orbit, producing an orbit of twice its length.

Proof. If F has degree N , then 

R(F )(1) R(F )( −1) = ( −1) N 22N F (1) F (−1) .

When −1 is a square or N is even, the square class is unchanged. The hypotheses ensure that the first transform preserves the square class; all subsequent degrees are even, so every later transform also preserves it. Successive application of the R-transform criterion in Chapter 11 proves irreducibility at every iteration. For a monic polynomial 

F of degree N , the leading and constant coefficients of R(F ) are both one, and 

X2N R(F )( X−1) = R(F )( X).

Hence all polynomials from the first step onward are monic and self-reciprocal. When choosing the initial polynomial, the nonsquare product of its values controls the first layer; when q ≡ 3 ( mod 4) , the additional even-degree condition keeps this square class nonsquare at the next layer. Over F5, one may start from X − 2, since the product of its values at 1 and −1 is 3, a nonsquare. The odd initial degree causes the first transform to change the square class. Thus one-step irreducibility and a continuing recursion impose different conditions: the former requires the current quadratic fiber to be irreducible, while the latter also requires this criterion to be preserved by the transform. 

# 14.6 Polynomial Iteration and Dynamical Irre-ducibility 

The preceding recursive constructions preserve a trace, a square class, or a multiplica-tive order at every step, so that each new root fiber continues to have a single return orbit. Repeated substitution of one fixed polynomial gives another class of towers of irreducible polynomials. The root-fiber criterion still applies, but we must explain why the conditions controlling the fibers hold at every level. 

## 14.6.1 Prescribed Targets and Successive Root Fibers Chapter 14 Orbit Composition, Recursive Lifting, and Trace Descent 429 

Definition 14.17 (Dynamical irreducibility) Let h ∈ k[X], with deg h = d ≥ 2, and set 

h◦0(X) = X, h◦(n+1) = h ◦ h◦n.

If h◦n is irreducible in k[X] for every n ≥ 1, then h is called dynamically irreducible ,or stable . More generally, if τ ∈ k and every h◦n(X) − τ is irreducible, then the pair 

(h, τ ) is called dynamically irreducible. Ordinary stability corresponds to the target τ = 0 . Iteration here takes place in the polynomial ring; the degree is dn, without reduction modulo Xq − X.

Corollary 14.18 (Fiber criterion for iteration) Suppose that h◦n(X) − τ is irreducible over k, where n ≥ 0, and choose a root βn. Then h◦(n+1) (X) − τ is irreducible if and only if h(X) − βn is irreducible over k(βn). For n = 0 , take β0 = τ ; for n ≥ 1, we have 

[k(βn) : k] = dn.

Proof. Apply Theorem 11.2 to the monic normalization of the outer polynomial h◦n(Y )−

τ and the inner polynomial h(X).When every level is irreducible, we may choose h(βn+1 ) = βn, obtaining 

k ⊆ k(β1) ⊆ k(β2) ⊆ · · · , [k(βn+1 ) : k(βn)] = d. 

Each multiplication of the degree by d corresponds to a full return orbit in a new root fiber. The iteration level n and a separate base-extension degree r have different roles: the former changes the polynomial to h◦n − τ while keeping k fixed; the latter keeps that polynomial fixed and replaces Frobenius σ by σr. If this level is irreducible over 

k, Theorem 5.15 gives gcd (dn, r ) distinct irreducible factors over Fqr , each of degree 

dn/ gcd (dn, r ). Thus a dynamically irreducible tower remains dynamically irreducible after base extension if and only if gcd (d, r ) = 1 ; see Exercise 14.6. 

Proposition 14.19 (Transforming the polynomial and target together) Let φ(X) = 

uX + v, where u ∈ k× and v ∈ k, and put g = φ ◦ h ◦ φ−1. Then 

g◦n(X) − φ(τ ) = u(h◦n(φ−1(X)) − τ ).

Thus (h, τ ) is dynamically irreducible if and only if (g, φ (τ )) is. 

Proof. Conjugation commutes with iteration, so g◦n = φ ◦ h◦n ◦ φ−1. Substitution of 

φ(τ ) = uτ + v gives the formula; invertible linear substitution and multiplication by a nonzero constant preserve irreducibility. 430 Chapter 14 Orbit Composition, Recursive Lifting, and Trace Descent 

We refer to this simultaneous change of polynomial and target as pointed affine conjugacy . Prescribing the target keeps every root fiber after an affine change of variables in correspondence with an original fiber. For example, stability corresponds to the new target v after conjugation by a translation; see [22]. 

## 14.6.2 Iteration of Power Maps and the Binomial Criterion 

Theorem 14.20 (Stability of translated power maps) Let d ≥ 2, ζ ∈ k×, and put 

f (X) = ( X + ζ)d − ζ. Then 

f ◦n(X) = ( X + ζ)dn

− ζ.

Proof. The map φ(X) = X + ζ gives φ ◦ f ◦ φ−1 = Xd, proving the iteration formula. A linear substitution reduces irreducibility at level n to that of Xdn

− ζ. Since dn and d

## 14.6.3 Quadratic Iteration and Finite Critical Orbits 

For a nonconstant polynomial H whose formal derivative H′ is nonzero, a root of H′

in a splitting extension is called a critical point , and the corresponding value of H is called a critical value . The successive images H◦j (γ), j ≥ 0, of a critical point γ form its critical orbit . We now take h = X2 + c in odd characteristic; its unique critical point is 0.

Theorem 14.22 (Square-class criterion for quadratic iteration) Let q be odd, h =

X2 + c ∈ k[X], and τ ∈ k. Then (h, τ ) is dynamically irreducible if and only if 

τ − c is a nonsquare , h◦j (0) − τ is a nonsquare (j ≥ 2) .

Here a nonsquare means an element of k× that is not a square. 

Proof. The first level is X2 − (τ − c), whose irreducibility condition is precisely that 

τ − c is a nonsquare. Suppose that level n is irreducible, with n ≥ 1, choose a root βn,and put E = k(βn). By Corollary 14.18, the next level is irreducible if and only if βn − c

is a nonsquare in E. The power-residue expression for the norm, formula (14.2), gives 

z(q2n −1)/2 = NE/k(z)(q−1)/2 (z ∈ E×).

Thus nonsquareness can be tested in k by taking the norm; the norm of zero is also zero. Since 2n is even, NE/k(βn − c) = h◦n(c) − τ = h◦(n+1) (0) − τ. 

Thus level n + 1 is controlled precisely by the listed critical-orbit value of index n + 1 .Induction on the levels proves the result. The critical-orbit criterion for quadratics is a basic result in the study of dynamical irreducibility; see [30, 22]. In this proof, the relevant critical-orbit value minus the target is the norm of the extension-field fiber parameter, so one square-class condition controls the entire two-element fiber. 

Corollary 14.23 (A finite test for quadratic stability) Retain the hypotheses of the preceding theorem. First test τ − c, then iterate point by point starting from h◦2(0) .If every value h◦j (0) − τ encountered is a nonsquare until an orbit point repeats, then 

(h, τ ) is dynamically irreducible. In particular, it suffices that h◦n(X) − τ be irreducible for 1 ≤ n ≤ (q + 3)/2 .432 Chapter 14 Orbit Composition, Recursive Lifting, and Trace Descent 

Proof. Once an orbit point repeats, all subsequent points repeat, so the preceding the-orem proves the first assertion. For the stated bound, put B = ( q + 3)/2 and suppose that h◦n(X)−τ is irreducible for 1 ≤ n ≤ B. The successive norm tests in the preceding proof show that τ − c and all values h◦j (0) − τ , 2 ≤ j ≤ B, are nonsquares. Hence the 

B − 1 = ( q + 1)/2 orbit points h◦j (0) , 2 ≤ j ≤ B, all lie in 

τ + {u ∈ k× : u is a nonsquare },

a set of (q − 1)/2 elements. Two of these points therefore coincide. Every subse-quent point repeats within this segment, so all later square-class conditions hold as well. Together with the first-level condition, the preceding theorem gives dynamical irreducibility. This finite test examines base-field elements in the critical orbit, without expanding iterate polynomials of degree 2n.

## 14.6.5 Mixed Compositions and Forward-Invariant Sets in the Base Field 

Definition 14.29 (Dynamically irreducible set) Let A = {f1, . . . , f s} ⊆ k[X], with deg fi ≥ 2 for every i. If, for every length r ≥ 1 and every choice of indices i1, . . . , i r,the composition fi1 ◦· · ·◦ fir is irreducible, then A is called a dynamically irreducible set .For translated power families, norm descent for power residues allows mixed compo-sitions of arbitrary length to be controlled by a forward-invariant set in the base field; see [56]. 

Theorem 14.30 (A finite criterion for translated power families of odd degree) Let 

d ≥ 3 be odd, suppose that every prime ` | d divides q − 1, and put 

fi(X) = ( X − ai)d + bi (1 ≤ i ≤ s), ai, b i ∈ k. 

Let S ⊆ k be the smallest set containing all bi and satisfying fi(S) ⊆ S. Then 

{f1, . . . , f s} is dynamically irreducible if and only if every element of S is nonzero and is not an `-th power in k for any prime ` | d.Chapter 14 Orbit Composition, Recursive Lifting, and Trace Descent 437 

Proof. Let G be an irreducible mixed composition, let D = deg G be odd, choose a root 

α, and put E = k(α). The fiber polynomial for the next substitution of fi on the right is 

fi(X) − α = ( X − ai)d − (α − bi).

By the binomial criterion, it is irreducible if and only if α − bi 6 = 0 and it is not an `-th power for any ` | d. The norm expression gives 

(α − bi)(qD −1)/ ℓ = NE/k(α − bi)(q−1)/ ℓ, NE/k(α − bi) = ( −1) DG(bi) = −G(bi).

All ` are odd, and −1 = ( −1) ℓ, so changing the sign does not change `-th-power status. Thus G ◦ fi is irreducible precisely when G(bi) satisfies the stated power-residue condi-tions. The same argument applies to the initial outer polynomial G = X, with D = 1 

and α = 0 , giving the irreducibility condition for each fi.The set S consists exactly of all G(bi), where G runs through all mixed compositions and the identity polynomial X. If S satisfies the conditions, the one-step equivalence above and induction on composition length ensure that all mixed compositions are irre-ducible. Conversely, if all mixed compositions are irreducible, applying the equivalence to each G and fi shows that every G(bi) satisfies the conditions, proving necessity as well. Starting from S0 = {b1, . . . , b s}, repeatedly adjoining every fi(x) produces S. At most q distinct elements occur; by recording the elements already processed, each ele-ment need only be evaluated once under each fi. Thus the condition on infinitely many mixed compositions in this family admits a finite test in the base field. 

Example 14.31 In F7, the nonzero cubes are 1, 6. Put 

f1 = X3 + 3 , f2 = X3 + 4 , S = {2, 3, 4, 5}.

For x = 2 , 4, we have (f1(x), f 2(x)) = (4 , 5) ; for x = 3 , 5, we have (f1(x), f 2(x)) = (2 , 3) .Thus S contains both constant terms, is closed under both polynomials, and consists entirely of noncubes. The preceding theorem ensures that every mixed composition is irreducible; a composition of length r has degree 3r.438 Chapter 14 Orbit Composition, Recursive Lifting, and Trace Descent 

## 14.6.6 Denominators of Rational Iterates and Inverse Stability 

Definition 14.32 (Inverse stability) Let ψ ∈ k[X], with deg ψ ≥ 2, and put Ψ = 1/ ψ.For each integer n ≥ 1, write its rational iterate as 

Ψ◦n(X) = An(X)

Bn(X), gcd (An, B n) = 1 , Bn monic .

If all Bn are irreducible and pairwise distinct, then ψ is called inversely stable .The roots of these denominators are the finite poles of the corresponding rational iterates: the points where the denominator vanishes and the numerator does not. The reciprocal additive recursion of Section 14.4 gives an example for a fixed rational map.

The constructions above preserve multiplicative orders, square classes, noncube classes, or nonzero traces after reciprocation. The quadratic critical-orbit criterion and the forward-invariant set for translated power families of odd degree give two explicit finite tests. General cubic fibers contain further information: in characteristic different from 2, 3, a nonzero square discriminant allows both irreducibility and complete split-ting, so the square class of the discriminant gives only partial factorization information. ## 14.7.1 Counting Sparse Families and Conjugate Roots 

Every irreducible f of degree at least two satisfies f (0) 6 = 0 , f (1) 6 = 0 , and gcd (f, f ′) = 1 .Hence an irreducible polynomial over F2 of degree at least two has an odd number of nonzero terms and at least one term of odd degree. These are only necessary conditions. 

Proposition 14.35 (A square-root estimate for a sparse family) Let n ≥ 2, q = pr,and p - 2n(n − 1) , and put 

Tn(q) = #{b ∈ Fq : Xn + X + b is irreducible }.

Then there is a constant Bn, depending only on n, such that 

∣∣∣Tn(q) − qn

∣∣∣ ≤ Bn

√q. 

This is a special case of Cohen’s polynomial distribution theorem; for a proof, see [17, Theorem 1 and p. 257]. Critical points and critical values are defined in Section 14.6. The restriction p - n(n − 1) on the characteristic has the following interpretation. Put 

H(X) = Xn + X; then H′(X) = nX n−1 + 1 . Its roots are all nonzero, and H′′ (X) = 

n(n − 1) Xn−2 is nonzero at these roots, so there are exactly n − 1 distinct critical points. If H′(β) = 0 , then 

βn−1 = − 1

n, H(β) = n − 1

n β. 

The coefficient (n − 1)/ n is nonzero, so the critical values are also pairwise distinct. The characteristic condition also excludes p = 2 , as required by the cited distribution theorem. For Xn +X +b with distinct roots, irreducibility is equivalent to Frobenius acting on its root set as an n-cycle. The factor 1/ n in the main term agrees with the proportion 

(n−1)!/ n! of n-cycles in the symmetric group Sn; turning this group-theoretic proportion into a distribution of parameters b, and controlling the square-root error, still requires the distribution theorem in the cited paper. For fixed n, the estimate ensures the existence of such irreducible trinomials over sufficiently large finite fields satisfying the characteristic condition; it does not ensure existence over every small finite field.

# Polynomial Functions and Fiber Permutations 

Functions on a finite field are determined by their values on a finite root set. Starting from low-degree representatives, this chapter studies permutations, value sets, differ-ence preservation, and compatibility between maps on fibers and on their base sets. Traces and power maps provide two natural projections: a map on the smaller base, together with control within each fiber, constructs a permutation and determines its cycles. Difference rigidity identifies functions forced to have linear or semilinear struc-ture; Section 17.12 will apply it to common permutation groups of cyclic codes. The prerequisites here are root-set evaluation, traces and norms, and linearized polynomials, not coding theory. 

# 15.1 Function Algebras and Low-Degree Polynomial Representatives 

Polynomial representatives of functions in this section are reduced modulo Xq − X.Dynamical irreducibility in Section 14.6 concerns the irreducibility of h◦n(X) − τ for a fixed target τ , and the successive root fibers arising in extension fields. Exercise 14.7 compares two families of iterates with the same function values on the base field.

An arbitrary polynomial vanishes everywhere if and only if it is divisible by ∏

# 15.2 Permutation Polynomials and Inverse Functions 

A polynomial F ∈ Fq[X] is called a permutation polynomial if it induces a bijection on Fq. Its inverse function is represented by a unique polynomial G of degree less than 

q, satisfying 

G(F (X)) ≡ F (G(X)) ≡ X (mod Xq − X).

These inverse relations hold modulo Xq − X; they need not hold as identities in the ordinary polynomial ring. In terms of root sets, F is a permutation polynomial if and only if 

∏

> a∈Fq

(T − F (a)) = T q − T, 

or, equivalently, if gcd (F (X)−b, X q −X) has degree exactly one for every b ∈ Fq. These conditions say, respectively, that distinct inputs have distinct images and that each fiber has exactly one element.

Theorem 15.3 (Lacunarity obstruction over a prime field) Let p be prime and g ∈

# 15.3 Difference Preservation and Algebraic Rigidity 

How much of a function is determined by its local differences? If parallel difference quo-tients are independent of the base point, the differences recover linearity over the prime field. Preservation of the multiplicative cosets of nonzero differences instead forces rigid-ity through low-degree function representatives and Frobenius automorphisms. A multi-plicative subgroup constraint on second divided differences recovers ordinary quadratics through compatibility between base points; constant values for a fixed shape recover lin-earity over its generated subfield. Over an integer residue ring, the same question is expressed by cyclotomic difference orbits and reduced by the Chinese remainder the-orem to prime-power moduli. These conditions link constraints on pairs or triples to Chapter 15 Polynomial Functions and Fiber Permutations 451 

global algebraic form. Over residue rings, however, certain additive blocks also allow extra non-affine permutations, so rigidity and its exceptions must both be identified.

## 15.3.2 Multiplicative Coset Preservation and Rigidity 

The preceding theorem recovers all Fp-affine maps from parallel difference quotients. We now impose a different condition—preservation of multiplicative cosets of nonzero differences—which yields a stronger rigidity conclusion without assuming parallel difference-quotient invariance. ## 15.3.4 Difference Orbits and Local Rigidity at Prime Powers 

Every nonzero difference in a field can be used as a divisor. Over a residue ring, a nonzero difference need not be a unit, so we retain the orbit condition rather than form a quotient. This connects multiplicative coset preservation over fields with the exponent orbits of Chapter 5. 

Definition 15.16 (Preservation of cyclotomic difference orbits) Let n ≥ 2, R = Z/nZ,and K ≤ R×. For z ∈ R, put Kz = {uz : u ∈ K}. A function f : R → R preserves cyclotomic difference orbits if 

f (x) − f (y) ∈ K(x − y) (x, y ∈ R). (15.14) Write RK (n) for the set of these functions, and put Aff K (n) = {x 7 → ux + b : u ∈ K, b ∈ R}.

Here K need not be generated by a field size; when K = 〈q〉, the sets Kz are the 

q-cyclotomic cosets modulo n. Multiplication by a unit cannot send a nonzero element to zero, so condition (15.14) makes f a permutation automatically. It gives the equality 

K(f (x) − f (y)) = K(x − y), so these permutations are closed under composition and inversion. Thus RK (n) is a group containing Aff K (n).If n = p is prime and K 6 = F× 

> p

, the Carlitz–McConnel theorem gives RK (p) = 

Aff K (p), since the prime field has no nontrivial automorphism. If K = F× 

> p

, every permutation satisfies the condition; all of them are affine precisely when p = 2 , 3. Indeed, the affine group has p(p − 1) elements, equal to 2! and 3! in these two cases. For p ≥ 5,a transposition fixing every other point is not affine. At a prime-power modulus we must also compare congruence layers. Theorem 15.20 (Multiple equal-difference structure and non-affine symmetries) Let 

p be an odd prime, a ≥ 2, R = Z/paZ, and K = 〈q〉 ≤ R×, where gcd (p, q ) = 1 . Put

It asserts the existence of extra permutations, not that every preserving map is non-affine. 

Proof. The unit group at an odd prime power is cyclic of order pa−1(p − 1) , so 0 ≤ t ≤

a − 1. For 1 ≤ s ≤ a, the group 1 + psR has order pa−s. Subgroups of a cyclic group are determined by their orders; hence 

1 + psR ⊆ K ⇐⇒ pa−s | τ ⇐⇒ a − s ≤ t. 

The additive stabilizer H+(C) is proper, so it is some psR. Proposition 5.22 shows that the largest admissible ideal is pa−tR. Now use κC = |H+(C)| and ωC = τ /κC from Theorem 5.21 to obtain the formulas and the equivalence of the first two conditions. For the modulus pa, only the second exception of Theorem 15.19 can occur. Its condition is 

∆pa (pa−1) = 1 + pa−1R ⊆ K. 

This subgroup has order p, so the containment is equivalent to p | τ , and hence to the third condition. When it holds, formula (15.16) already supplies the non-affine permutation; no further existence argument is needed. 466 Chapter 15 Polynomial Functions and Fiber Permutations 

Multiple equal-difference structure does not always strengthen rigidity. Here it re-tains a complete additive direction, allowing perturbations within the corresponding congruence layers to preserve each difference orbit. The result also follows from the odd-characteristic Galois-ring classification of Evdokimov–Ponomarenko [25, Theorem 1.4]; the unit-group structure and local rigidity already established here give a direct proof. The equivalence is restricted to the stated odd prime-power case: modulo 8, the group 

K = 〈5〉 = {1, 5} has H+(K) = {0, 4}, but Lemma 15.18 gives RK (8) = Aff K (8) . Thus nontrivial equal-difference blocks and extra non-affine symmetries cannot be identified without further conditions at powers of two. 

Example 15.21 (The field of nine elements and the residue ring modulo nine) The field F9 in Example 15.10 admits a nontrivial Frobenius automorphism. The ring Z/9 Z

is different: its additive group is cyclic, so an additive automorphism is determined by the image of 1. For K = {1, −1} ≤ (Z/9 Z)×, we have ∆9(3) = {1, 4, 7} 6 ⊆ K. Thus its difference-orbit-preserving maps are exactly ±x + b, numbering 18 . For K = 〈4〉 =

{1, 4, 7}, the second exception holds and x 7 → x + 3( x mod 3) 2 is nonaffine. The residue-ring exceptions therefore arise from local perturbations of congruence layers, not from field Frobenius automorphisms. These results recover prime-field linearity from parallel differences, Frobenius from multiplicative cosets of field differences, quadratic polynomials from second divided dif-ferences on all triples, and, after excluding the stated exceptions, a common multiplier from residue-ring difference orbits. Their underlying sets and permitted local variations differ; in particular, Fpa and Z/paZ are distinct algebraic structures when a > 1. Sec-tion 17.12 will apply the last rigidity theorem to the coordinate symmetries common to all cyclic codes, using root-of-unity Fourier projections. 

# 15.4 Value Sets, Fibers, and Minimal Value Set Poly-nomials 

Every fiber of a permutation polynomial has one element. For a general polynomial, computing the nonempty fibers and their sizes determines the number of values actually attained. The root bound gives a general restriction, and subspace polynomials provide constructions attaining it. Chapter 15 Polynomial Functions and Fiber Permutations 467

# 15.6 The AGW Criterion and Additive and Multi-plicative Fibers 

Descending a map to a smaller set separates the permutation property into two con-ditions: images of distinct fibers must remain separate, and no collisions may occur within a fiber. This set-theoretic principle is called the AGW criterion ; see [2, 26]. Trace fibers are cosets of an additive subgroup, whereas nonzero power-map fibers are cosets of a multiplicative subgroup; the two constructions therefore have the same form of criterion. 

## 15.6.1 A Fiber Criterion for Finite Sets 

Lemma 15.34 (AGW criterion) Let A, S, S be finite sets with |S| = |S|, and suppose that 

λ : A −→ S, λ : A −→ S

are surjective. If maps F : A → A and ϕ : S → S satisfy λ ◦ F = ϕ ◦ λ, then F is a permutation if and only if ϕ is bijective and F is injective on every fiber λ−1(s). When these conditions hold, each restriction 

F : λ−1(s) −→ λ−1(ϕ(s)) 

is bijective. 

Proof. If F is bijective, then λF is surjective, and commutativity implies that ϕ is surjective. Since the two base sets are finite and have equal size, ϕ is bijective; the restriction of F to each fiber is certainly injective. Conversely, if F (x) = F (y), applying 

λ to both sides gives ϕ(λ(x)) = ϕ(λ(y)) . By injectivity of ϕ, the elements x, y lie in the same fiber; injectivity within that fiber then gives x = y. Hence F is injective and therefore bijective on the finite set A. Finally, each point in the target fiber has an 

F -preimage, which commutativity and injectivity of ϕ force to lie in λ−1(s). Thus the restriction is also surjective. 476 Chapter 15 Polynomial Functions and Fiber Permutations 

The commutativity relation is expressed by the following diagram: 

A AS SFϕλ λ

When S = S and λ = λ = π, this is the fiber permutation criterion compatible with 

πF = ϕπ . To compute the cycles of F as well, choose one fiber over each cycle of ϕ and apply Lemma 11.1: the total cycle length is the product of the base-cycle length and the fiber return period. 

## 15.6.2 Constructing Permutations Along Trace Fibers 

Theorem 15.35 Let E = Fqn , k = Fq, and a ∈ k×, and let g : k → E be any function. Put 

F (x) = ax + g(Tr E/k(x)) , ϕ(t) = at + Tr E/k(g(t)) .

Then F permutes E if and only if ϕ permutes k. In this case, 

F −1(z) = a−1(z − g(ϕ−1(Tr E/k(z))) ).

Proof. Linearity of the trace gives Tr ◦F = ϕ◦Tr. The trace is surjective, and every fiber has qn−1 elements. On the fiber Tr (x) = t, F is the affine map x 7 → ax + g(t), which is injective because a 6 = 0 , and hence maps bijectively onto the corresponding target fiber. Lemma 15.34 gives the permutation criterion. If F (x) = z, then Tr (x) = ϕ−1(Tr (z)) ;substituting into the definition and solving for x gives the inverse formula. By interpolation, g can always be represented by a polynomial with coefficients in 

E, so this construction does give permutation polynomials. If g takes values in k, then 

ϕ(t) = at + ng (t). In particular, when p | n, every such g gives a permutation. This is a nonlinear application of k ⊆ ker Tr in Proposition 6.11. 

Choosing parameters from a base-field permutation. One may instead prescribe a permutation ϕ of k and a scalar a ∈ k×, and then construct g. By surjectivity of the trace, choose θ ∈ E with Tr E/k(θ) = 1 . For any function u : k → ker Tr E/k, put 

g(t) = θ(ϕ(t) − at ) + u(t).

Then Tr E/k(g(t)) = ϕ(t) − at , so Theorem 15.35 gives the permutation F (x) = ax +

g(Tr E/k(x)) . For fixed θ, a, ϕ , every g satisfying this trace condition has the displayed Chapter 15 Polynomial Functions and Fiber Permutations 477 

form; u changes the actual maps between fibers without changing ϕ on the base field. This choice does not require division by n, and therefore also applies when p | n.Along a cycle of ϕ of length `, choose an initial trace fiber and an origin in it. The first return then has the form v 7 → aℓv + δ, where v, δ ∈ ker Tr E/k. The translation term records the accumulated values of g along the base cycle, so the slope aℓ alone does not determine all cycles. Exercise 15.13 gives this term explicitly and determines the resulting cycle decomposition. 

Example 15.36 Over F16 /F2, F (x) = x + Tr (x) = x2 + x4 + x8 is an involutory permutation. Indeed, Tr (F (x)) = Tr (x), so F (F (x)) = x. If the extension degree four is replaced by any odd integer, the same expression x + Tr (x) always has trace zero and cannot permute the extension field.

## 15.7.1 Norms and Changes of Origin 

Lemma 15.41 (Hilbert 90 for any generating automorphism) Let H ⊆ E be finite fields, and let γ generate Aut H (E). Then im (γ − id ) = ker Tr E/H , {γ(u)/ u : u ∈ E×} = ker N E/H .

Proof. The powers of γ run through all conjugates, so the difference has trace zero and the quotient has norm one. The kernel of the first map is H, and that of the second homomorphism is H×. Comparing dimensions and group orders, respectively, and using surjectivity of the trace and norm proves both equalities. This is the proof of Theorem 6.8 and does not depend on the chosen generating automorphism.

## 15.7.4 The Sign and Determinant of a Linear Permutation 

A permutation of a finite set is a product of disjoint cycles. The permutation sign of a cycle of length r is (−1) r−1; the sign of the whole permutation is the product of its cycle signs, with value 1 or −1, corresponding to an even or odd permutation, respectively. If the finite set has Q elements and cr denotes the number of cycles of length r, then sgn (f ) = ( −1) ∑  

> r(r−1) cr

= ( −1) Q−∑  

> rcr

.

The sign also equals the determinant over Q of the associated permutation matrix, and is therefore multiplicative under composition. For linear permutations, this cycle invariant can also be determined directly by linear algebra.

# 15.8 Dickson Polynomials: Power Maps Descending Along Conjugate Fibers 

The behavior of a power map on a cyclic group is determined by its exponent. Identifying two mutually inverse roots as a single value allows this group action to descend to a nonlinear permutation of a finite field. Given a quadratic polynomial, raise both of its roots, counted with multiplicity, to the same power. The sum of the resulting roots, expressed as a polynomial in the sum and product of the original roots, is a Dickson polynomial. We first consider the case in which the product of the two roots is one. 

Definition 15.55 The Dickson polynomials of the first kind with parameter one are defined by the recurrence 

D0(X) = 2 , D1(X) = X, Dm+1 (X) = XD m(X) − Dm−1(X) (m ≥ 1) .

After reducing the integer coefficients, we use the same notation over a base field of any characteristic. For m ≥ 1, Dm is monic of degree m.The first few terms are D2 = X2 − 2, D3 = X3 − 3X, and D4 = X4 − 4X2 + 2 . The recurrence directly gives, for every nonzero element u of any extension field, 

Dm(u + u−1) = um + u−m. (15.42) Indeed, the identity holds for m = 0 , 1, and substitution of two consecutive terms into the recurrence cancels the two middle terms. 

Lemma 15.56 (Root parameters for inversion orbits) In F× 

> q2

, put U = μq−1 ∪ μq+1 and define π(u) = u + u−1. Then π : U → k is surjective, and 

π(u) = π(v) ⇐⇒ v = u or v = u−1.

Thus each fiber is exactly one orbit of the involution u 7 → u−1; the fiber is a singleton when u = u−1.

Proof. If u ∈ μq−1, then uq = u; if u ∈ μq+1 , then uq = u−1. In both cases, π(u)q = π(u),so π(u) ∈ k. Conversely, for x ∈ k, the quadratic polynomial Y 2 − xY + 1 splits in Fq2 ,with nonzero roots u, u −1. Frobenius permutes these two roots, so uq = u or uq = u−1.Hence u ∈ U and π(u) = x. Finally, multiplying π(u) = π(v) by uv gives the equivalent equation (u − v)( uv − 1) = 0 , proving the fiber description. This calculation also covers the case of a repeated root of the quadratic polynomial. Chapter 15 Polynomial Functions and Fiber Permutations 493
