Dm(π(ζ)) = 2 = Dm(2) .

Thus Dm is not injective. The argument remains valid in characteristic two, where 

2 = 0 .For example, over F8, the polynomial D5 = X5 +X3 +X is a permutation polynomial because gcd (5 , 63) = 1 . Here q − 1 comes from the multiplicative group of the base field, and q + 1 from the norm-one group of the quadratic extension. On the root parameters, Frobenius either fixes u or exchanges u, u −1, and the power map descends simultaneously along both types of fibers. The self-reciprocal constructions of Chapter 11 use the same root parameter u + u−1: there the question is transitivity of the return map, whereas here it is whether taking powers preserves all inversion orbits. The polynomial X3 + X

in Theorem 14.26 is exactly D3 in characteristic two; the noncube condition in the same reciprocal coordinate ensures dynamical irreducibility with the prescribed target, as stated in that theorem. For related classical results, see [37, Chapter 7, Section 2]. The Dickson polynomials of this section, the Dickson matrices of Section 8.7, and the Dickson invariants of Chapter 19 are distinct objects. 494 Chapter 15 Polynomial Functions and Fiber Permutations 

## 15.8.1 Reciprocal-Orbit Root Polynomials and a Frobenius Equation 

The root parameter above identifies a root of unity with its inverse. Forming a new root polynomial from these parameter values allows us to compare the Frobenius equations arising from roots of unity of different orders. For odd m = 2 r + 1 , define 

Pm(Y ) = 1 + 

> r

∑

> j=1

Dj (Y ), P1(Y ) = 1 . (15.43) Formula (15.42) gives the Laurent polynomial identity 

Xm − 1

X − 1 = XrPm(X + X−1). (15.44) When p - m, the r distinct roots of Pm are the sums over the two-element reciprocal orbits of the nonidentity mth roots of unity, with each pair counted once. We therefore call Pm the corresponding reciprocal-orbit root polynomial . For m > 1, Dr is monic, so Pm is monic of degree r; moreover, z + z−1 = w + w−1 holds precisely when 

w = z or z−1. Since m is odd, inversion fixes no nonidentity root, giving exactly r roots. 

Theorem 15.58 (Root-set decomposition of a Dickson–Frobenius equation) For every odd prime power q, the following identity holds in Fq[Y ]:

Y q − Y 2 + 2 = ( Y − 2) Pq+2 (Y )Pq−2(Y ).

The nonconstant factors on the right are squarefree and pairwise coprime; they need not be irreducible. 

Proof. If zq+2 = 1 , then zq = z−2; if zq−2 = 1 , then zq = z2. In either case, y = z + z−1

satisfies 

yq = z2 + z−2 = y2 − 2 = D2(y).

After excluding z = 1 , the two sets of reciprocal-orbit sums have (q + 1)/2 and (q − 3)/2 

elements, none equal to 2. They are disjoint: equality between two parameter values would make the corresponding roots equal or inverse, with order dividing both q + 2 

and q − 2. These odd integers are coprime, leaving only the excluded root 1. Including 

2, we obtain q distinct roots. Both sides are monic of degree q, proving the identity. Squarefreeness also follows directly: the derivative of the left side is −2Y , while its value at 0 is 2 6 = 0 .Chapter 15 Polynomial Functions and Fiber Permutations 495 

For q = 3 , one has Pq−2 = P1 = 1 , and the identity and root count still apply. All roots are considered in a common algebraic closure; the equation yq = D2(y) does not require y to lie in the base field. Likewise, z + z−1 is first a reciprocal-orbit sum. It is the trace from the quadratic extension only when z ∈ Fq2 and zq = z−1.

Corollary 15.59 (Explicit interpolation weights) Put H = Pq+2 and J = Pq−2. For every root t of H,

H′(t) = − 2t

(t − 2) J(t) 6 = 0 .

Proof. Differentiate the preceding identity and substitute H(t) = 0 to obtain −2t =(t − 2) H′(t)J(t). Coprimality of the factors and t 6 = 0 show that the denominators are nonzero. The factor 1/ H′(t) is exactly the normalization weight in the Lagrange interpolation of Chapter 7. Thus the root-set decomposition supplies not only the factors but also the weights by which root evaluations recover the highest coefficient; see Exercise 15.19. 

Example 15.60 (The roots need not lie in a quadratic extension) For q = 5 , one has 

P3 = Y + 1 and P7 = Y 3 + Y 2 − 2Y − 1, so 

Y 5 − Y 2 + 2 = ( Y − 2)( Y + 1)( Y 3 + Y 2 − 2Y − 1) .

The cubic takes the values 4, 4, 2, 4, 1 at 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, and is therefore irreducible. Its roots lie in F125 , not in F25 . The reciprocal orbits of seventh roots thus have Frobenius period three, in agreement with the cubic factor.

# Linear Recurrences and Recovery from Finite Observations 

A linear recurrence is governed by a shift on a finite-dimensional state space. Identify-ing the shift with multiplication by a coordinate element in a quotient algebra gives a common model for minimal polynomials, periods, and transients arising from repeated factors. In the separable case the coefficient pairing becomes a trace representation; finite observations, in the reverse direction, recover an unknown recurrence. We pro-ceed through shifts, quotient algebras and root spaces, trace models, maximum periods, transients, and generating functions, ending with Berlekamp–Massey recovery. The underlying tools are polynomial orders from Chapter 4, the coefficient pairing from Chapter 7, and cyclic modules from Chapter 9; see also [37, Chapter 8]. 

# 16.1 The Shift Operator and Linear Recurrence Re-lations 

Let s = ( s0, s 1, . . . ) be a sequence with values in k = Fq, and define the shift operator 

S(s)t = st+1 . For a monic polynomial 

f (T ) = T d + cd−1T d−1 + · · · + c0, d ≥ 1,

the equation f (S)s = 0 is exactly the recurrence relation 

st+d + cd−1st+d−1 + · · · + c0st = 0 (t ≥ 0) .

A sequence satisfying some recurrence of this form is called a linear recurring se-quence . For a given f , a solution is uniquely determined by its first d terms, so the solution space is a d-dimensional k-space. The tuple (st, . . . , s t+d−1) is called the state 

501 502 Chapter 16 Linear Recurrences and Recovery from Finite Observations 

at time t. If c0 6 = 0 , the recurrence also recovers each state uniquely from the next one. The state transition is therefore a bijection of a finite set, so every state orbit is cyclic from the start. 

Definition 16.1 The minimal polynomial hs(T ) of a linear recurring sequence s

is the monic polynomial of least degree satisfying hs(S)s = 0 . The zero sequence is assigned minimal polynomial 1. If st+N = st holds for all t ≥ 0, then N is called a period of the sequence; the smallest positive period is its least period .Division with remainder again shows that the polynomials annihilating the sequence 

s are exactly the multiples of hs. This is the same operator principle as for the Frobenius annihilator polynomial of an element, with Frobenius replaced by the shift. 

Theorem 16.2 Suppose that f (S)s = 0 and f (0) 6 = 0 . Then hs | f , and the least period of the sequence is per (s) = ord (hs).

If f is irreducible, every nonzero solution sequence has minimal polynomial f and least period ord (f ).

Proof. The first assertion follows from division with remainder. Moreover, N is a period if and only if (SN − 1) s = 0 , equivalently, hs | T N − 1. Thus the least period is the polynomial order defined in Chapter 4. If f is irreducible, hs | f allows only hs = 1 or 

f ; the former corresponds precisely to the zero sequence. The orders of irreducible factors determine the part of the period coprime to the characteristic, and their multiplicities determine the additional p-power part. For a nonzero recurring sequence satisfying hs(0) 6 = 0 , if hs = ∏ 

> i

f ai 

> i

and b is the least nonnegative integer satisfying pb ≥ max i ai, then per (s) = pb lcm i ord (fi).

Thus the multiplicities of irreducible factors affect the sequence period through an ad-ditional power of p.Chapter 16 Linear Recurrences and Recovery from Finite Observations 503 

# 16.2 A Quotient-Algebra Model of the Recurrence Space 

A normal basis represents Frobenius as an action on a cyclic module. For recurring sequences, the corresponding operator is multiplication by the coordinate element in a quotient algebra. The coefficient pairing provides a common linear model for these two representations while retaining the nilpotent structure of repeated factors. 

## 16.2.1 The Coefficient Pairing and the Recurrence-Space Isomor-phism 

Theorem 16.3 (The coefficient-pairing model of the recurrence space) Let f ∈ k[T ]

be monic, with deg f = d ≥ 1, and put A = k[T ]/( f ) and α = T . Define λ : A → k to be the coefficient of T d−1 in the canonical remainder. Then the pairing 

(u, v ) 7 −→ λ(uv )

is nondegenerate, and the map 

c 7 −→ s(c), s(c)t = λ(cα t), t ≥ 0,

is a linear isomorphism from A to the solution space of the recurrence f (S)s = 0 . Under this isomorphism, the shift S corresponds to multiplication by α. If c is represented by a remainder of degree less than d, then 

hs(c) = f

gcd (f, c ).

Proof. Nondegeneracy of the coefficient pairing was proved in Theorem 7.7. This pairing gives a concrete model of the recurrence solution space. Since f (α) = 0 , the sequence s(c) satisfies the recurrence. If its first d terms vanish, then λ(cα i) = 0 for 0 ≤ i < d . These αi form a basis of A, so nondegeneracy gives 

c = 0 . Both the domain and the solution space have dimension d, hence the map is an isomorphism. The identity s(c)t+1 = λ(( αc )αt) shows that the shift corresponds to multiplication. For g ∈ k[T ], the condition g(S)s(c) = 0 is equivalent to λ(g(α)cα t) = 0 for all 

t ≥ 0; by nondegeneracy of the pairing, this is equivalent to g(α)c = 0 , that is, f | gc .Write b = gcd (f, c ), f = bf 1, and c = bc 1, where gcd (f1, c 1) = 1 . Then f | gc if and only 504 Chapter 16 Linear Recurrences and Recovery from Finite Observations 

if f1 | g. The monic annihilating polynomial of least degree is therefore f1. The zero element corresponds to b = f and f1 = 1 , and is included in the formula. 

Corollary 16.4 For each monic divisor h | f , exactly ϕq(h) solution sequences have minimal polynomial h. If f (0) 6 = 0 , all these sequences have least period ord (h).

Proof. The condition f / gcd (f, c ) = h is equivalent to c = ( f /h)u, where u is taken modulo h and is coprime to h. There are exactly ϕq(h) choices. The period assertion follows from Theorem 16.2. This uses the same Euler totient function for polynomial quotient rings as the count of normal elements: both count vectors in a cyclic module with a prescribed minimal annihilating polynomial. Multiplicative generation of the field and the cyclic-vector property for Frobenius must still be checked separately. If f (0) 6 = 0 , formula (15.38) also gives #{s : f (S)s = 0 , S ts = s} = qdeg gcd (f,T t−1) (t ≥ 1) .

Substitution into (15.36) yields all cycle counts for recurrence states.

# 16.4 Primitive Polynomials and Maximum-Length Sequences 

Suppose that a nonzero purely periodic sequence has a minimal polynomial of degree d.No d consecutive terms can all vanish, since the recurrence would make all subsequent terms zero, and pure periodicity would then make the whole sequence zero. States cannot repeat within one least period either: equal states determine the same subsequent terms, and pure periodicity would give a shorter period. There are only qd − 1 nonzero states, so the least period is at most qd − 1. The following definition describes sequences attaining this bound. 512 Chapter 16 Linear Recurrences and Recovery from Finite Observations 

Definition 16.12 A linear recurring sequence whose minimal polynomial has degree 

d ≥ 1 and whose least period is qd − 1 is called a maximum-length sequence , or an 

m-sequence. 

Theorem 16.13 If f is a primitive polynomial of degree d, every nonzero solution sequence is an m-sequence; the states formed by d consecutive terms run through kd \{ 0}

exactly once in one period. In one period, the symbol 0 occurs qd−1 − 1 times, and each nonzero symbol occurs qd−1 times. Conversely, if a sequence with minimal polynomial of degree d has least period qd − 1, its minimal polynomial is primitive. 

Proof. Let α be a root of f . For nonzero c, the elements cα t run through E×. The linear isomorphism from the trace representation associates them with all nonzero states, whose first coordinate is Tr (cα t). Each trace fiber has qd−1 elements; removing the zero element of the extension field gives the symbol distribution. Conversely, let the sequence have minimal polynomial h, with deg h = d. Periodicity gives h | T qd−1 − 1, hence h(0) 6 = 0 . By Theorem 16.2, ord (h) = qd − 1. Proposition 4.14 therefore shows that h is primitive. This reduces the converse for maximum-length sequences directly to the criterion for multiplicative order in a quotient algebra to attain its upper bound.

# 16.5 Transients, Eventual Periods, and Rational Generating Functions 

## 16.5.1 The Exact Decomposition into Transient and Periodic Parts 

For a sequence s = ( sj )j≥0, suppose that there exist u ≥ 0 and N ≥ 1 such that 

sj+N = sj for all j ≥ u. Then s is called eventually periodic. The smallest such u is its 

minimal preperiod ; the least positive integer N for which the equality holds on some tail is its least eventual period . A sequence with preperiod zero is purely periodic. Below we adopt the convention ord (1) = 1 .

Theorem 16.15 (Preperiods and eventual periods of general recurrences) Let s be a linear recurring sequence over k = Fq with minimal polynomial 

hs(T ) = T ag(T ), a ≥ 0, g(0) 6 = 0 ,

where g is monic. Then s is eventually periodic, with minimal preperiod = a, least eventual period = ord (g).

More precisely, for every u ≥ 0 and N ≥ 1,

sj+N = sj (j ≥ u) ⇐⇒ u ≥ a and g | T N − 1. (16.4) 

Proof. The tail-period relation is equivalent to Su(SN − 1) s = 0 for the whole sequence. By the definition of the minimal polynomial and division with remainder, this is equiv-alent to hs | T u(T N − 1) . Since T - T N − 1 and g(0) 6 = 0 , the last divisibility splits exactly into u ≥ a and g | T N − 1. If g 6 = 1 , the quotient ring k[T ]/( g) is finite and 

T is a unit, so some positive integer N satisfies g | T N − 1; for g = 1 , take N = 1 .Thus the least possible u is a and the least possible N is ord (g), and both are attained simultaneously. The zero sequence corresponds to hs = g = 1 and a = 0 and is included in the conclusion. A Bézout identity gives explicit projections for this decomposition. Choose U, V ∈

k[T ] such that 

U (T )T a + V (T )g(T ) = 1 ,514 Chapter 16 Linear Recurrences and Recovery from Finite Observations 

and define

sends 1 to s. The Chinese remainder decomposition k[T ]/( T ag) ' k[T ]/( T a) × k[T ]/( g)

then sends V g and U T a to (1 , 0) and (0 , 1) , respectively. Hence 

hsnil = T a, hsper = g. 

When a modulus polynomial is one, its component is zero, interpreted as having minimal polynomial one. Since Sasnil = 0 , the first component vanishes from index a onward; if 

a > 0, then Sa−1snil 6 = 0 , so its a − 1th term is nonzero. The second component has least period ord (g) from index zero. This gives the unique decomposition of s as the sum of a finitely supported sequence, meaning one with finitely many nonzero terms, and a purely periodic sequence: the difference of two such decompositions would be both finitely supported and purely periodic and must therefore vanish. Thus only the zero-root factor causes a transient phase. Repeated factors at nonzero roots remain in the invertible part and may enlarge the p-power part of the period as in Theorem 4.12. Proposition 16.5 realizes the invertible component as Frobenius on a linearized root space, while (16.5) explicitly gives the map from the original sequence to that component. A nonzero T -primary component on which the shift is nilpotent cannot be realized as Frobenius on a Frobenius-stable subspace of an extension field, because the latter is always injective. This restriction depends on the specified linear action. Again take, as in Exam-ples 7.10 and 16.8, A = F2[ε]/( ε2), and let Ma denote the linear operator of multiplica-tion by a. Then

# 16.6 Recovering Recurrences from Finite Observa-tions: The Berlekamp–Massey Algorithm 

A minimal polynomial describes the shift relations of the entire sequence; computations usually begin with finitely many terms. A finite prefix determines connection relations over a finite range; recovering a recurrence for the entire sequence also requires an order bound. For distinct exponential nodes, the Hankel–Vandermonde formula (13.29) reads the minimum recurrence order from the Hankel rank of the complete sequence. The present section concerns more general finite prefixes, which may include transients or may not yet reveal the eventual minimum recurrence order. 

Definition 16.18 Let N ≥ 0. For a finite prefix s0, . . . , s N −1 ∈ k, if 0 ≤ L ≤ N and 

C(Z) = 1 + c1Z + · · · + cLZL satisfy 

sj + c1sj−1 + · · · + cLsj−L = 0 (L ≤ j < N ),

then (L, C ) is called a connection relation for this prefix, where L is the connection length and C the connection polynomial . The smallest possible L is the linear complexity of the prefix. Since cL = 0 is allowed, the length L must be retained; recording only deg C does not suffice. For L = N there are no equations to check, so the minimum always exists. For a connection relation (L, C ), the value computed at a new index j ≥ L, δ =

sj +∑Li=1 cisj−i, is called the discrepancy there. It vanishes precisely when the previous connection relation remains valid at that position.

The Berlekamp– Massey algorithm solves the shortest linear feedback shift register synthesis problem: it finds a shortest linear recurrence generating a given prefix; see [41].

At the start of iteration j, one has L ≤ j, so the discrepancy uses no negative sequence index. The stored b is nonzero after initialization and after every update, so division by 

b is defined. For N = 0 or an all-zero input, the output is (0 , 1) . A zero final coefficient does not change the connection length L; it must not be replaced by deg C.

Theorem 16.20 The algorithm outputs the minimum linear complexity of the given prefix and a corresponding connection relation. If the final complexity is LN , a straight-forward implementation uses O(N (LN + 1)) arithmetic operations in k; apart from storing the input, the stored polynomials contain O(LN + 1) coefficients. 

Proof. Induct on the number of processed terms. The zero prefix has minimum length zero; if no discrepancy ever occurs, the algorithm keeps L = 0 , C = 1 and the conclusion 520 Chapter 16 Linear Recurrences and Recovery from Finite Observations 

follows. If the first nonzero term occurs at position j, the update gives C = 1 − sj Zj+1 

and L = j + 1 . There are then no recurrence relations to check, so this is feasible; Lemma 16.19 requires length at least j + 1 , proving minimality. Thereafter, suppose that the stored B first failed at position t with discrepancy 

b 6 = 0 , when the minimum length was `. The update at the most recent complexity increase ensures that 

L = t + 1 − `, deg B ≤ `, 

and B satisfies all connection relations at indices from ` through t − 1. If the current discrepancy is zero, the old relation remains valid. Any shorter relation would also apply to the old prefix, contradicting the induction hypothesis. If the current discrepancy δ 6 = 0 , every new relation has length at least the old minimum L and, by the discrepancy lemma, at least j + 1 − L. Its length is therefore at least 

L1 = max {L, j + 1 − L}.

The polynomial C′ = C − (δ/b)Zj−tB constructed by the algorithm has degree at most 

L1, since j − t + ` = j + 1 − L. For every L1 ≤ v < j , the old relation C is valid at position v, while the shifted B corresponds to position v − j + t, satisfying 

` = t + 1 − L ≤ v − j + t < t. 

Thus the correction term vanishes at these positions. At position j, its discrepancy is 

(δ/b)b = δ, exactly cancelling the old discrepancy. Hence (L1, C ′) is feasible and attains the lower bound. When L1 > L , equivalently 2L ≤ j, storing the old relation and the current discrepancy restores the invariant; otherwise the previous record is retained. This proves correctness of all updates and of the final output. Complexity is nondecreasing. Each discrepancy computation and polynomial update costs O(LN + 1) field operations, and polynomial lengths are also bounded in terms of 

LN , giving the stated costs. 

Corollary 16.21 (Information needed to recover an infinite sequence) Let D ≥ 0, and suppose that the minimal polynomial of an infinite sequence is known to have degree at most D. Run the algorithm on its first 2D terms. The output H(T ) is the minimal polynomial of the entire sequence. 

Proof. Let the true minimal polynomial be h, of degree d ≤ D. If d = 0 , then h = 1 

and the sequence is zero, so the algorithm also returns H = 1 . Assume henceforth Chapter 16 Linear Recurrences and Recovery from Finite Observations 521 

that d ≥ 1. It gives a prefix relation of length d, so the output length satisfies L ≤ d.Put w = H(S)s. Since H(S) and h(S) commute, w also satisfies h(S)w = 0 . The connection relation ensures that the first 2D − L ≥ d terms of w vanish. A monic recurrence of degree d is determined by its first d terms, so w = 0 ; thus H annihilates the entire sequence. Minimality gives h | H, which together with deg H = L ≤ d yields 

H = h.Recovering the minimal polynomial of the entire sequence requires a known degree bound. A finite prefix can have arbitrary continuations, so its shortest connection relation need not annihilate the entire sequence. The recovery statement also applies when H(0) = 0 . For example, the sequence 1, 0, 0, . . . has minimal polynomial T , with connection length one and constant connection polynomial one.

# Root Sets and Coding 

Root sets and finite-field linear algebra turn distance requirements into vanishing con-ditions, column relations, or bounds on root-space dimensions. We begin with linear codes, two weights, and distance bounds, then study linearized evaluation, cyclic and constacyclic structures, consecutive root constraints, support root polynomials, and pro-jective evaluation. Trace representations of recurrences were established in Chapter 16. Here a period becomes a coordinate vector: root orbits determine code spaces, while root sets recover coefficient fields and permutation symmetries. The emphasis is on how finite-field structures yield constructions and criteria; decoding theory is not developed. 

# 17.1 Linear Codes, Weights, and Distance Bounds 

## 17.1.1 Hamming Distance, Duality, and the Column Criterion 

A linear code over a field K is a linear subspace of KN . The integer N is the code length , and the vector-space dimension is the dimension of the code . Its elements are called codewords . A code of length N and dimension r is briefly called an [N, r ]

code. The Hamming weight of a codeword c = ( c0, . . . , c N −1) is wt H (c) = #{j : cj 6 = 0 },and the Hamming distance between two codewords is wt H (c − c′). The minimum Hamming distance of a nonzero linear code C is 

dH (C) = min   

> 0̸=c∈C

wt H (c),

equivalently, the minimum distance between two distinct codewords. A linear code of length N , dimension K, and minimum distance d is denoted by [N, K, d ].In the following discussion take k = Fq, and write N, K for length and dimension. 525 526 Chapter 17 Root Sets and Coding 

A matrix whose rows form a basis of a code C is its generator matrix .With respect to the standard inner product, its dual code is 

C⊥ = {y ∈ kN : ∑N −1 

> j=0

cj yj = 0 for all c ∈ C}.

A set of K coordinates is an information set if restriction to those coordinates gives an isomorphism C → kK . The next proposition gives the Hamming Singleton bound and the column criterion for equality. An [N, K, d ] linear code is maximum distance separable , or MDS , if d = N −

K + 1 . It is called nontrivial when 2 ≤ K ≤ N − 2. The following linear-algebraic criterion translates this equality into independence of a root set. 

Proposition 17.1 (Distance, column ranks, and scalar extension) Let G ∈ kK×N have full row rank, with 1 ≤ K ≤ N , and let C be its row space. Then 

dH (C) = N − max {| I| : rank GI < K } ≤ N − K + 1 . (17.1) Equality holds if and only if every K columns are independent, equivalently every set of at most K columns is independent. For every extension L/k, the code CL generated by the same G over L has the same dimension and distance, and CL ∩ kN = C and 

(C⊥)L = ( CL)⊥. If C is MDS and K < N , then C⊥ is an [N, N − K, K + 1] MDS code. Imposing zeros on any s < K coordinates and then deleting these coordinates gives a 

shortened code with parameters [N − s, K − s, N − K + 1] .

Proof. The condition rank GI < K says precisely that some 0 6 = u ∈ kK gives a word 

uG vanishing on I, which proves the distance formula. Any K − 1 columns have rank less than K, giving the Singleton bound. A smaller dependent set can be enlarged to a dependent set of K columns, proving the equivalence of the independence conditions. The rank of every submatrix is determined by its nonzero minors, which are unchanged by scalar extension. Hence dimension and distance are preserved. Choose an invertible submatrix GI of K columns. If uG ∈ kN , then u = ( uG )I G−1 

> I

∈ kK , proving the inter-section formula. The extended dual contains (C⊥)L, and both spaces have dimension 

N − K, so they agree. For an MDS code, any K coordinates allow a generator matrix of the form (IK | A); a generator of the dual is (−AT | IN −K ). Since the original K coordinates were arbitrary, their complement is always an information set for the dual, which therefore satisfies the column criterion. For shortening, the selected s columns impose zero-coordinate Chapter 17 Root Sets and Coding 527 

conditions of rank s, leaving dimension K − s. Deleting zero coordinates preserves weight. The resulting distance is at least N − K + 1 , and the Singleton bound gives the reverse inequality. 

## 17.1.2 Rank Weight and the Rank-Metric Singleton Bound 

Let E = Fqm , with 1 ≤ K ≤ n ≤ m. For c = ( c1, . . . , c n) ∈ En, its rank weight is wt R(c) = dim Fq 〈c1, . . . , c n〉.

The rank distance between two vectors is wt R(c − c′). The minimum rank distance 

of a nonzero E-linear code C is 

dR(C) = min   

> 0̸=c∈C

wt R(c).

If dim E C = K, imposing zero values in any K − 1 coordinates gives a linear map 

C → EK−1 with nonzero kernel. A nonzero vector in this kernel has at most n − K + 1 

nonzero coordinates, so the span of its coordinates has dimension at most n − K + 1 .Hence 

dR(C) ≤ n − K + 1 .

This is the rank-metric Singleton bound for E-linear codes when n ≤ m. A code attaining it is called a maximum rank distance code .

# 17.3 Root Orbits, Cyclic Codes, and Fourier Coordi-nates 

Restricting a purely periodic sequence to one period gives a vector of finite length, and the shift becomes a cyclic shift on these vectors. Definition 17.9 (Constacyclic codes) Let λ ∈ k×. A linear code C ⊆ kN invariant under

# 17.5 Consecutive Root Constraints and the BCH Bound 

Taking the union of the Frobenius orbits meeting an interval of consecutive exponents and using the corresponding roots of unity as the zeros of the generator polynomial gives a BCH code . Explicitly, given integers b and 2 ≤ δ ≤ N , its generator polynomial is

Example 17.13 (A binary cyclic code from consecutive roots) Retain k = F2, N = 7 ,and ζ from Example 17.8, but take M (X) = X3 + X + 1 as the generator polynomial. Its roots are ζ, ζ 2, ζ 4, so its defining set is {1, 2, 4}. The first two roots correspond to consecutive exponents one and two, and Theorem 17.12 gives dH (C) ≥ 3. On the other hand, M itself is a nonzero codeword of weight three, so dH (C) = 3 . Since dim k C = 7 − deg M = 4 , this gives a [7 , 4, 3] code. Example 17.8 uses the same polynomial as a check polynomial, retaining the field component corresponding to C1 and giving dimension three; here it is the generator polynomial, removing that component and giving dimension four. The same example shows why the consecutive exponents in the BCH argument matter. The polynomial c(X) = 1 + X + X3 has three nonzero coefficients and vanishes at ζ, ζ 2, ζ 4. Thus the Fourier submatrix 

(ζij )i∈{ 1,2,4}  

> j∈{ 0,1,3}Chapter 17 Root Sets and Coding 537

annihilates (1 , 1, 1) T and is singular. The seven-point Fourier transform of the coefficient vector of c has exactly four nonzero coordinates, since these three points are all the roots of c. Even at prime transform length, arbitrary square submatrices of a finite-field Fourier matrix need not be nonsingular. Frobenius closure determines which root constraints descend to the base field, while consecutive exponents make the evaluation equations form an invertible Vandermonde submatrix. Thus root sets determine not only cyclic-code dimensions but also the minimum number of nonzero coefficients. The distinction from the Moore matrices of trace codes is made precise at 17.51.

# 17.6 Support Root Polynomials and the Distance of Binary Goppa Codes 

The BCH bound turns a small set of nonzero codeword coefficients into evaluation equations. Multiplicative cosets and square roots of derivatives. The preceding example starts with a split root polynomial and uses its derivative to verify attainment of the distance bound. Thus the distance criterion for binary Goppa codes can be used not only to test a given root set but also to construct one from admissible orbits. The support root polynomial has coordinate positions as roots and degree equal to the codeword weight. It differs from the polynomial whose coefficients form the code-word. In the binary case, the coefficients are zero or one, so the root set already records the entire word. This is why the logarithmic derivative directly expresses the check condition. The coefficient representation of cyclic codes also relates support periods to coordinate decompositions.

## 17.7.2 Affine Symmetries and Code Subspaces 

A support period gives a direct sum by coordinate interleaving. Affine symmetry also involves a center and translation directions, which give rise to code subspaces through the semi-invariant spaces of Section 12.4.1. We first test divisibility in the polynomial space, then return to the original coefficient coordinates to compute Hamming weights. Continue with k = Fq, and fix C = ( f ) ⊆ k[X]/( XN − λ), where λ 6 = 0 and 

0 < τ = deg f < N . Equation (17.3) specifies the polynomial representatives and their degree range. 546 Chapter 17 Root Sets and Coding 

Proposition 17.25 (A criterion for affine substitutions to preserve a code space) Let 

K/k be an extension field, with a ∈ K× and b ∈ K. In the space of polynomials of degree less than N , the substitution g(X) 7 → g(aX + b) preserves C ⊗k K if and only if 

f (aX + b) = aτ f (X).

Its affine stabilizer is therefore exactly the root-multiplicity-preserving affine stabilizer of its generator polynomial. 

Proof. If the identity holds, f q is sent to aτ f (X)q(aX + b), and the multiplier still satisfies the original degree bound; the inverse substitution gives equality of the code spaces. Conversely, f (aX + b) belongs to the code space and has degree τ , so by (17.3) it is a constant multiple of f ; comparing leading terms gives the constant aτ .The action here is in the specified polynomial coordinates. If b 6 = 0 , then X is sent to 

aX +b, and its Hamming weight changes from one to two. Thus a substitution generally does not preserve weight. Put s = sp (f ) and write f (X) = fsp (Xs). Replacing −1 by 

−λ in the proof of Proposition 17.23 gives s | N , fsp | Y N /s −λ, and the same coordinate interleaving with additive Hamming weights. The resulting blocks also determine every decomposition along disjoint sets of coordinates. 

Definition 17.26 (Coordinate direct sums) For B ⊆ { 0, . . . , N − 1}, let kB ⊆ kN

denote the subspace of vectors supported on B. A partition B1, . . . , B m of the coordinate set gives a coordinate direct-sum decomposition of C if 

C =

> m

⊕

> i=1

(C ∩ kBi ).

A nonzero summand is coordinate-indecomposable if it cannot be split further into two nonzero subcodes supported on disjoint coordinate sets. 

Proposition 17.27 (The indecomposable coordinate blocks) Let C = (f ) ⊆

k[X]/( XN − λ), where f is monic, f | XN − λ, λ 6 = 0 , and 0 < deg f < N . Put 

s = sp (f ). The sets 

Rj = {i : 0 ≤ i < N, i ≡ j (mod s)}, 0 ≤ j < s, 

are precisely the indecomposable coordinate blocks of C. Every coordinate direct-sum decomposition of C is obtained by grouping these blocks. Chapter 17 Root Sets and Coding 547 

Proof. A nonzero codeword is called support-minimal if no nonzero codeword has strictly smaller support contained in its support. Since f | XN − λ, we have f (0) 6 = 0 . If a nonzero codeword g is supported inside Supp X (f ), its standard representative has degree at most deg f . Divisibility by f then makes g a nonzero scalar multiple of f . Thus f

is support-minimal. The constacyclic shift is invertible and permutes the coordinates while multiplying one coordinate by a nonzero scalar, so every constacyclic shift of f is also support-minimal. Identify the coordinate set with Z/N Z, and join two coordinates whenever they occur in the support of the same shifted generator. These supports are all translates of Supp X (f ). Because 0 ∈ Supp X (f ), the connected component of zero is the subgroup generated by the positive support indices: each such index gives edges from a to its translate by that index, and every edge difference belongs to the subgroup they generate. Since their greatest common divisor is s and s | N , the connected components are exactly the Rj .The shifted generators span C, and each lies within one Rj , so these blocks give a coordinate direct sum. In any coordinate direct sum, a support-minimal word must lie in one summand; otherwise projection onto a nonzero summand would give a nonzero codeword with strictly smaller support. Consequently no support of a shifted generator, and hence no connected component Rj , can be split between two summands. This proves both assertions. 

Corollary 17.28 (A distance bound from the compressed code) Under the hypotheses of Proposition 17.27, put τ = deg f and

If C has parameters [N, k C , d H (C)] , then D has parameters 

[N /s, k C /s, d H (C)] , kC = N − τ, 

and 

dH (C) ≤ τs + 1 .

Proof. Interleaving gives C ' D⊕s, so dimensions add and the two minimum distances agree. For a nonzero linear code of length M and dimension K, imposing zero values in any K −1 coordinate positions leaves a nonzero word, whose weight is at most M −K +1 .Applying this Singleton bound to D gives the stated inequality. 548 Chapter 17 Root Sets and Coding 

For the [6 , 4, 2] code in Example 17.24, the even and odd positions are therefore its two indecomposable coordinate blocks. The bound obtained from the [3 , 2, 2] com-pressed code is attained.

Proposition 17.30 (The divisibility matrix and effective support) Let W ⊆ k[X]<N

The jth coefficient vanishes identically on D if and only if the linear functional rj vanishes on ker M , equivalently, rj belongs to the row space of M . This proves the support formula. Put d = l − ρ > 0. Requiring any d − 1 coordinates in the effective support to vanish on D imposes at most d − 1 linear conditions, leaving a nonzero solution of weight at most | Supp X (D)| − d + 1 . Finally, D ⊆ C gives the first inequality.

# 17.8 Projective Evaluation and Interpolation Duality 

## 17.8.1 Projective Root Forms and Evaluation Spaces 

A univariate root polynomial records affine points; after adding the point at infinity, a binary homogeneous form records the root set. Homogenization preserves the root bound while relating changes of coordinates, Frobenius descent, and evaluation spaces. For a fixed set of evaluation points, the image of a polynomial vector space under Chapter 17 Root Sets and Coding 553 

pointwise evaluation is called an evaluation space ; viewed as a linear code, it is an 

evaluation code . We continue to write k = Fq for the base field and use N, K for code length and dimension, respectively. Recall the projective line P1(k) from Subsection 15.4.4: its points are the one-dimensional subspaces of k2. The point represented by a nonzero vector (u, v ) is de-noted by [u : v], with [u : v] = [ λu : λv ] for λ ∈ k×. Every point has a unique representative [a : 1] , a ∈ k, or ∞ = [1 : 0] , so there are q + 1 points. The zeros of a homogeneous form F (U, V ) do not depend on the representatives; its values generally do, since F (λu, λv ) = λdeg F F (u, v ). Evaluation at these fixed representatives is called 

projective evaluation ; on forms of a fixed degree, the corresponding map is a homo-geneous evaluation map . Throughout, projective evaluation uses the representatives fixed above.

Proposition 17.36 (Kernel and dimension of homogeneous evaluation) Let Rd =

There is an important distinction from the affine function algebra k[X]/( Xq −X). The extra coordinate retains exactly this highest-degree information. These assertions concern each fixed homogeneous degree; forms of different degrees are not identified as the same kind of function without choosing representatives. 

Corollary 17.37 (Elementary parameter restrictions) A nontrivial [N, K ] MDS code satisfies 

N ≤ q + K − 1, K ≤ q − 1, N ≤ 2q − 2.

Proof. Shorten on K − 2 coordinates to obtain a two-dimensional MDS code. Its gen-erator columns represent distinct points of P1(k), so N − K + 2 ≤ q + 1 . Applying this inequality to the dual gives K ≤ q − 1, and substitution gives the last bound. 556 Chapter 17 Root Sets and Coding 

Proposition 17.38 (The root bound and Reed–Solomon evaluation codes) Let S ⊆ k,with |S| = n ≥ 1. For 1 ≤ K ≤ n, the Reed–Solomon code 

RS K (S) = {(f (a)) a∈S : f ∈ k[X], deg f < K }

is an [n, K, n − K + 1] MDS code. For 1 ≤ K ≤ n + 1 , the extended Reed–Solomon code 

ERS K (S) = {(( f (a)) a∈S ; fK−1) : deg f ≤ K − 1}

is an [n + 1 , K, n − K + 2] MDS code, where fK−1 denotes the coefficient of XK−1.

Proof. In ordinary evaluation, a nonzero f vanishes at at most K − 1 points. Thus evaluation is injective and the distance is at least n − K + 1 . Extended evaluation is the evaluation of F (U, V ) = V K−1f (U /V ) on {[a : 1] : a ∈ S} ∪ {∞} . The projective root bound gives injectivity and distance at least n − K + 2 . The Singleton bound gives equality in both cases. When S = k = Fq, the set S is the full evaluation set , and RS K (k) is a full-length Reed–Solomon code , of length q. When S = H ≤ k×, we call H a multiplicative subgroup evaluation set ; the code length is |H|. The term “full-length” modifies the code, not the evaluation set. The extended code obtained by adjoining the coordinate at infinity is distinct from the full-length code of length q.More generally, PK−1(k) is the set of one-dimensional subspaces of kK . A set of at least K points for which every K representative vectors are independent is a projec-tive arc . For K ≥ 2, the columns of an MDS generator matrix give precisely such an arc. Changing the representatives only rescales the corresponding code coordinates by nonzero scalars and does not change distance. For example, the columns of ERS K (k)

are (1 , a, . . . , a K−1)T and (0 , . . . , 0, 1) T. The BCH bound starts with a small coefficient support and obtains evaluation equations; here a small root set of an evaluation poly-nomial controls the zero coordinates of a word. Both arguments use root bounds or Vandermonde independence, but the polynomials record different objects. 

Example 17.39 (An extra evaluation direction in characteristic two) Here an evalu-ation direction means the projective class of the linear functional defining a code coor-dinate; an additional coefficient functional need not be evaluation at another ordinary point. Suppose that q is a power of two. Take the columns 

(1 , t, t 2)T (t ∈ Fq), (0 , 0, 1) T, (0 , 1, 0) T.Chapter 17 Root Sets and Coding 557 

Any three are independent. For three finite parameters, the determinant is a Vander-monde product. For two finite parameters a 6 = b and one of the last two columns, it equals, up to sign, b − a or b2 − a2 = ( b − a)2, respectively. For one finite parameter and both special columns, it equals one. The columns therefore generate an [q + 2 , 3, q ]

MDS code, whose dual has parameters [q + 2 , q − 1, 4] . Such an arc of q + 2 points in the projective plane is called a hyperoval . The independence is verified directly, without a classification of general projective arcs. For q = 2 , the dimensions are three and one, respectively, so both codes are trivial boundary cases. Quotienting by the span of s points of an arc, with 0 ≤ s ≤ K − 2, leaves an arc in the quotient: a dependence there lifts to a dependence involving at most K original columns. For s = K −2, the quotient is two-dimensional and contains N −K +2 distinct occupied directions. The remaining q + K − 1 − N directions can be recorded by the product of their linear forms. The root forms of the occupied and missing directions multiply to a nonzero scalar multiple of Bq. This is a factorization within each two-dimensional quotient; it does not assert that the missing-direction forms from different quotients automatically come from one global polynomial.

## 17.8.4 Compatible Restrictions and Recovery of Homogeneous Polynomials 

Univariate interpolation recovers a polynomial from point values. In three-dimensional space, a homogeneous form can also be recovered from compatible restrictions to sev-eral two-dimensional subspaces. The restrictions below are polynomial restrictions in coordinate rings, not merely equality as functions on the rational points of a finite field. 

Proposition 17.45 (Compatible recovery on linear sections) Let k be any field and let 

L1, . . . , L N ∈ k[X1, X 2, X 3]1 \ { 0} be pairwise nonproportional, with any three distinct forms linearly independent. Put Hi = ker Li. For 0 ≤ d < N , suppose that each Hi

carries a homogeneous binary form gi of degree d, and that 

gi|Hi∩Hj = gj |Hi∩Hj (i 6 = j).

There is a unique G ∈ k[X1, X 2, X 3]d satisfying G|Hi = gi for every i.

Proof. First lift g1 to a ternary homogeneous form. Suppose that G has already been constructed correctly on H1, . . . , H j−1. The residual form gj − G|Hj vanishes on each 

Hi ∩Hj , i < j , so it is divisible by Li|Hj . Independence of any three original forms makes these restricted factors pairwise nonproportional. Their product therefore divides the residual form. If j − 1 > d , the residual form is zero by degrees. Otherwise lift the quotient to a ternary homogeneous form Q of degree d − j + 1 , and replace G by 

G + ( L1 · · · Lj−1)Q. This preserves all previous restrictions and corrects the one on Hj ,proving existence inductively. If G, ˜G have the same restrictions, each Li divides their difference. Their product of degree N therefore divides a form of degree d < N , forcing the difference to be zero. The proof applies over an arbitrary field and uses only divisibility by linear forms and a degree comparison. Over a finite field, homogeneity makes one value at a nonzero representative determine the entire restriction to a one-dimensional intersection. With-out homogeneity, equality at one point does not justify this conclusion. The condition 

d < N controls uniqueness: at d = N , adding cL 1 · · · LN to any solution preserves every restriction. Chapter 17 Root Sets and Coding 565 

Example 17.46 (A binary code glued from three local quadratic forms) Over k = F2,order the seven points of P2(k) as 

e1, e 2, e 3, e 1 + e2, e 1 + e3, e 2 + e3, e 1 + e2 + e3.

Let C2 be the evaluation code of all ternary quadratic homogeneous forms. The three coordinate lines Xi = 0 cover the first six points. On each line, a binary quadratic form aU 2 + bU V + cV 2 has values (a, c, a + b + c) at [1 : 0] , [0 : 1] , [1 : 1] ; these values can be prescribed arbitrarily and determine the local form uniquely. Arbitrary values on the first six coordinates therefore give three local forms agreeing on their pairwise intersections. Proposition 17.45, with d = 2 < 3 = N , glues them to a unique ternary quadratic form. Thus the first six coordinates form an information set of C2. Each square monomial is one at four of the seven points, and each mixed monomial is one at two, so every evaluation vector has coordinate sum zero. Consequently

# 17.9 Trace Codes, Sparse Multiples, and Multiplica-tive Subgroup Rigidity 

The trace model of an irreducible cyclic code already identifies cyclic shift with multi-plication by a field element. # 17.10 Residue Layers and Balance of Fourier Sup-ports 

An irreducible trace code retains a single root orbit; a general cyclic code may retain several. Expanding these orbits into a Fourier basis over a splitting field preserves their Frobenius descent information and makes it possible to compare support sizes in different residue layers. These factors can change under Frobenius, so the other classes cannot automatically be treated as the same kind of base-field cyclic code. This distinction parallels the interleaved direct sums obtained from support periods: exponent layers and coefficient blocks are related but are not the same decomposition. 574 Chapter 17 Root Sets and Coding 

# 17.11 The Smallest Field of Definition of a Cyclic Code 

Root-set descent determines not only the coefficient field of a polynomial but also whether a cyclic code can already be defined over a smaller alphabet. Coordinates are fixed here: no coordinate scalings or permutations are allowed before fields of definition are compared. Let q = pf , N > 1, and gcd (N, p ) = 1 , and let C ⊆ FNq be cyclic. For b | f , say that 

C is defined over Fpb in the fixed coordinates if C = span Fq C0 for some C0 ⊆ FNpb .The least such subfield is the smallest field of definition of this cyclic realization.

Proof. For the zero code and the whole space, the defining sets are Z/N Z and the empty set, respectively; both have s = 1 , and the assertions are immediate. We prove the remaining cases below. Multiplication by p permutes Z/N Z; the return times of T

The generator and check polynomials have the same coefficient field: they are monic with product XN − 1, and monic division recovers either from the other over that field. This proves s = gcd (e, f ). Over Fps , the orbit of α has length e/s = K, so the check polynomial remains irreducible and the dimension stays K.This unifies descent of a general root set with descent of a single Frobenius orbit; the precise irreducible case also appears in[67, Theorem 5.1]. The smallest field belongs to the fixed cyclic realization ; it has not thereby been shown to be smallest among all equivalent codes.

Example 17.59 (Coefficient-field descent without changing coordinates) Take q = 9

No search through codewords is required. Nor is the dimension of a general cyclic code being identified with ord N (q):that equality applies here because the check polynomial consists of one irreducible orbit. 

# 17.12 Common Permutation Symmetries of Cyclic Codes 

Root constraints determine the vectors in a cyclic code. We now ask the reverse ques-tion: which coordinate permutations preserve every cyclic code simultaneously? This is a problem of recovering common symmetries from a family of linear subspaces. Cyclo-tomic orbits, idempotent decompositions of quotient algebras, and the finite-field-valued Fourier transform provide the three descriptions needed to answer it. Throughout this section, assume n ≥ 2, gcd (n, q ) = 1 , and put R = Z/nZ, K = 〈q〉 ≤ R×. The-orems 17.60 and 17.61 correspond to Theorems A and B of Wu and Xiang [66], re-spectively. Here we give proofs based on finite-field-valued Fourier spectral projections and the difference-orbit rigidity established earlier, without developing the theory of cyclotomic association schemes.

Root orbits give field com-ponents, these give idempotent projections, and the matrix entries of the projections separate difference orbits. Local rigidity then turns the orbit constraints into a common affine multiplier. For repeated-root cyclic codes, n is not invertible in the base field, so these Fourier projections are unavailable. For an individual code, the common-group theorem likewise does not replace an analysis of its full automorphism group. 

## 17.12.3 Multiplier Preservation and Fixed-Point Rigidity for One Code 

The preceding two subsections studied permutations preserving every cyclic code. For a fixed code, the MDS condition constrains the multipliers that preserve its Fourier support. The quantifiers are different: the full automorphism group of one code cannot generally be read off from the common group. Continue to assume gcd (N, q ) = 1 and use the support S = S(C) and negative-exponent basis of Section 17.10. Define the multiplier stabilizer 

H(S) = {u ∈ (Z/N Z)× : uS = S}.

It is a subgroup of the unit group and contains 〈q〉. If (Pux)j = xuj , then Puvd = vud .The Fourier model and the intersection formula for scalar extension show that u ∈ H(S)

if and only if Pu preserves C.Chapter 17 Root Sets and Coding 581 

Theorem 17.63 (A nonidentity multiplier has at most two fixed points) If C is a nontrivial cyclic MDS code, then every u ∈ H(S), u 6 = 1 , satisfies #{j ∈ Z/N Z : uj = j} = gcd (u − 1, N ) ≤ 2. (17.46) 

Proof. First suppose that u has prime order r. Its coordinate orbits have length one or 

r. Let ν be the number of fixed points and b the number of other orbits, so N = ν + rb .Since uS = S, the support contains a of the fixed points and t of the orbits of length 

r, giving K = a + rt . One has 0 < t < b . Indeed, if t = 0 , every d ∈ S is fixed by u

and hence divisible by N /ν. Columns zero and ν of the Fourier generator matrix are equal, with 1 ≤ ν < N , contradicting the column criterion for K ≥ 2. If t = b, the dual support contains no orbit of length r, and the same argument applied to C⊥ gives a contradiction. Over the splitting field E, put P = Pu and W = ( P −I)CE . On the space spanned by a Fourier orbit of length r, the kernel of P −I consists of vectors with all coefficients equal and has dimension one; on a fixed basis vector the map is zero. Thus dim E W = ( r −1) t.On the coordinate side, every w = ( P − I)c is zero at the fixed coordinates and satisfies 

∑ 

> j∈O

wj = 0 on each orbit of length r, since P permutes that orbit. These facts remain valid when the characteristic divides r; no division by r has occurred. Impose zeros on t − 1 whole coordinate orbits of length r, and on r − 2 coordinates of one more orbit. Each whole orbit contributes at most r − 1 independent conditions because its coordinate sum is zero. The total rank is at most 

(t − 1)( r − 1) + ( r − 2) = t(r − 1) − 1 < dim E W. 

A nonzero w ∈ W therefore still satisfies these conditions, and wt H (w) ≤ rb − (r(t − 1) + r − 2) = r(b − t) + 2 .

On the other hand, W ⊆ CE and the MDS property give wt H (w) ≥ N − K + 1 = ν − a + r(b − t) + 1 .

Hence ν − a ≤ 1. The dual support (Z/N Z) \ (−S) contains ν − a fixed points and b − t

long orbits. Applying the same argument to the dual gives a ≤ 1, so ν ≤ 2.For general order h > 1, choose a prime r | h and put v = uh/r. Then v ∈ H(S)

has order r. Every point fixed by u is fixed by v, so there are at most two. Finally, the congruence (u − 1) j ≡ 0 ( mod N ) has gcd (u − 1, N ) solutions, as required. 582 Chapter 17 Root Sets and Coding 

This fixed-point restriction appears in[39, Lemma 3.1]. The subcode distance esti-mate here follows directly from the zero-sum relations on the orbits and rank–nullity. The restriction therefore comes not from the multiplier action alone, but from its preser-vation of a linear space with strong column independence. 

Corollary 17.64 (Synchronization of orders on divisors) Under these hypotheses, for every d | N , d ≥ 3, reduction induces an injection 

H(S) −→ (Z/dZ)×.

In particular, writing m = ord N (q), one has ord d(q) = m (d | N, d ≥ 3) . (17.47) For odd N , all nonzero q-cyclotomic cosets have size m. For even N , all cosets other than {0} and {N /2 } have size m. The dimension K of a general cyclic code may be the sum of the sizes of several such orbits and need not equal m.

Proof. If u belongs to the kernel of reduction, then d | u−1, hence gcd (u−1, N ) ≥ d ≥ 3.Theorem 17.63 forces u = 1 , proving injectivity. Its restriction to 〈q〉 preserves the order of q, giving (17.47). The coset of an exponent i has size ord N / gcd (N,i )(q). This modulus is less than three only for i = 0 , or for even N and i = N /2 . Apply synchronization of orders in every other case. The subgroup argument for an irreducible trace code gives order K for every d > 1,and also excludes even length. The multiplier argument for a general cyclic code only requires d ≥ 3, and does not identify K with m. The two rigidity statements therefore share a Frobenius-period mechanism but have different hypotheses and boundary cases. In particular, the restriction d ≥ 3 in (17.47) is essential. 

Corollary 17.65 (Two fixed directions and parity of dimension) Let C be a nontrivial 

[N, K ] cyclic MDS code, with gcd (N, q ) = 1 . If gcd (N, q 2 − 1) = 2 and m = ord N (q),then 

K ≡ N − K ≡ 1 (mod 2m), min {K, N − K} ≥ 2m + 1 .

Proof. Here N is even and q is odd, and N /2 is odd: otherwise 4 | N and 4 | q2 −1 would contradict the hypothesis. Also m > 2, since otherwise N | q2 − 1 would force N = 2 ,contrary to nontriviality. Choose a nonidentity element u of prime order in 〈q〉. It fixes 

0, N /2 , so it has exactly two fixed points. The prime-order proof of Theorem 17.63 also shows that S contains exactly one of them. Chapter 17 Root Sets and Coding 583 

Every other q-orbit has size m, and since q is odd it preserves exponent parity. Suppose that S contains x even-exponent orbits and y odd-exponent orbits. Put ε = 1 

if 0 ∈ S, and ε = 0 otherwise. Balance modulo two gives 

|mx + ε − (my + 1 − ε)| = |m(x − y) + 2 ε − 1| ≤ 1.

Since m > 2, one has x = y, and hence K = 1+2 mx . Nontriviality gives x ≥ 1. The dual code satisfies the same hypotheses, so the same conclusion applies to its dimension. Root-set descent determines which frequencies combine to form a code over the base field. Residue layers constrain their distribution, and multiplier preservation then constrains the common periods of those layers. For a single irreducible orbit, these conditions also return to full-degree multiplicative subgroups, normality, and the ob-struction from sparse multiples. They arise from the same Frobenius cyclic structure, tested through coefficients, orbits, and linear relations, respectively.

# Fourier Duality, Quadratic Forms, and Character Sums 

The trace pairing makes field elements into parameters for additive characters. The Fourier transform describes changes of frequency parameters through adjoint operators and converts solvability into orthogonality. Polynomial indicator functions first give root-count congruences for low-degree equations; polarization and linearized root spaces determine the structure of quadratic forms, and character sums then determine their exact value distributions. Joint expansions in additive and multiplicative characters count primitive elements of prescribed trace and, combined with the local Frobenius decomposition, prove the primitive normal basis theorem; weighted orbit products orga-nize extension-field character sums into finite-order recurrences, and trace fibers recover extension-field point counts for a family of curves in characteristic two. The same or-thogonality relation also converts moments of character sums into counts of solutions of power-sum equations, and correlations of orbit sequences into character sums. 

# 18.1 Additive and Multiplicative Characters 

Throughout this chapter write K = FQ and Q = pm, and put ζp = exp (2 πi /p). An 

additive character is a map K → C× satisfying ψ(x + y) = ψ(x)ψ(y). A multiplica-tive character is a group homomorphism χ : K× → C×. A character identically equal to one is called trivial. 589 590 Chapter 18 Fourier Duality, Quadratic Forms, and Character Sums 

Writing trace duality as four rows of signs. Temporarily take K = F4 = F2(ω),with ω2 + ω + 1 = 0 . The absolute trace is Tr (x) = x + x2, so Tr (0) = Tr (1) = 0 , Tr (ω) = Tr (ω2) = 1 .

Each nontrivial row has two plus signs and two minus signs, and the entrywise product of any two distinct rows sums to zero. This displays both the trace parametrization of characters and their orthogonality. Arithmetic with the table entries takes place in C; its −1 must not be identified with 1 in characteristic two.

# 18.6 Short Linear Relations in Multiplicative Sub-groups and Gaussian Periods 

Multiplicative order first determines the least field containing one element, and Frobe-nius orbits then organize its conjugates; neither determines all additive relations among several elements. Even when every nontrivial orbit in a multiplicative subgroup is a normal basis, elements chosen from different orbits may be dependent. Passing from orbit structure to the linear position of the entire subgroup therefore requires recording the support of a shortest relation. We first obtain necessary restrictions from multiplica-tive orders, then detect joint independence using trace hyperplanes, and finally count intersections and relations through moments of Gaussian periods. The trace-code in-terpretation has appeared in Section 17.9; here the main objects are linear relations in finite fields. 

## 18.6.1 Linear relation length and multiplicative orders 

Let n > 1, gcd (n, q ) = 1 , and k = ord n(q) ≥ 2. Put L = Fqk and let H = 〈β〉 be the unique subgroup of L× of order n. Since Fq(β) = L, the Fq-span of H is L. Define the 

linear relation length of H by 

λq(H) = min 

{

#{h ∈ H : ch 6 = 0 } : ∑

> h∈H

chh = 0 , (ch) ∈ FHq \ { 0}

}

. (18.8) Its support counts distinct subgroup elements, independently of the coefficient values. Any k + 1 elements of H are dependent, while 0 / ∈ H; hence 

2 ≤ λq(H) ≤ k + 1 .

The extreme value λq(H) = k + 1 says that every set of at most k distinct elements of H is linearly independent. We call this maximal linear general position . It is stronger than requiring every nonidentity element to have degree k, since the latter merely excludes elements contained in proper subfields. 602 Chapter 18 Fourier Duality, Quadratic Forms, and Character Sums

## 18.6.2 When every Frobenius orbit is a normal basis 

The equality λq(H) = k + 1 first forces every nontrivial subgroup to generate the full extension and then restricts the linear relations within each Frobenius orbit. 

Proposition 18.15 (Cyclotomic and normality consequences of general position) If 

λq(H) = k + 1 , then: (1) ord d(q) = k for every d | n, d > 1, and n | Φk(q);(2) every nonzero q-cyclotomic coset modulo n has length k, and n ≡ 1 ( mod k);(3) H \ { 1} is partitioned into (n − 1)/ k Frobenius orbits, each of which is a normal basis of L/Fq. In particular, Tr L/Fq (h) 6 = 0 for h 6 = 1 ;(4) the minimal polynomial mh(X) of every h ∈ H \ { 1} has all its coefficients nonzero. 

Proof. The order equality follows from Proposition 18.14. If ` | n is prime, then k =

ord ℓ(q) | ` − 1, so ` - k. Moreover, ` cannot divide qd − 1 for a proper divisor d of k.The factorization qk − 1 = ∏ 

> d|k

Φd(q) therefore yields n | Φk(q), including prime-power multiplicities. Every nonidentity nth root of unity has degree k, giving the uniform Frobenius orbit lengths. Each orbit consists of k distinct elements of H and is linearly independent by general position; hence it is a normal basis, and its sum, the trace, cannot vanish. Finally, the order of h is at least k + 1 . If its minimal polynomial had Chapter 18 Fourier Duality, Quadratic Forms, and Character Sums 603 

a zero coefficient, mh(h) = 0 would give a nontrivial relation involving at most k of the distinct elements 1, h, . . . , h k, a contradiction. One must distinguish uniform Frobenius orbit lengths from linear indepen-dence of the elements of an orbit . Even when every orbit is a normal basis, one cannot infer that arbitrary k elements drawn from different orbits are independent. The primitive normal basis theorem guarantees an element that generates L× and is normal; here the assertion is that every nonidentity element of a specified subgroup is normal. The objects and quantifiers are different.

Proof. Any k distinct elements of H are dependent precisely when their span is proper, in which case a nonzero trace-linear functional vanishes simultaneously on them. Now suppose gcd (n, q − 1) = 1 . The projective image of the subgroup is

Here PG (k −1, q ) is the projective space of one-dimensional Fq-subspaces of L; the copri-mality condition makes the n displayed points distinct. An n-point set is a projective arc , or an n-arc , if representatives of every k of its points are linearly independent. This condition is unchanged by nonzero rescaling of representatives and is equivalent to every projective hyperplane containing at most k − 1 of the points. ## 18.6.7 Base-field descent, a seven-element example, and Fourier minors 

The length of a shortest relation is unchanged by certain extensions of scalars. If q = pf ,

e0 = ord n(p), and a = gcd (e0, f ), then 

Fpe0 ∩ Fq = Fpa , Fpe0 Fq = Fqk , k = e0/a. 

The two finite fields are linearly disjoint over their intersection. Consequently, any finite subset of the subgroup of order n is linearly independent over Fpa if and only if it is independent over Fq. Hence 

λpa (H) = λq(H). (18.22) This corresponds to the smallest coefficient field in Section 17.11, but its formulation here does not involve a code. This identity compares the same subgroup inside an algebraic closure of one fixed characteristic p; linear disjointness ensures that extending scalars introduces no new dependent subsets. The following example of order seven instead changes the char-acteristic from two to eleven, comparing subgroups in different characteristics rather than a scalar extension of this kind. It shows that the same multiplicative orders and cyclotomic-coset partition can accompany different additive relations, without contra-dicting (18.22). 

Example 18.26 (The same cyclotomic order data with different three-term relations) Take n = 7 . For both q = 2 and q = 11 one has k = 3 , and the two nonzero Frobenius cosets modulo seven are {1, 2, 4} and {3, 5, 6}. Over F8, the subgroup is H = F×

Thus the same multiplicative orders and Frobenius coset partition do not determine λ: what changes is the joint additive position of the subgroup elements. Two Fourier descriptions must also be distinguished here. The Gaussian periods above use complex-valued characters of the additive group (L, +) : orthogonality counts intersections, and the periods are eigenvalues of an additive Cayley graph. The matrices below instead use root-of-unity characters of the cyclic group Z/nZ, with minors first considered in a characteristic-zero cyclotomic field and then reduced to characteristic 

p. The former frequencies are parameterized by the trace pairing; the latter indices are organized into cyclotomic cosets, and finite-field-valued inversion requires p - n. When the latter row indices form a Frobenius orbit, the reduced submatrix is a Moore matrix testing base-field linear independence. This connects with the comparison at 17.51; it does not identify complex character sums with nonsingularity of finite-field minors. For fixed n, characteristic-dependent behavior can also be explained through Fourier minors over a cyclotomic number field. Put Γ = 〈q mod n〉, with |Γ| = k, and let 

S ⊂ Z/nZ have size k. Consider 

DΓ,S (ζn) = det (ζγj n )γ∈Γ, j ∈S .

Choose a prime ideal above p in the cyclotomic integer ring and identify the image of ζn

with a primitive nth root of unity in characteristic p. Ordering the rows as 1, q, . . . , q k−1,the reduced minor is the Moore determinant of the corresponding k subgroup elements and hence tests linear independence. If the cyclotomic integer is nonzero in characteristic zero, its integer norm is nonzero. Each conjugate determinant has absolute value at most 

k!, giving an absolute norm bound (k!) φ(n). Accordingly, if all these minors are nonzero in characteristic zero , the inequality p > (k!) φ(n) ensures λq(H) = k + 1 . When n = `

is prime, Chebotarëv’s nonvanishing theorem for all minors of a prime-order Fourier matrix guarantees the hypothesis [59, 24], yielding the sufficient, though very coarse, condition 

n = ` prime , p > (k!) ℓ−1 =⇒ λq(H) = k + 1 . (18.23) 612 Chapter 18 Fourier Duality, Quadratic Forms, and Character Sums 

This deduction uses the classical Fourier-minor theorem, which is not proved here. At composite n, the possibility of minors vanishing already in characteristic zero must not be ignored. From Theorem 18.24, short linear relations can be analyzed in successive layers: mul-tiplicative orders provide quick necessary bounds; one cyclotomic intersection number detects all three-term dependencies; and factorial moments of Gaussian periods recover dependencies of greater length. Group theory, additive counting, and character sums are linked by the linear position of the same subgroup.

These Weil-type bounds for diagonal equations [1, Chapter 11] come entirely from the square-root magnitude of Gauss sums. Multiplicative characters expand the fibers of power maps, and the additive constraint combines these characters into Jacobi sums; whether their product character is trivial determines the two scales of the error term. Exact counts and square-root estimates are therefore two consequences of the same character expansion. 

# 18.8 Primitive Elements of Prescribed Trace 

Primitivity is characterized by order in the multiplicative group, whereas prescribing the trace specifies an additive affine subspace. Expanding both conditions in characters reduces their common solution count to multiplicative character sums over trace fibers. These fiber sums are determined by a Gauss sum over the extension field and the restriction of the character to the base field. This application connects the trace fibers of Chapter 6 with the square-root estimates of this chapter; for a classical discussion, see [26, Chapter 8].

# 18.9 The primitive normal basis theorem: a joint count of two generation conditions 

Section 9.12 expresses normality as nonvanishing in the local Frobenius components and uses weighted traces to describe affine fibers consisting entirely of normal elements. Primitivity, in turn, requires an element to generate the multiplicative group of the field. We expand the two conditions in characters and use Gauss sums to control the number of elements satisfying both. A normality-preserving scaling group first reduces the multiplicative prime factors that must be tested; a local density sieve retains the density of each remaining condition and handles the boundary cases of the basic estimate. This approach is related to the classical character-sum proofs of the primitive normal basis theorem[34, 19]. Throughout this section, write 

k = Fq, E = Fqn , Q = qn, N = Q − 1, σ(x) = xq.

Theorem 18.45 (The primitive normal basis theorem) For every prime power q and positive integer n, the extension Fqn /Fq has a primitive normal element. 

Proof. The case n = 1 is immediate. For n = 2 , if a primitive element x were not normal, then xq = cx for some c ∈ k×. Applying Frobenius again gives c2 = 1 , so 

x2( q−1) = 1 , contradicting ord x = q2 − 1 > 2( q − 1) .For n ≥ 3, Proposition C.3 in the appendix and the basic joint estimate cover every pair except the eight boundary cases. The scaling lemma turns the resulting generators of the quotient into primitive elements while preserving normality. This exhausts all cases. The proof places the two generation conditions in a single counting formula: the local Frobenius decomposition provides additive frequencies, the multiplicative quotient pro-vides multiplicative characters, and Gauss sums control their interaction. Appendix C gives the complete arithmetic coverage from the uniform estimates to the eight bound-ary cases and is part of the proof for all parameters. # 18.12 Polarization, Radicals, and Classification of Quadratic Forms 

In this section take k = Fq, and let V be a k-space of dimension m ≥ 1. Solution counts for quadratic equations are controlled by the polar form and the remaining quadratic information; the trace pairing further turns the former into the kernel of a linearized operator. For the classification of quadratic forms and solution-count formulas, see [37, Chapter 6, Section 2]. 

Definition 18.50 A map Q : V → k is called a quadratic form if Q(cx ) = c2Q(x)

and 

BQ(x, y ) = Q(x + y) − Q(x) − Q(y)

is bilinear. The form BQ is called the polar form of Q. Write 

R = rad BQ = {x ∈ V : BQ(x, y ) = 0 for all y ∈ V }.

A nonzero vector satisfying Q(x) = 0 is called isotropic ; a quadratic form with no such vector is called anisotropic . Quadratic forms Q : V → k and Q′ : V ′ → k are called 

isometric if there is a k-linear isomorphism T : V → V ′ such that Q′(T x ) = Q(x).For any basis (ei), the quadratic-form axioms give

Thus the definition is equivalent to a homogeneous quadratic polynomial in coordinates. In odd characteristic, BQ(x, x ) = 2 Q(x), so the polar form determines the quadratic form completely; in characteristic two, BQ is always alternating, and the square terms cannot be recovered from it. Chapter 18 Fourier Duality, Quadratic Forms, and Character Sums 635 

Example 18.51 (A trace quadratic form with known polarization and undetermined type) Over E = F64 , take Q(x) = Tr E/F2 (x3), retaining the notation σ(x) = x2. For

The second equality follows from invariance of the trace under σ: Tr (x2y) = Tr (xy 32 ).The trace pairing is nondegenerate and σ is invertible, so rad BQ = ker (σ + σ−1) = ker (σ2 − 1) = F4.

Thus BQ has rank 6 − 2 = 4 . For x ∈ F4, we have x3 ∈ F2, hence Q(x) = 6 x3 = 0 .For every r ∈ F4, Q(x + r) = Q(x) + Q(r) + BQ(x, r ) = Q(x), so Q descends to the four-dimensional quotient E/F4 with nondegenerate polar form. Polar rank still does not determine the solution count: the classification below leaves two quadratic types, and Example 18.66 uses Gauss sums to determine the type and value distribution in this example. If V = U ⊕ W and BQ(U, W ) = 0 , then Q(u + w) = Q(u) + Q(w). This is an 

orthogonal sum of quadratic forms, denoted by Q|U ⊥ Q|W . The binary quadratic form H(x, y ) = xy is called a hyperbolic plane ; H⊥s denotes the orthogonal sum of s

hyperbolic planes, with H⊥0 the zero form on the zero-dimensional space. In character-istic two also write Nδ(x, y ) = x2 + xy + δy 2. For a nondegenerate alternating bilinear form, a basis (e1, f 1, . . . , e s, f s) satisfying B(ei, e j ) = B(fi, f j ) = 0 and B(ei, f j ) = δij is called a symplectic basis .

## 18.15.2 Differential Kernels and Trace Components of a Field-Valued Quadratic Map 

The preceding arguments fix a quadratic form and examine its polar operator. When a quadratic map takes values in an extension field, the direction and trace parameters give two families of operators whose kernels are related by the trace pairing. 

Definition 18.59 Let E = F2n , with n ≥ 1. A map F : E → E is a field-valued quadratic map if F (0) = 0 and

# 18.16 Character Lifts to Extensions and Weighted Orbit Products 

The trace and norm lift additive and multiplicative characters, respectively, from the base field to an extension. In an extension-field sum, the number of repetitions of a base-field Frobenius orbit controls both lifts simultaneously. Thus the geometric-series contribution of each orbit in (3.7) can be weighted by its trace and norm; the lifting formula below follows from the same unique-factorization expansion and formal logarithm calculation.

# 18.17 Generating Polynomials and Linear Recur-rences for Extension-Field Character Sums 

The Hasse–Davenport formula expresses lifted Gauss sums of fixed base-field characters over successive extensions as signed powers of a single base-field Gauss sum. More generally, if a weighted orbit product is a polynomial, the corresponding extension-field character sums are power sums of finitely many numbers and hence satisfy a linear recurrence of fixed order. We first prove the polynomial-phase case, then give a complete calculation for Kloosterman sums, which include an inverse term [26, Chapter 8].

The diagonal-equation estimate of Theorem 18.29 comes from the explicit absolute-value formula for Gauss sums, not as a general consequence of this formal recurrence.

# 18.18 From Kloosterman Sums to Curve Point Counts and Zeta Functions 

Kloosterman sums can also record solution counts in fibers of two-variable equations. We apply the Artin–Schreier trace criterion to a family of curves in characteristic two, then recover their extension-field point counts from the second-order recurrence of the preceding section. 

## 18.18.1 The Curve Model and Trace Fibers 

Fix k = Fq, q = 2 m, and b ∈ k×, and write kn = Fqn . To include both affine solutions and points at infinity, first specify projective coordinates. The projective plane P2(K) over a field K consists of equivalence classes of nonzero triples (X, Y, Z ) under multiplication by a common nonzero scalar, denoted by [X : Y : Z]. For Z 6 = 0 , take the unique representative [x : y : 1] , where x = X/Z and y = Y /Z; points with Z = 0 are called

Section 19.10 connects these fixed-point counts with Euler products over orbits. In elliptic curve theory, Pb(T ) = T 2 − aT + q is the characteristic polynomial of Frobenius ; see [57, Chapter V]. Here α, β are complex characteristic roots of a recurrence, not conjugates of an element of a finite field; the permutation πb of the curve points is also distinct from the earlier k-linear operators on extension fields. The recurrence and rationality of the generating function alone do not imply |α| = |β| = √q; this absolute-value statement requires a separate proof. Remark 18.80 (The Hasse bound and recurrence roots) We invoke the Hasse bound 

for elliptic curves: every elliptic curve E/Fq satisfies 

∣∣#E(Fq) − (q + 1) ∣∣ ≤ 2√q;

see [57, Chapter V, Theorem 1.1] for a proof. Applying it to Eb, whose nonsingularity was checked above, gives 

|a| = |q + 1 − N1| ≤ 2√q, |K1(1 , b )| ≤ 2√q. 

Since a is real, the discriminant of T 2 − aT + q is nonpositive. Its roots are complex conjugates, or a repeated real root in the equality case. Together with αβ = q, this yields |α| = |β| = √q, and hence, for every n ≥ 1,

|Nn − (qn + 1) | = |Kn(1 , b )| ≤ 2qn/2 .

The additional input for the absolute-value bound is Hasse’s theorem. The phase x+b/x

remains rational, so the later theorem for polynomial phases does not apply directly. 

# 18.19 Weil bounds for polynomial character sums 

Throughout this section, write k = Fq and p = char k. The generating polynomial expresses the character sums over all extension fields as power sums of finitely many complex numbers, but does not yet bound their absolute values. This section supplies the missing step. The argument again starts from root sets and Frobenius: an auxil-iary polynomial bounds trace and power-value fibers over extension fields, and power sums then bound the characteristic roots. The auxiliary construction only needs a square-root estimate whose constant is independent of the extension degree; the degree of the generating polynomial subsequently supplies the precise constant in the final bound. The construction of high-multiplicity zeros by counting coefficient parameters is called Stepanov’s method . We use a form adapted to polynomial phases, proving nonvanishing and the multiplicity conditions separately[16]. 662 Chapter 18 Fourier Duality, Quadratic Forms, and Character Sums 

Figure 18.3 separates two necessary inputs: the finite recurrence bounds the number of characteristic roots, and a rough bound uniform over extensions controls their moduli. The final constant follows only after both inputs are combined.

R is constant, the character sum can have absolute value qr, and the exact formula of Corollary 18.70 applies instead. Thus phase reduction identifies the nondegeneracy condition, while counting high-multiplicity zeros establishes square-root cancellation.

# Exact-Period Layers, Affine Compression, and Orbit Counts 

Exact-period layers separate orbits of prescribed length from the full fixed-point sets. Polynomial divisibility, coefficient gaps, and affine invariants refine this decomposition, while Euler products reconnect local orbits with global point counts. Parity cancellation follows by comparing multiplicities in finite products, and invari-ants are determined by compatibility between translations and dilations. The former describes the coefficient structure of exact-period layers; the latter compresses affine orbits in a layer into new root coordinates, whose factorization is recovered by return maps. 

# 19.1 Fixed-Point Sets and Exact-Period Layers 

Fix k = Fq, and write 

Aq,m (X) = Xqm

## 19.5.2 Base-Field Extension and Reciprocal Pairing 

For an order class satisfying ord e(q) = n, extend the base field to Fqr and put g =

gcd (n, r ). Then ord e(qr) = ng .

By Theorem 5.15, each original orbit splits into g orbits of length n/g, so Φe has exactly gϕ (e)/ n irreducible factors over the new base field. Correspondingly, the whole polynomial Eq,n splits into gI q(n) irreducible factors of degree n/g. All roots of the original layer lie in the exact-period layer of period n/g over the new base field, but the latter may also contain roots of other original periods; the two exact-period polynomials therefore cannot in general be identified. Inversion preserves multiplicative order, so reciprocal pairing occurs separately within each Φe. If ord e(q) = n > 1, Corollary 4.21 shows that the irreducible factors in this order class are self-reciprocal if and only if 

n is even , qn/2 ≡ − 1 (mod e). (19.4) This condition depends only on e, so all irreducible factors in an order class are either self-reciprocal or paired with distinct reciprocals. In particular, factors in an exact-period layer of odd degree occur in pairs. Self-reciprocity of the exact-period polynomial can 690 Chapter 19 Exact-Period Layers, Affine Compression, and Orbit Counts 

therefore arise either from self-reciprocal individual factors or from pairings of distinct factors.

# 19.7 Compressed Periods, Return Orders, and Fac-tor Lifting 

The Frobenius period of a compression value determines the first return time of its fiber. The return permutation within the fiber further determines the degrees of the original roots and the degrees and number of lifted factors.
