## 19.7.3 Lifting Irreducible Factors 

Corollary 19.22 (Lifting compressed factors and decomposing fibers) Retain the no-tation of Proposition 19.19, put e = n/t = ord (g), and let H ∈ k[T ] be the monic minimal polynomial of c. Then: (1) Over k(c), the polynomial Θq(X)−c splits into q(q−1)/ e distinct monic irreducible factors, each of degree e.(2) Over k, the polynomial H(Θ q(X)) splits into q(q − 1)/ e distinct monic irreducible factors, each of degree n.In particular, if H | Gq,n and deg H = t, the number of lifted factors is q(q − 1) t/n, and every lifted factor has degree n.

Proof. Since α /∈ k, we have c 6 = 0 . Proposition 19.16 gives q(q − 1) distinct roots of 

Θq(X) − c, namely AGL 1(k)α. This polynomial also has degree q(q − 1) , so these are all its roots, each simple. The Frobenius of the base field k(c) = Fqt is σt. Under the fiber identification above, it corresponds to right multiplication h 7 → hg on the group, every cycle having length e. The correspondence between root orbits and irreducible factors immediately gives the first assertion. The roots of H(Θ q) lie in disjoint fibers over c, c q, . . . , c qt−1

. Every root in each fiber is simple. By Lemma 11.1, each return orbit of length e extends to a total orbit of length 

te = n, and return orbits correspond bijectively to total orbits. Thus the number of factors is unchanged, and every degree is multiplied by t, proving the second assertion. Starting instead from H | Gq,n , choose a root c and adjoin a root α of Θq(X) − c. The identity Eq,n = Gq,n (Θ q) shows that α has degree exactly n, so the conclusions above still apply. Chapter 19 Exact-Period Layers, Affine Compression, and Orbit Counts 699 

The order of the return transformation thus gives both the relative extension degree and the factor degrees of the fiber polynomial. In affine compression, the general fiber factorization of Theorem 11.3 becomes a case in which all return orbits have equal length; the same integer e therefore determines both the number and the degrees of the factors. 

Corollary 19.23 (Computing the lifted factorization type from a compressed factor) Let H(T ) = T t + ht−1T t−1 + · · · + h0 ∈ k[T ] be monic irreducible, with H 6 = T . Put 

a = ( −1) th0 ∈ k×, r(T ) = Rq,t (T ) mod H(T ), deg r < t.

Proof. Choose a root c of H. It has degree t, and H 6 = T ensures c 6 = 0 . The product of the roots gives N k(c)/ k(c) = ( −1) th0 = a. Since H is the minimal polynomial of c,we have Rq,t (c) = 0 if and only if H | Rq,t , or r = 0 . Proposition 19.20 therefore gives degree te for each lifted root; Corollary 19.22 then gives the number of factors and the absence of repeated roots. If q > 2, the return order is p or a divisor of q − 1, both strictly smaller than q(q − 1) ,so there is more than one factor. If q = 2 , the fiber has size two, so irreducibility of the composition is equivalent to e = 2 . Corollary 19.21 reduces this to Tr k(c)/ F2 (c) = 1 .The sum of the roots shows that this trace equals ht−1, giving the final criterion. This corollary determines a base-field element from the constant term, computes its multiplicative order, and, when needed, takes one polynomial remainder to determine the degrees and number of all lifted factors. In the binary case, it agrees with the Artin–Schreier composition criterion of Chapter 11.

## 19.7.4 Return Mechanisms for Power and Affine Compression 

The power map of Chapter 5 and the affine invariant of this chapter both send one Frobenius orbit to another. The image period records motion between fibers, while the ratio of the original period to the image period records the first-return period within a fiber. Lemma 11.1 applies in both cases; the specific return maps on the fibers must be determined separately. 

Power compression. In the notation of Section 5.6, let C = Ci and α = ζi, take 

r = κC , t = ωC , and put β = αr. Proposition 5.31 gives 

[k(α) : k] = τ = rt, [k(β) : k] = t. 

On the conjugate root set of α, the map x 7 → xr sends each complete equal-difference root block of size r to a single value. The fiber over β is precisely αμ r, and σt forms a single cycle of length r on this fiber. Use ε 7 → αε as fiber coordinates, and put 

Q = qt, δ = αQ−1.

Since βQ = β, we have δr = 1 , so δ ∈ μr. Direct calculation gives the first-return map 

σt(αε ) = αδε Q, R(ε) = δε Q (ε ∈ μr). (19.10) Since the original root set is a single orbit of length rt , the least period of R starting from 1 is exactly r. Thus the period-reduction factor here equals the size of the entire root block. 

Affine compression. For c = Θ q(α) 6 = 0 , put n = [ k(α) : k] and t = [ k(c) : k], and write σt(α) = g(α), with e = ord (g) = n/t. Equation (19.7) shows that the full fiber has 

q(q − 1) elements, whereas its intersection with one original orbit has only e; the first return is right multiplication h 7 → hg in group coordinates. Thus the period-reduction factor is the return period of the chosen root and need not equal the size of the full fiber. In power compression above, the whole of αμ r lies in one original orbit, so the two sizes agree. Both cases satisfy 

[k(α) : k] = [ k(π(α)) : k] [ k(α) : k(π(α))] ,

where π is the power map or Θq, respectively, and the relative degree is precisely the return period of the chosen root within the fiber. The internal period is κC for power compression and ord (g) for affine compression. 704 Chapter 19 Exact-Period Layers, Affine Compression, and Orbit Counts 

The forms of the two return maps differ. The map ε 7 → εQ in (19.10) is the identity only when r | Q − 1; in general, R cannot simply be written as multiplication by δ. Its iterates are in fact 

Rj (ε) = δ1+ Q+··· +Qj−1

εQj

(j ≥ 1) ,

as follows by successive composition. For example, when q = 5 , N = 32 , C = C1, we have τ = 8 , κC = 8 , and ωC = 1 . Take α to be a primitive 32nd root of unity, and put ξ = α4. Then μ8 = 〈ξ〉, and the return map is ε 7 → ξε 5. In coordinates ε = ξj , it becomes 

j 7 −→ 1 + 5 j (mod 8) .

Exercise 19.5 gives the full return calculation and compares this permutation with mul-tiplication by ξ alone. In the affine case, the right-multiplication formula follows from the commutativity of the group elements with Frobenius. Thus the common period multiplication law comes from equivariance of the compression map with Frobenius, while the specific return-order test also depends on the group action on the fiber.

# Field Extensions and Polynomial Tools 

This appendix treats extensions and polynomial operations over arbitrary fields. The basic concepts of field extensions relate the base field, vector-space coordinates, and algebraic relations; division with remainder, Bézout’s identity, and interpolation provide the computational tools for adjoining roots and decomposing root sets. The proofs of these general results do not depend on the existence or structure theorems for finite fields. 

# A.1 Field Embeddings and a Specified Base Field 

Field homomorphisms preserve addition, multiplication, and the identity element. Every field homomorphism ι : k → E is injective: if a nonzero a ∈ k satisfies ι(a) = 0 , then 

1 = ι(1) = ι(aa −1) = ι(a)ι(a−1) = 0 ,

contrary to 1 6 = 0 in a field. Thus ι is an injective field homomorphism, called a field embedding ; it gives an isomorphism from k to the subfield ι(k). Identifying k with 

ι(k) through this isomorphism allows us to write the inclusion k ⊆ E. A field equipped with a specified embedding ι : k → E is therefore also regarded as an extension field of 

k. Scalar multiplication in its k-vector space structure is explicitly a · x = ι(a)x.Let ι : k → E and ι′ : k → E′ be specified embeddings. A field homomorphism 

τ : E → E′ satisfying τ ◦ ι = ι′ is called a k-homomorphism ; if it is also bijective, it is called a k-isomorphism . When both images of the base field are denoted by k, this condition says that τ (a) = a for every a ∈ k. Thus a k-homomorphism is automatically a k-linear map. A k-isomorphism from a field E to itself is called a k-automorphism ;these maps form the group Aut k(E) under composition. 713 714 Appendix A Field Extensions and Polynomial Tools 

For example, in the quotient construction obtained by adjoining a single root 

k[X]/( f ), the specified embedding is a 7 → a. Identifying constant classes in the quotient with elements of the original field through this map gives the inclusion 

k ⊆ k[X]/( f ) used in the main text. Similarly, a k-isomorphism between two models obtained by adjoining a root must map the chosen root to a corresponding root and preserve the specified embedding of the base field. 

# A.2 Bases, Extension Degrees, and Restriction of Scalars 

For a finite tuple e1, . . . , e n in a field extension E/k, spanning means that every x ∈ E

is a k-linear combination of these elements; linear independence means that ∑ 

> i

aiei = 0 

with ai ∈ k holds only when all ai = 0 . Together, these two conditions are precisely the existence and uniqueness of coordinate representations used to define the extension degree in the main text. Dimension is determined by linear relations over the base field; the same elements may have different linear relations over different base fields. 

Example A.1 (Finite extensions and finite fields) Every complex number has a unique expression a+bi with a, b ∈ R. Thus 1, i is a basis of C/R and [C : R] = 2 , although both fields have infinitely many elements. If the base field k has q elements, a coordinate tuple of length n has exactly qn possible values, so every extension E/k of degree n satisfies 

|E| = qn. Conversely, if E is a finite set, the length of every k-linearly independent tuple is bounded by |E|; successively extending a linearly independent tuple therefore produces a finite basis. Let k ⊆ L, and let V be an L-vector space. Keeping addition in V and allowing only elements of k as scalars gives the k-vector space obtained from V by restriction of scalars . If u1, . . . , u a is a basis of L/k and v1, . . . , v b is a basis of V over L, the two successive expansions and coefficient comparison in Lemma 1.3 apply equally to V ,giving the k-basis uivj . Hence dim k V = [ L : k] dim L V. 

Taking V = E gives the tower formula for dimensions. This identity describes the further expansion of each L-coordinate into several k-coordinates. Appendix A Field Extensions and Polynomial Tools 715 

If k ⊆ L ⊆ E and [E : k] < ∞, then L is a k-linear subspace of E, so [L : k] < ∞.Also, a k-basis of E spans E over L, so [E : L] < ∞. The tower formula therefore applies and gives [L : k] | [E : k]. Thus divisibility of intermediate-field degrees follows from successive basis expansions, independently of the classification of subfields. 

# A.3 Generated Subfields and Algebraic Extensions 

Chapter 2 defines k(S) as the smallest subfield containing k ∪ S, and k[α] as the set of all polynomial values at α. For any α ∈ E, the generated subfield k(α) also has the following description in terms of fractions. 

Proposition A.2 (Fractions in a generated subfield) Let k ⊆ E and α ∈ E. Then 

k(α) = 

{ A(α)

B(α) : A, B ∈ k[X], B (α) 6 = 0 

}

.

More generally, if S ⊆ E, every element of k(S) belongs to a subfield generated by some finite subset of S.

Proof. Sums, differences, and products of fractions on the right have the same form, and the inverse of a nonzero fraction is obtained by interchanging numerator and denomi-nator. Thus the right-hand side is a subfield containing k and α, and hence contains 

k(α). Conversely, every subfield containing k and α contains all these fractions, proving equality. For the second assertion, let U be the union of all k(S0), where S0 ranges over the finite subsets of S. If x ∈ k(S0) and y ∈ k(S1), both belong to k(S0 ∪ S1), so their sum, difference, product, and quotient when the denominator is nonzero all belong to U . Hence U is a subfield containing k ∪ S; since every k(S0) ⊆ k(S), we obtain 

U = k(S).If E = k(α1, . . . , α r), then E/k is called a finitely generated extension . Finite generation restricts only the number of generators; it does not require them to be algebraic over the base field. 716 Appendix A Field Extensions and Polynomial Tools 

Example A.3 (One generator and infinite dimension) Let t be an indeterminate, and let k(t) be the rational function field consisting of fractions A(t)/ B(t) with A, B ∈ k[T ]

and B 6 = 0 . Then k(t)/ k is generated by the single element t, but 1, t, t 2, . . . are linearly independent over k, since a polynomial in k[t] is zero precisely when all its coefficients are zero. Thus [k(t) : k] = ∞. Moreover, t−1 ∈ k(t) whereas t−1 /∈ k[t], so k[t] 6 = k(t).If every element of E is algebraic over k, then E/k is called an algebraic extension .An element that is not algebraic over k is called a transcendental element . For an algebraic element α, Proposition 2.2 has already established 

k(α) = k[α], [k(α) : k] = deg mα,k .

The key is that a relation of least degree both expresses higher powers in terms of lower powers and excludes nontrivial linear relations among those lower powers.

Corollary A.5 (Algebraic elements form a subfield) In any extension field E/k, the elements algebraic over k form a subfield of E.

Proof. Every element of the base field is algebraic. If α, β are algebraic over k, then 

k(α, β )/ k is finite. It contains α ± β and αβ , and also α/β when β 6 = 0 . By the preceding proposition, these elements are algebraic over k, proving closure under the field operations. Every element of an algebraic extension belongs to a finite extension, but the entire algebraic extension need not be finite. The algebraic closure of a finite field constructed in Theorem B.2 provides such an example: it is an increasing union of finite extensions whose degrees are unbounded. 

# A.4 Simple Extensions, Splitting Fields, and Separa-bility 

If α is algebraic over k, Proposition 2.2 gives 

k[X]/( mα,k ) ' k(α), A 7 −→ A(α).

This isomorphism identifies the field defined by the quotient with the subfield gener-ated by a root in a specified extension field. Different images of the root determine different embeddings; the precise statement and proof of the extension lemma appear in Lemma 2.3. Adjoining all roots of a specified polynomial gives its splitting field as in Definition 2.4. A splitting field is generated by finitely many algebraic elements and is therefore a finite extension; its existence is guaranteed by Lemma 1.9. Proposi-tion 2.5 shows that any two splitting fields admit an isomorphism preserving the base field, although this isomorphism need not be unique. An algebraic element α is separable over k if its minimal polynomial has no repeated roots in a splitting field. If every element of an algebraic extension E/k is separable over 

k, then E/k is called a separable extension . The criterion relating repeated roots to the formal derivative is given in Proposition A.16 of this appendix. A finite extension over a general field can be inseparable. 718 Appendix A Field Extensions and Polynomial Tools 

Example A.6 (Power relations and an inseparable extension) Let u be an indetermi-nate, with E = Fp(u) and k = Fp(up). The element u satisfies the polynomial Xp − up

# A.5 Divisibility, Bézout’s Identity, and Unique Fac-torization 

The root bound and its inductive proof are given in Lemma 1.11. We first establish division with remainder and the associated algebraic results. 

Lemma A.7 (Division with remainder) Let k be a field, and let A, B ∈ k[X] with 

B 6 = 0 . There exist unique Q, R ∈ k[X] such that 

A = QB + R, R = 0 or deg R < deg B. 

Consequently, a is a root of A if and only if X − a divides A.

Proof. Successively cancel the highest-degree term of A using the leading term of B.The degree strictly decreases, giving division with remainder. If two representations Appendix A Field Extensions and Polynomial Tools 719 

had different quotients, subtracting them would express a nonzero multiple of B as a polynomial of degree less than deg B, which is impossible. The quotient is therefore unique, and so is the remainder. Division by B = X −a has remainder exactly A(a).

Definition A.8 A polynomial f ∈ k[X] of positive degree is called an irreducible polynomial if it cannot be expressed as a product of two polynomials of positive degree. A polynomial with leading coefficient 1 is called a monic polynomial .

Lemma A.9 (Existence of irreducible factors) Every nonconstant polynomial has a monic irreducible factor and can be expressed as a constant times a finite product of monic irreducible polynomials. 

Proof. If the polynomial is irreducible, divide by its leading coefficient. Otherwise, factor it into two nonconstant polynomials of smaller degree and treat each in turn. Induction on the degree shows that this process terminates. This factorization result does not prescribe factor degrees; it therefore applies to adjoining finitely many roots without assuming the existence of irreducible polynomials of specified degrees. 

Lemma A.10 (Bézout’s identity) Let A, B ∈ k[X] be not both zero, and let D be their monic greatest common divisor. Then there exist U, V ∈ k[X] such that 

U A + V B = D. 

In particular, if A, B are coprime, there exist U, V such that U A + V B = 1 .

Proof. Among all nonzero U A + V B , choose one of least degree and make it monic; denote it by D. Divide A by D: A = QD + R. The remainder R = A − QD is still a polynomial linear combination of A, B . If R 6 = 0 , it has smaller degree, a contradiction. Hence D | A, and similarly D | B. Every common divisor also divides U A + V B = D,so D is precisely the monic greatest common divisor. 

Example A.11 In F2[X], let f = X2 + X + 1 . Then 

(X + 1) X + f = 1 .

Thus in the quotient ring modulo f , the element X + 1 is the multiplicative inverse of 

X. This is the role of Bézout’s identity in the root-adjoining construction. 720 Appendix A Field Extensions and Polynomial Tools 

Corollary A.12 (Primality of irreducible factors and unique factorization) If an irre-ducible polynomial f | AB , then f | A or f | B. Every nonzero polynomial factors uniquely, up to the order of the factors, as a constant times a product of monic irre-ducible factors. 

Proof. If f - A, then gcd (f, A ) = 1 , so we can write U A + V f = 1 . Multiplying by 

B gives f | B. Compare two irreducible factorizations. Every factor in the first must divide some factor in the second; both are monic and irreducible, so they are equal. Cancelling these factors successively proves uniqueness. 

# A.6 The Chinese Remainder Theorem and Interpo-lation 

Decomposing a root set divides a polynomial problem into local problems. The Chi-nese remainder theorem combines local congruence conditions into a single polynomial residue class. 

Definition A.13 An ideal of a commutative ring R is a nonempty subset I closed under addition and subtraction and satisfying rI ⊆ I for r ∈ R. The congruence a ≡ b

(mod I) modulo an ideal means a − b ∈ I; operations on representatives make the congruence classes into the quotient ring R/I.In k[X], every nonzero ideal has the form (g) = {gh : h ∈ k[X]}: choose a monic nonzero polynomial g of least degree in the ideal and divide any element by g. The remainder is still in the ideal and must be zero. The kernel of a ring homomorphism is an ideal. If a homomorphism ψ : R → S has kernel I, then R/I → im ψ, ¯a 7 → ψ(a) is an isomorphism, since it is well defined and surjective with zero kernel. An evaluation homomorphism therefore factors through the corresponding quotient ring.

# Algebraic Closures and Compatible Finite Periods 

An algebraic closure of a finite field can be constructed as an increasing union of finite extension fields. This extends the process of adjoining finitely many roots to a common extension field for all algebraic equations. 

Definition B.1 A field Ω is called an algebraically closed field if every nonconstant polynomial in Ω[ X] has a root in Ω. Equivalently, every nonconstant polynomial splits completely over Ω: after finding a root, divide out the corresponding linear factor and proceed by induction. If, in addition, Ω/ k is algebraic, meaning that every element of 

Ω is algebraic over k, then Ω is called an algebraic closure of k.

Theorem B.2 Every finite field k has an algebraic closure, which can be constructed as a union of finite extension fields. 

Proof. Put K0 = k. After constructing a finite field Kj , consider all monic polynomials in Kj [X] of degrees from 1 to j+1 . There are only finitely many, since each coefficient has finitely many choices. Their product is a nonconstant polynomial Pj . By the splitting-extension construction in Lemma 1.9, there is a finite extension field Kj+1 ⊇ Kj in which Pj splits completely. Each of the polynomials above then splits completely in 

Kj+1 . This gives an increasing sequence of fields 

K0 ⊆ K1 ⊆ K2 ⊆ · · · .

Put Ω = ⋃ 

> j≥0

Kj . Any finite collection of elements belongs to some common Kj , so sums, differences, products, and inverses of nonzero elements remain in Ω; hence Ω is a field. Take any nonconstant A ∈ Ω[ X] of degree D. It has only finitely many coefficients, all of which therefore belong to some KN . Choose j ≥ N with j + 1 ≥ D. by its leading coefficient, A is one of the polynomials considered in constructing Kj+1 ,so it splits completely in Kj+1 ⊆ Ω. Thus Ω is algebraically closed. Finally, α ∈ Ω belongs to some finite field Kj . Hence α|Kj | = α, so α is a root of the nonzero polynomial X|Kj | − X, whose coefficients lie in the prime field and hence in k.Thus α is algebraic over k, and Ω is an algebraic closure of k.Adjoining finitely many roots makes each stage possible; the increasing union ensures that any finite set of coefficients eventually belongs to a single stage. Together, these properties ensure that the resulting field is algebraically closed.

# B.1 Compatible Finite Periods and Absolute Auto-morphisms 

In Ω = Fq, every element belongs to some finite subfield. Thus an Fq-automorphism is completely determined by its restrictions to these finite subfields. Each restriction is a power of Frobenius, and the restrictions must agree on common subfields. 

Definition B.3 Define the additive group ̂

Z = {(an)n≥1 : an ∈ Z/nZ, am ≡ an (mod n) whenever n | m} ,

with componentwise addition; componentwise multiplication makes it a ring. It is called the profinite completion of the ring of integers, and is also denoted by lim 

←−n Z/nZ.

Theorem B.4 Let σ(x) = xq. Every τ ∈ Aut Fq (Ω) corresponds uniquely to an (an) ∈̂

Z through the rule 

τ |Fqn = σan |Fqn .

This correspondence gives a group isomorphism Aut Fq (Ω) '̂ Z.

Proof. Every τ preserves the root set of xqn

= x and therefore maps the unique subfield 

Fqn to itself. The classification of finite-field automorphisms gives a unique residue class 

an (mod n). If n | m, compatibility of restrictions gives am ≡ an (mod n).Conversely, given a compatible family, define τ (x) = σan (x) when x ∈ Fqn . If x

also lies in another finite subfield, take their compositum; compatibility ensures that the two definitions agree. Any two elements belong to a common finite subfield, so this map preserves sums, products, and the identity. The compatible family (−an)

defines its inverse, so it is an automorphism. Composition corresponds to addition of exponents, and the finite subfields have union Ω, so the resulting correspondence is a group isomorphism. An ordinary integer a gives the family (a mod n)n. These do not exhaust the com-patible families. For example, for each n use the Chinese remainder theorem to prescribe 

an ≡ 0 (mod 2v2(n)), an ≡ 1 (mod n/2 v2(n)).

These congruences define a compatible family. If it came from an integer, that integer would be divisible by every power of two and hence would be zero; yet the condition modulo three requires it to be one, a contradiction. 726 Appendix B Algebraic Closures and Compatible Finite Periods 

For τ ∈ Aut Fq (Ω) and n ≥ 1, put 

Un(τ ) = {η ∈ Aut Fq (Ω) : η|Fqn = τ |Fqn }.

These sets form a neighborhood basis at τ : any finite set of restriction conditions can be expressed simultaneously on the compositum of the corresponding finite subfields. This defines a topology on the automorphism group, corresponding to the topology on ̂

Z defined by finitely many residue-class conditions. In this topology the subgroup of integer powers of Frobenius is dense: for any τ and n, choose an integer a representing an;then σa ∈ Un(τ ). An inverse limit of finite groups, equipped with the topology defined by finitely many coordinate conditions, is called a profinite group. Its elements are tuples satisfying the compatibility conditions imposed by the transition homomorphisms. A profinite group with a dense cyclic subgroup is called a procyclic group . Thus Aut Fq (Ω) is procyclic. To see that it is not cyclic as an abstract group, identify it with ̂

Z. If some a ∈̂ Z generated this group, then 1 = (1 mod n)n would equal ma for an integer m. The case m = 0 is impossible after reduction modulo two. If |m| > 1,reduction modulo any prime divisor of |m| would give 1 = 0 . Hence m = ±1, so a = ±1.These elements generate only the embedded copy of Z, which is a proper subgroup, as shown by the compatible family constructed above. 

# B.2 Pointwise Periods and a Common Period 

Proposition B.5 Let K be a field containing Fq, and put σ(x) = xq. Then (1) K/Fq is algebraic if and only if every x ∈ K satisfies some σmx (x) = x, where 

mx ≥ 1 may depend on x;(2) K is finite if and only if there is an N ≥ 1 such that σN = id K .

Proof. If K/Fq is algebraic, then for every x the simple extension Fq(x) is a field of qmx

elements for some exponent, so xqmx 

= x. Conversely, this identity makes x a root of the nonzero polynomial Xqmx 

− X ∈ Fq[X], so every x is algebraic over Fq. This proves the first assertion. If K is finite, write |K| = qN ; then σN = id K . Conversely, if the same N works for every element, all elements of K are roots of XqN

− X, and the root bound gives |K| ≤ qN , so K is finite. Every element of an algebraic closure has finite period, but no common finite period controls all elements: it contains finite extensions of every degree and is therefore infinite. Appendix B Algebraic Closures and Compatible Finite Periods 727 

For a finite field, a single integer is a common multiple of all pointwise periods. The root bound converts a common period into finiteness of the whole field, connecting this with the Frobenius fixed-point construction in Chapter 1. 

# B.3 Intermediate Fields Determined by Allowed Pe-riods 

Fix an algebraic closure Ω of k = Fq, and put σ(x) = xq. Inclusion and composita of finite subfields are governed by divisibility and least common multiples; these rules also characterize arbitrary intermediate fields in Ω.

Example B.7 (An infinite field allowing only power-of-two periods) The set D = {2j :

j ≥ 0} is closed under positive divisors and least common multiples, so 

K = ⋃

> j≥0

Fq2j

is an intermediate field in Ω, and D(K) = D. Its finite subfields have unbounded orders, so K is infinite; nevertheless, every element has Frobenius period a power of two. Since 

3 / ∈ D (K), we have Fq3 * K. No irreducible cubic over k can have a root in K, since such a root would generate the subfield Fq3 . Thus K/k is an infinite algebraic extension, but K is not algebraically closed. Proposition B.5 also shows that Frobenius on K has no common finite period valid for every element. Inside a fixed algebraic closure, specifying a subfield containing the base field is equivalent to specifying a family of exact periods closed under positive divisors and least common multiples. The first condition corresponds to inclusion of finite subfields; the second puts any finite collection of elements in a common finite extension field. Together, they express closure under field operations as closure of periods. 

# B.4 Uniqueness of the Isomorphism Type and Choice of an Isomorphism 

Finite fields of the same order have a unique isomorphism type, but choosing an iso-morphism between two concrete models usually still requires specifying the image of a root. This distinction occurs in quotient-ring representations, explicit isomorphisms, and compatible identifications of finite extension fields. Exercise 1.10 Solution A subfield is closed under multiplication. Conversely, if V is closed under multiplication, it is a finite subring with identity and has no zero divisors as a subring of a field. For a ∈ V \ { 0}, the multiplication map x 7 → ax is injective on V , hence surjective by finiteness, so some x ∈ V satisfies ax = 1 . Thus V is a subfield, and the proposition on root polynomials of finite subfields gives the stated identity. If that identity holds, V is the full fixed-point set of the pnth-power map and is therefore a subfield. Appendix D Solutions to the Exercises 747

Exercise 3.8 Solution Specifying a homomorphism A → B is equivalent to independently speci-fying its component homomorphisms A → Fqej . The latter must select one field factor of A: the coordinate idempotents are pairwise orthogonal and sum to one, and their images can only be zero or one. Orthogonality prevents two images from both being one, while their sum ensures that at least one is one. A factor Fqdi embeds in the target if and only if di | ej , in which case there are exactly di embeddings. Summing over the choice of factor and multiplying over target coordinates gives the formula; an empty sum is zero, meaning that no homomorphism exists. Equivalently, a cycle of length ej

maps equivariantly into one of length di if and only if di | ej ; then the first point has di

possible images, determining all the others. An automorphism can only permute factors of the same degree; for degree d there are md! permutations, and d field automorphisms for each factor, giving the final product. 

Exercise 3.9 Solution The map σA raises each coordinate to the qth power; in every field factor the fixed field of σrA is Fqgcd (di,r ) , giving the stated fixed algebra and dimension. On evaluation points, a cycle of length di splits into gcd (di, r ) cycles under step r. Its number of fixed points is di if di | r and zero otherwise. For example, the q-Frobenius of a cubic field has a one-dimensional fixed field, but its three evaluation points form a three-cycle with no fixed point.

Exercise 6.3 Solution Every x satisfying the conditions is a root of P (X) = X2 − tX + u. Put

Exercise 14.1 Solution In the tensor-product basis, multiplication by u⊗v has matrix Mu ⊗Mv. Its diagonal entries are all products of diagonal entries of the two matrices, so its matrix trace is tr (Mu) tr (Mv), giving the first identity. In the product-of-fields model, the multiplication matrix is block diagonal, each block being the multiplication matrix in the corresponding field; hence the algebra trace is the sum of the field traces of the blocks. This also shows that the two models compute the same linear functional. Appendix D Solutions to the Exercises 809

Exercise 19.2 Solution An element of degree 12 over Fq has degree 12/ gcd (12 , 2) = 6 over Fq2 .Conversely, an element of degree six over Fq2 is fixed by the q12 th-power map; its q-period d satisfies d | 12 and d/ gcd (d, 2) = 6 . Comparing the 2-adic valuations and odd parts gives d = 12 . If the base field is instead Fq3 , an element of degree four over Fq

still has degree four over Fq3 , since gcd (4 , 3) = 1 . Thus relative degree four does not distinguish original degree four from degree 12. 

Exercise 19.3 Solution Both two and three are prime, so Gq,ℓ = Rq,ℓ . Substitution into the explicit formula for R gives both identities. By Corollary 19.18, compression identifies elements in the same affine-group orbit; the degree of a compressed root is determined by its Frobenius period on the orbit quotient. In the quadratic case that quotient has one element, so the period is one.

From a problem to its structure. Let k = Fq ⊆ E = Fqn , with σ(x) = xq. To choose a model, first identify what the problem asks us to control. For coefficient descent and factor degrees, begin with Frobenius stability and orbits of the root set; for linear relations among conjugates, normality, and kernels, examine linear operators and cyclic modules; for multiplicative orders, power classes, and norms, first test compatibility in the cyclic group. For composition and periods, finding a compatible projection and then analyzing return on one fiber is often clearer than working with all roots at once. In a construction, one must also distinguish satisfying a desired property from attain-ing the target exactly . A prescribed annihilator can be obtained by choosing a divisor of T n − 1 and then acting on a normal element. A prescribed base-field permutation can be lifted by solving a trace condition and retaining free parameters in the trace kernel; see Prescribing the Frobenius annihilator and Choosing parameters from a base-field permutation. For recursion, check in addition that the conditions needed at the next step are preserved. The choice of model depends on the problem; there is no need to use all models at once. The table below is for reference once the relevant object has been identified; the hypotheses remain those in the cited definitions and theorems. Fields, orbits, and linear subspaces. All fixed points of a Frobenius iterate form a subfield because Frobenius preserves the operations. A finite Frobenius-stable root set ensures that its monic root polynomial is defined over the base field. A Frobenius-invariant k-linear subspace of E corresponds to a monic divisor of T n − 1. These state-ments depend, respectively, on preservation of field operations, stability of the root set, and the cyclic-module structure of Frobenius; each requires its own hypotheses. In par-ticular, k[T ]/( T n − 1) ' E is a module isomorphism supplied by a normal element, and is generally not a ring isomorphism. Field multiplication also compares subspaces: the scalars preserving a subspace form a subfield, while the ranks of quotient multiplication measure its intersections with dilates. Trace duality converts these multiplicative con-ditions into orthogonality; when Frobenius acts semisimply, products of eigenvalues in conjugate coordinates determine products of invariant subspaces. 

The root bound and generation. The root bound excludes low-degree polynomial relations holding on an entire finite field or an excessively large subspace. Cyclicity of the multiplicative group, nondegeneracy of the trace pairing, the Moore criterion, and the normal basis theorem thereby share a common proof mechanism; see Section 9.2.1. The bound constrains the possible relations, while preservation of the operations by Frobenius determines the structures in which they occur. 

Three degrees and periods. For α 6 = 0 , set m = ord (α), and let μα be its Frobenius annihilator polynomial. Then 

[k(α) : k] = min {j ≥ 1 : αqj

= α} = ord m(q) = ord (μα).

Here ord 1(q) = 1 . On the other hand, deg μα is the dimension of the span of its conjugates, which need not equal the field extension degree. Normality requires μα =

T n − 1, while multiplicative primitivity requires m = qn − 1.

Subfields, representations, and relative traces. Fix E = k(α). The subfield 

Kd is determined by a Frobenius fixed-point condition, but its intersections with low-degree power-basis spaces depend on the choice of generator. Weighted relative traces 864 Appendix D Solutions to the Exercises 

turn these intersection spaces into orthogonal complements in the subfield; a shortest recurrence for the same sequence recovers the root-block polynomial of α over Kd. Thus base-field linear rank, subfield linear recurrences, and root-block coefficient rank record, respectively, representation degree, relative algebraic relations, and whether rational representations attain the degree lower bound. Intermediate traces then give the profiles of divisor subfields; Möbius inversion separates counts of elements lying in a subfield into counts of elements generating it.

Every finite extension has a normal basis. A self-dual basis exists if and only if q is even or n is odd. A self-dual normal basis exists if and only if n is odd, or q is even and n ≡ 2 ( mod 4) . These results involve different generation and pairing conditions, whose connections are made explicit by cyclic modules and trace adjoints. Index of Notation
